In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Tafsir of Surat al-Anfal

It is entirely Medinan, so said most people. Muqatil said: it is Medinan except for one verse, which is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when those who disbelieved plotted against you﴾ [al-Anfal: 30], the whole verse. This verse was revealed concerning an incident that occurred in Makkah, though it is possible that the verse was revealed in Medina concerning that. There is no disagreement that this surah was revealed concerning the Day of Badr and the matter of its spoils.

The Exalted and Majestic said:

﴿They ask you about the spoils. Say: The spoils belong to Allah and the Messenger. So fear Allah, set right what is between you, and obey Allah and His Messenger, if you are believers.﴾

Al-nafl (the voluntary, extra portion), al-nafal and al-nafilah in the speech of the Arabs mean: an addition beyond what is obligatory. The spoils were called nafl because they are an addition beyond standing in jihad, defending the religion, and calling to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. From this is the saying of Labid:

"Indeed, the piety of our Lord is the best nafl..."

That is, the best spoil. And the saying of 'Antarah:

"Indeed, when the battle reddens, we quench our spears [with blood], and we abstain at the division of the spoils (al-anfal)."

(p-127) Questioning in the speech of the Arabs comes to seek knowledge of a matter within the one questioned, and it may come to seek wealth or the like. In this verse, the majority view is that the question was really about the ruling concerning the spoils, so it belongs to the first type. But a group said: they asked him for the spoils themselves, that he would give them to them, and they argued for this by the recitation of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, 'Ali ibn al-Husayn, Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn 'Ali, Zayd ibn 'Ali, Ja'far ibn Muhammad, Talhah ibn Musarrif, 'Ikrimah, al-Dahhak, and 'Ata': (They ask you the spoils—al-anfal). They said that in the recitation of one who reads "'an" (about), it has the meaning of "min" (from). This is the second type of question.

People differed over what is meant by al-anfal in this verse. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrimah, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Qatadah, 'Ata', and Ibn Zayd said: they are the spoils in general. They said: the cause of the verse was what happened on the Day of Badr, namely that the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ divided into three groups on the Day of Badr: a group that remained with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in the shelter (al-'arish) that was made for him, guarding and comforting him; a group that surrounded the enemy's army and their war gear when they were routed; and a group that pursued the enemy, killing and taking prisoners. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said in the book of al-Tabari: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ had urged the people before that, saying: "Whoever kills an enemy or takes a prisoner, for him is such and such, and for him is such and such." The young men hastened, and the elders remained by the banners. When the fighting ended and the people gathered, each group saw itself as having the greater merit, and said: "We have the better right to the booty," and their conduct in this worsened. Then the verse was revealed that the spoils belong to Allah and the Messenger, so they desisted. Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ divided it equally.

Al-Tabari and others related, through a chain, from Abu Umamah al-Bahili, who said: "I asked 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit about al-Anfal, and he said: 'It was revealed concerning us, the people of Badr, when we differed and our conduct worsened, so Allah took it from our hands and placed it in the hands of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he divided it among us, peace be upon him, equally (ʿan bawa').'"

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

He means "'an sawa'" (equally). Thus in that was the fear of Allah, obedience to His Messenger ﷺ, and the reconciliation of relations among them.

From what also occurred on the Day of Badr, it is said that the cause was what al-Tabari related, through Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, who said: "On the Day of Badr my brother 'Umayr was killed, and I killed Sa'id ibn al-'As and took his sword, which was called Dhu al-Kathifah. I brought it to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, this is the sword with which Allah has healed [my heart] from the polytheists, so give it to me.' He said: 'This is neither mine nor yours; throw it into the spoils heap (al-qabad).' So I threw it, and I returned with what no one knows except Allah of the killing of my brother and the taking of my spoils. He said: I had not gone far when the surah al-Anfal was revealed to him, and he said: 'Go and take your sword, for you asked me for the sword and it was not mine, but now it has become mine, so it is yours.'"

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

In some of the chains of this hadith: "Sa'd said: When he told me, 'Put it in the heap,' I said: 'I fear that you will give it to someone who has not endured my trials.' He said: Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was behind me. He said: I said: 'I fear that something has been revealed concerning me.' He said: 'Indeed the sword has become mine,' and he gave it to me, and the verse was revealed: ﴿They ask you about the spoils﴾." Al-Tabari also related, through Abu Usayd Malik ibn Rabi'ah, who said: "(p-129) I took the sword of Ibn 'A'idh on the Day of Badr, which was called al-Marzaban. When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ ordered that what was in their hands of the nafl be returned, I came with it and threw it into the nafl. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ did not refuse anything that was asked of him, and al-Aqram al-Makhzumi saw it and asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ for it, and he gave it to him."

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

From the totality of these reports it results that the hearts of the people of Badr were at odds, and there occurred in them what occurs in human souls of desire for preference, especially in those who had distinguished themselves. So Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, revealed the verse, and the Muslims were content and submitted. Thus Allah reconciled their relations and returned their spoils to them. Some of the people of this interpretation, 'Ikrimah and Mujahid, said: this ruling from Allah was to remove dispute, and then it was abrogated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And know that whatever you obtain of anything﴾ [al-Anfal: 41], the verse. Ibn Zayd said: no abrogation occurred in the verse, but it was informed that the spoils belong to Allah in that they are His possession and provision, and to the Messenger in that he explains by them the rulings of Allah and proclaims them so that submission to them may come from the people, while the ruling on division descends within that. There is no doubt that the spoils and other things and the entire world belong to Allah and the Messenger.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Ibn 'Abbas also said: al-anfal in the verse is what the Imam gives to whoever he sees as deserving, such as a sword, a horse, or the like. This also agrees with the verse and with what we have mentioned of the reports about the Day of Badr. 'Ali ibn Salih ibn Hayy and al-Hasan, as related by al-Mahdawi, said: al-anfal in the verse is what the raiding detachments (al-saraya) alone bring.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This view is far from the verse and does not fit with the causes mentioned; rather it falls outside the Day of Badr. Mujahid said: al-anfal in the verse is the one-fifth (al-khums). The Emigrants said: this fifth did not come out from us, so Allah the Exalted said: it belongs to Allah and the Messenger. This view too has little relevance to the verse. (p-130) Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ata' also said: al-anfal in the verse is what was seized of the polytheists' property that came to the Muslims, such as a stray horse or a runaway slave, and it belongs to the Prophet ﷺ, who may do with it as he wills. Ibn 'Abbas also said: al-anfal in the verse is what was obtained of the polytheists' property after the division of the spoils; it belongs to Allah and His Messenger.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

These two views do not take the verse out of the causes that were related concerning the Day of Badr, nor does the verse become restricted to the Day of Badr according to them. It seems that these two sayings refer only to what the army obtained without fighting, after the war was over and fear had lifted. The most preferred and clearest of these views is the first, whose causes are widely attested in reports, and which fits the time in which the verse was revealed. Al-Naqqash related from al-Sha'bi that he said: al-anfal are the prisoners.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is only by way of example, for it means every kind of spoil.

It is fitting in the interpretation of this verse that we mention some of the scholarly disagreement concerning the Imam granting extra portions (tanfil) to whoever he sees among the people of valour and effort, what is permissible of that and what is forbidden, and what is disputed regarding the spoils of the slain (al-salab). One group said: there is no tanfil after the Prophet ﷺ. The majority said: tanfil remains until the Day of Resurrection; the commander of the army gives whatever he sees fit to whomever he sees deserving, but in accordance with judgment and the interest of the Muslims, to urge people to valour and to spur them to confront the enemy and strive in war. Then they differed. Ibn al-Qasim related from Malik in the "al-Mudawwanah": the Imam grants extra portions only from the one-fifth, not from the whole of the spoils, and he may grant them at the beginning of the booty and at its end according to his judgment. A group said: the Imam grants extra portions only before the fighting; once the spoils have been gathered, there is no tanfil.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This, according to this view, occurs when the Imam says: "Whoever kills an enemy, for him is such and such," (p-131) or says to a detachment: "If you reach such and such a place, for you is such and such." Al-Shafi'i and Ibn Hanbal said: there is no tanfil except after the spoils are gathered and before the fifth is taken out. Ibrahim al-Nakha'i said: the Imam may grant extra portions whenever he wishes before the fifth is taken out. Anas ibn Malik, Raja' ibn Haywah, Makhul, al-Qasim, and a group including al-Awza'i, Ahmad, Ishaq, and 'Adi ibn 'Adi said: there is no tanfil except after the fifth is set aside; then the Imam grants extra portions from the four-fifths, and then the remainder is divided among the people. Ibn al-Musayyab said: the Imam grants extra portions only from the fifth of the fifth. Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said: it is not permissible for the commander to say: "Whoever demolishes such and such part of the fortress, for him is such and such, and whoever reaches such and such, for him is such and such." I do not like for anyone to shed blood for the sake of something like this. Sahnun said: if such a thing happens, it is binding, for it is a contract (mubayaah). Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said: it is not permissible for the Imam to say to a detachment: "What you take, one-third of it is for you." Sahnun said: he means at the outset; if it happens, it stands, and they have their shares in the remainder. Sahnun also said: if the Imam says to a detachment: "What you take, no fifth is due from you on it," this is not permissible; if it happens, I would reject it, for this is an anomalous ruling that is not permissible and is not upheld. According to the school of Malik, it is recommended, if the Imam grants extra portions, that he grant what is visible, such as a turban, a horse, or a sword. Some scholars forbade the Imam from granting gold, silver, pearls, or the like. Others said: tanfil is permissible in anything whatsoever.

As for the salab (spoils of the slain): Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said: the spoils of the slain are part of the booty and are divided among the whole army, unless the Imam stipulates otherwise; and so said others. Al-Layth, al-Awza'i, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Abu Thawr, Abu 'Ubayd, and Ibn al-Mundhir said: the salab is the right of the slayer by the ruling of the Prophet ﷺ. Al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Abu 'Ubayd, and Ibn al-Mundhir said: whether the Imam says so or not. Malik said: when the Imam says, "Whoever kills an enemy, for him is his salab," that is binding; but it is in accordance with the Imam's judgment and the circumstances, the constraints, and the calls for reinforcements. Al-Shafi'i and Ibn Hanbal said: the salab is taken out of the booty, then the fifth is taken from it, and the salab is given to the slayers. Ishaq ibn Rahawayh said: if the salab is small, it belongs to the slayer; if it is large, a fifth is taken from it. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, did this with al-Bara' ibn Malik when he challenged the marzaban and killed him; the value of his belt and bracelets was thirty thousand, and he took a fifth of that. A hadith from the Prophet ﷺ is also related on this, the hadith of 'Awf ibn Malik in the Musannaf of Abu Dawud. Makhul said: the salab is booty, and in it there is the fifth. Something similar is related from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

He means: a fifth is taken from it, on the slayer alone. The majority of jurists said: the slayer is not given the salab unless he establishes evidence of his killing. Most of them said: one witness suffices, based on the hadith of Abu Qatadah. Al-Awza'i said: he is given it on the mere strength of his claim.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is weak.

Al-Shafi'i said: the slayer is not given it unless his victim was advancing, challenging, and fighting openly; but whoever kills one who is fleeing, he is not given it. Abu Thawr and Ibn al-Mundhir, author of "al-Ashraf," said: the slayer has the salab whether the victim was fleeing or not.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is more sound, because of the hadith of Salamah ibn al-Akwa' concerning his pursuit of a scout of the unbelievers at the battle of Hunayn, his seizing the rein of their camel, and his killing of him while he was fleeing; the Messenger of Allah ﷺ gave him his salab. Ibn Hanbal said: the salab belongs to the slayer only in single combat (al-mubarazah) alone.

Ibn 'Atiyya's commentary (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 8, verse 1 (part 2 of 2):

They differed concerning the spoils (salab). As for weapons and everything needed for fighting, I do not know of any disagreement that it is part of the salab, and likewise his horse if he fought on it and was unhorsed from it. Ahmad ibn Hanbal said regarding the horse: it is not part of the salab. Likewise, if there are dinars or jewels in his money-belt (himyan) or his waist-belt (mintaqa), or the like of these things which he prepares, I do not know of any disagreement that they are not part of the salab. There was disagreement concerning what is adorned for war and used to strike terror in it, such as the crown, the two armlets, the earrings, and the waist-belts weighted with gold and gems. Al-Awza'i said: all of that is part of the salab. A group said: it is not part of the salab, and this is narrated from Sahnun, may Allah have mercy on him, except the waist-belt, which he considered to be part of the salab. Ibn Habib said in al-Wadiha: the two armlets are part of the salab. Al-Shafi'i wavered over whether all of these are part of the salab or not.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
If the Imam says: "Whoever kills a slain enemy, his salab is for him," and a dhimmi kills a slain enemy, the well-known view is that he has no share. According to the view of Ashhab, "the People of the Dhimma are given a portion (yarda') of the spoils," it would follow that he should be given the salab. If the Imam himself kills a slain enemy with his own hand after this statement, then the salab is for him.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
As for the safi (the choice portion), it was exclusively for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

As for the words of the Exalted and Majestic: ﴿So fear Allah﴾, their meaning in speech is: make between yourself and what is feared a protection (wiqaya). His words: ﴿and set right what is between you﴾ are an explicit statement that disagreement had arisen among them and souls had inclined toward contention. The word "dhat" (essence) in this context is intended to mean the very self and reality of a thing. What is understood from "baynikum" (between you) is a meaning encompassing all connection, bonds, and affections, and the "dhat" of that is what is commanded to be set right, that is, its very self and essence. So Allah, the Exalted and Majestic, urged the setting right of those components, and when they are set right, the setting right of what encompasses them, which is the relationship that is theirs, is achieved. The term "dhat" may also be used to mean something that is a necessary attribute of what it is attached to, even if it is not its very self and essence. This is found in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Knower of what is in the breasts (dhat al-sudur)﴾, and ﴿dhat al-shawka﴾ (the one with the thorn/might), where it is the feminine form of their saying: "The wolf is envied for its dhu-batn (possessor of a belly)," and the saying of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him: "It is only the dhu-batn of Bint Kharija." "Dhat al-bayn" may be understood in this sense. "Dhat" may also be used with another meaning, though it is close to this one, namely their saying: "I did such-and-such dhat yawm (on a certain day)," and from it the words of the poet:
♦ No dog barks in it except once, nor do its vipers move at dhat al-'isha' (nightfall).

Al-Tabari reported from some of them that he said: ﴿dhat baynikum﴾ means the state that belongs to your relationship, just as "dhat al-'isha'" means the hour in which the evening prayer ('isha') falls.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
Al-Tabari preferred this view, but it is a view whose weakness is clear. Al-Zajjaj said: "al-bayn" here means connection, and similar to it is the saying of the Exalted and Majestic: ﴿Indeed, your bonds have been severed (laqad taqatta'a baynakum)﴾ [al-An'am: 94].

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
In all of this there is room for consideration. His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And obey Allah and His Messenger﴾ are a general expression, and its occasion is the command to refrain from what the Messenger of Allah ﷺ implements regarding the spoils. His words: ﴿if you are believers﴾ mean: those of perfect faith, just as you say to a man: "If you are a man, then do such-and-such," meaning: if you are of perfect manhood. The answer to the conditional in his earlier words is ﴿and obey﴾. The position of Abu al-'Abbas is that the answer is an elided, postponed element indicated by what precedes it, its estimated form being: "If you are believers, obey." And his position in this is that the answer should not precede the condition.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 8, verses 2–4:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿The believers are only those who, when Allah is mentioned, their hearts tremble, and when His verses are recited to them, they increase them in faith, and upon their Lord they rely. Those who establish prayer and spend from what We have provided them. Those are the believers in truth; for them are degrees with their Lord, and forgiveness and generous provision.﴾

"Innama" (only, indeed) is a particle that never leaves emphasis and affirmation wherever it occurs, and it is also suitable for restriction (hasr). When it enters a narrative and the meaning of the context supports restriction, that is valid and fits, as in His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Your God is only one God﴾ [al-Kahf: 110], and other examples. When the context does not allow restriction, "innama" remains only for emphasis and affirmation, as in his, peace and blessings be upon him, saying: "Usury is only in credit (nasi'ah)," and as in their saying: "The brave one is only 'Antarah." As for one who says that "innama" is for specifying the subject (bayan al-mawsuf), this is a weak expression, since specifying the subject occurs in mere statement without "innama." His, glory be to Him, saying here ﴿innama al-mu'minun﴾ — its apparent meaning is that it is for emphasis and affirmation only, i.e., "the perfect ones."

And ﴿wajilat﴾ means: feared, grew soft, and was afraid, and the scholars interpreted it with these meanings. Ibn Mas'ud read (p-136) "faraqat," and Ubayy ibn Ka'b read "fazi'at." It is said: wajila yawjalu, and yajal (irregular), and yijal with the first yā' vowelled with kasra. The reasoning behind these forms is that when they changed the waw into yā', there was no regular analogical basis for it, so they vowelled the first yā' with kasra so that the yā' replacing the waw would come by a cause. Sibawayh, may Allah have mercy on him, recorded these four dialectal forms. ﴿Tuliyat﴾ means: was recited and read aloud, and "the verses" here means the recited Qur'an. The increase in faith occurs in ways all of which lie outside the essence of assent itself. Among them: a believer who had not heard a ruling of Allah's in the Qur'an, which was revealed to the Prophet ﷺ, hears it and believes in it, his faith increases in addition to all that he already believed, since each ruling has a specific assent attached to it. This applies to anyone who receives legal rulings he did not have until the Day of Resurrection. The increase of faith follows the increase of proofs. For this reason Malik said: "Faith increases and does not decrease." The increase in righteous deeds also follows according to the view of those who take the term "faith" to apply to both assent and acts of obedience; these say: it increases and decreases.

His, the Exalted, saying ﴿and upon their Lord they rely﴾ is a comprehensive expression for the interests of this world and the Hereafter, when it is taken into account and acted upon accordingly, in that a person carries out what he is commanded, exerts his utmost effort without weakness, and awaits what has been guaranteed to him of victory, provision, or other things.

These are beautiful attributes with which Allah described the excellent believers, making them the goal for the community so that the virtuous may race toward them. Then He followed this by counting and marking them with the establishment of prayer, praising them for it, as an incitement to it.

As for His saying: ﴿and from what We have provided them they spend﴾, a group of exegetes said: it is zakat.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

What led them to this is the juxtaposition of the speech with the establishment of prayer; otherwise it is a general term covering zakat, voluntary good deeds, and giving to those who deserve. The statement of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, in this sense is open to interpretation.

(p-137) His, the Exalted, saying ﴿Those are the believers in truth﴾ means: all the believers. "Haqqan" (in truth) is an emphatic infinitive (masdar mu'akkid); so stated Sibawayh, and it is the infinitive that does not shift, and its governing verb is "ahuqqu dhalika haqqan" (I affirm that truly). His saying ﴿darajat﴾ — its apparent meaning, and it is the view of the majority, is that what is meant is the ranks and abodes of Paradise, and their rank is according to their deeds. Al-Tabari related from Mujahid that they are the ranks of worldly deeds. His saying ﴿and generous provision﴾ means by it: the foods and drinks of Paradise. "Karim" (generous) is an attribute that entails the removal of blemishes, as in your saying: a generous garment (thawb karim) and a noble lineage (hasab karim).

When it enters a narrative and the meaning of the context supports restriction, that is valid and fits, as in His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Your God is only one God﴾ [al-Kahf: 110], and other examples. When the context does not allow restriction, "innama" remains only for emphasis and affirmation, as in his, peace and blessings be upon him, saying: "Usury is only in credit (nasi'ah)," and as in their saying: "The brave one is only 'Antarah." As for one who says that "innama" is for specifying the subject (bayan al-mawsuf), this is a weak expression, since specifying the subject occurs in mere statement without "innama." His, glory be to Him, saying here ﴿innama al-mu'minun﴾ — its apparent meaning is that it is for emphasis and affirmation only, i.e., "the perfect ones."

And ﴿wajilat﴾ means: feared, grew soft, and was afraid, and the scholars interpreted it with these meanings. Ibn Mas'ud read (p-136) "faraqat," and Ubayy ibn Ka'b read "fazi'at." It is said: wajila yawjalu, and yajal (irregular), and yijal with the first yā' vowelled with kasra. The reasoning behind these forms is that when they changed the waw into yā', there was no regular analogical basis for it, so they vowelled the first yā' with kasra so that the yā' replacing the waw would come by a cause. Sibawayh, may Allah have mercy on him, recorded these four dialectal forms. ﴿Tuliyat﴾ means: was recited and read aloud, and "the verses" here means the recited Qur'an. The increase in faith occurs in ways all of which lie outside the essence of assent itself. Among them: a believer who had not heard a ruling of Allah's in the Qur'an, which was revealed to the Prophet ﷺ, hears it and believes in it, his faith increases in addition to all that he already believed, since each ruling has a specific assent attached to it. This applies to anyone who receives legal rulings he did not have until the Day of Resurrection. The increase of faith follows the increase of proofs. For this reason Malik said: "Faith increases and does not decrease." The increase in righteous deeds also follows according to the view of those who take the term "faith" to apply to both assent and acts of obedience; these say: it increases and decreases.

His, the Exalted, saying ﴿and upon their Lord they rely﴾ is a comprehensive expression for the interests of this world and the Hereafter, when it is taken into account and acted upon accordingly, in that a person carries out what he is commanded, exerts his utmost effort without weakness, and awaits what has been guaranteed to him of victory, provision, or other things.

These are beautiful attributes with which Allah described the excellent believers, making them the goal for the community so that the virtuous may race toward them. Then He followed this by counting and marking them with the establishment of prayer, praising them for it, as an incitement to it.

As for His saying: ﴿and from what We have provided them they spend﴾, a group of exegetes said: it is zakat.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

What led them to this is the juxtaposition of the speech with the establishment of prayer; otherwise it is a general term covering zakat, voluntary good deeds, and giving to those who deserve. The statement of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, in this sense is open to interpretation.

(p-137) His, the Exalted, saying ﴿Those are the believers in truth﴾ means: all the believers. "Haqqan" (in truth) is an emphatic infinitive (masdar mu'akkid); so stated Sibawayh, and it is the infinitive that does not shift, and its governing verb is "ahuqqu dhalika haqqan" (I affirm that truly). His saying ﴿darajat﴾ — its apparent meaning, and it is the view of the majority, is that what is meant is the ranks and abodes of Paradise, and their rank is according to their deeds. Al-Tabari related from Mujahid that they are the ranks of worldly deeds. His saying ﴿and generous provision﴾ means by it: the foods and drinks of Paradise. "Karim" (generous) is an attribute that entails the removal of blemishes, as in your saying: a generous garment (thawb karim) and a noble lineage (hasab karim).

[p-137]

The Exalted's words:

﴿Just as your Lord brought you forth from your house in truth, though a party of the believers were averse,﴾ ﴿arguing with you concerning the truth after it had become clear, as though they were being driven to death while looking on.﴾ ﴿And when Allah promised you one of the two groups, that it would be yours, and you wished that the unarmed one would be yours, while Allah intended to establish the truth by His words and cut off the last of the disbelievers.﴾

People differed over what the particle *al-kaf* (the "like" in His words "just as," *kamā*) is connected to. I will show which of the views we shall mention later, by Allah's power, fits the meaning and makes the sequence of words good. There are two views, and I begin with them.

Al-Farrā' said: The implied sense is: "Proceed with your command concerning the spoils, and grant extra shares (*nafl*) to whom you wish, even if they dislike it, just as your Lord brought you forth." This is the wording of his view as recorded in *Hidāyat* of Makkī. However, the expression "proceed with your command and grant extra shares to whom you wish" is not precise. My own clarification of this meaning is that this *kāf* likens this narrative, which is his bringing you out of your house, to the earlier narrative, which is their asking about the spoils (*anfāl*). It is as though they asked about the extra share and quarreled, and Allah removed that matter from them, and in it there was the choice (*khīra*). Their quarreling over the extra share is thus equivalent to their aversion here to going out, and Allah's ruling on the spoils, that they belong to Allah and the Messenger and not to them, is equivalent to His bringing out His Prophet ﷺ from his house. Then the choice in both narratives lay in what Allah did. On this interpretation, His words "they argue with you" can be a new, independent statement referring to the disbelievers, meaning [p-138] that they argue with you about the law of Islam after the truth in it has become clear, as though they were being driven to death in calling to faith.

The judge Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

What I have mentioned, that "they argue with you" refers to the disbelievers, is explicitly stated.

The second view, stated by Mujāhid, al-Kisā'ī and others, is that the meaning of this verse is: just as your Lord brought you out of your house while a party of them disliked it, so too they argue with you about fighting the disbelievers of Makkah, and they wish for the unarmed one, after it has become clear to them that you are only doing what you were commanded, not what they want.

The judge Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The implied sense on this interpretation is: they argue with you about the truth with an argument like their aversion to your Lord bringing you out of your house. So on this interpretation the arguing is equivalent to the aversion, and the comparison occurs in meaning in this way. The proponent of this view says that the ones arguing are the believers. The proponent of the first view says that the ones arguing are the polytheists. These are two consistent views, by which the meaning is completed and the arrangement of the wording is good.

Al-Akhfash said: The *kāf* is an adjective (*na't*) of *ḥaqqan* (truly), and the implied sense is: "They are the believers truly, just as He brought you out."

The judge Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The meaning on this interpretation, as you see, is not coherent.

It was also said: The *kāf* is in the nominative position (*raf'*). The implied sense is: "Just as your Lord brought you out, so fear Allah." It is as though it is an inceptive (*ibtidā'*) with a predicate (*khabar*).

The judge Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This meaning was devised by this commentator, and it is not among the words of the verse in its wording or its context.

Abū 'Ubayda said: It is an oath, meaning: "For them are ranks, forgiveness, and generous provision, by He who brought you out." The implied sense is: "And by He who brought you out," so the *kāf* carries the meaning of the particle *wa* (and, by), and *mā* carries the meaning of *alladhī* (the one who).

[p-139] Al-Zajjāj said: The *kāf* is in the accusative position (*naṣb*). The implied sense is: "The spoils belong to you firmly, just as your Lord brought you out."

It was also said: The *kāf* is in the nominative position. The implied sense is: "For them are ranks with their Lord, forgiveness and generous provision. This is a true promise, just as He brought you out."

It was also said: The meaning is: "And set right the matters between you; that is better for you, just as He brought you out," with the *kāf* being an adjective of the predicate of an omitted inceptive. It was also said the implied sense is: "Say: the spoils belong to Allah and the Messenger, just as He brought you out," and this is similar to the first view I mentioned.

'Ikrima said: The implied sense is: "Obey Allah and His Messenger if you are believers, just as your Lord brought you out," meaning: obedience is better for you, just as your going out was better for you.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿from your house﴾ mean: from the city of Yathrib (Madīna). This was said by the majority of the exegetes. Ibn Bakīr said the meaning is: "just as He brought you out of Makkah at the time of the emigration (*hijra*)." 'Abd Allāh ibn Mas'ūd, may Allah be pleased with him, read: "in the truth after it was made clear," with a *ḍamma* on the *bā'* and without a *tā'*. As for the pronoun in His words ﴿they argue with you﴾, it was said it refers to the believers, and it was said it refers to the polytheists. Whoever says it refers to the believers makes "the truth" the fighting against the polytheists of Quraysh, and whoever says it refers to the polytheists makes "the truth" the law of Islam. His words ﴿as though they were being driven to death﴾ mean: in their being driven, on the view that the arguers are the believers, and in their being called to the law, on the view that they are the polytheists. His words ﴿while looking on﴾ are a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) that increases the terror of the driving and indicates the severity of their state.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿And when Allah promised you one of the two groups, that it would be yours﴾, to the end of the verse. In this verse there is a fine narrative which I will abridge, since it is fully recorded in the *Sīra* of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ by Ibn Hishām. Its abridgement is that when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ learned, or it was said that it was revealed to him, that Abū Sufyān ibn Ḥarb had come from Syria with the caravan carrying the trade and wealth of Quraysh, he said to his companions: "The caravan of Quraysh has come upon you; go out to it, perhaps Allah will grant it to you as spoils." He said: So he dispatched those with him who were light and those who were burdened, and some people disliked going out. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ hastened, not turning back for anyone who was excused, nor waiting for anyone who was absent. So he set out with three hundred and thirteen of his companions, among the Emigrants and the Helpers. The people all thought that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ would not meet a battle, so their preparation was not great. Abū Sufyān in the meantime was investigating and being cautious. When he learned of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ's departure, he sent Ḍamḍam ibn 'Amr al-Ghifārī to Makkah to call its people to arms. Ḍamḍam did so, and the people of Makkah came out, a thousand men or about that number. When the news of their coming out reached the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, Allah revealed to him a revelation not recited (*ghayr matlū*) promising him one of the two groups. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ informed his companions of this, and they were pleased and wished that the caravan, which had no fighting with it, would be theirs. When Abū Sufyān learned of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ's nearness, he took the road along the coast, went far away, and escaped. Only the meeting with the people of Makkah remained. Some of the disbelievers advised others to turn back, and they said: "Our caravan has been saved, so let us turn back." But Abū Jahl stirred things up and insisted until the matter of the battle came about. Some of the believers said: "We did not come out for fighting and we did not prepare for it." So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ gathered his companions while he was in a valley called Dhafirān, and said: "Advise me, O people." Abū Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, stood up, spoke well, and urged the meeting with the enemy. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ repeated his request for counsel. 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, stood up and said the same. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ repeated his request for counsel. Then al-Miqdād al-Kindī spoke and said: "We do not say to you, O Messenger of Allah ﷺ, 'Go, you and your Lord, and fight; we are sitting here.' Rather we say: 'We are fighting with you.' By Allah, if you were to lead us to Barak al-Ghimād" (the judge Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: this is a city of Abyssinia) "we would fight with you on the way to it." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was pleased with his words and prayed good for him. Then he said: "Advise me, O people." Sa'd ibn Mu'ādh spoke to him, or it was said Sa'd ibn 'Ubāda.

The judge Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

"It is possible that both of them spoke on that day." He said: "O Messenger of Allah, do you mean us, the group of the Helpers?" The Prophet ﷺ said: "Yes." He said: "We have believed in you and followed you, so proceed with the command of Allah. By Allah, if you were to lead us into this sea, we would plunge into it with you." The Prophet ﷺ said: "Proceed in the blessing of Allah; for I see as though I am looking at the places where the people will fall." Then they met, and it was the battle of Badr. [p-141] Muslima ibn Muḥārib read: "And when He promises you" with the *dāl* jussed (*jazm*), and Abū al-Fatḥ said: this is because of the succession of vowels (*tawālī al-ḥarakāt*). Ibn Muḥaysin read: "And when Allah promises you the one of the two groups," with the hamza of *iḥdā* joined, and the *hā'* joined with the *ḥā'*.

*Al-shawka* is an expression for weapons and sharpness, and from it is the saying of al-A'war: "Indeed the 'arfaj has become sharp." Abū 'Amr, as related by Abū Ḥātim, read "*al-shawka* *tukawn*" with the *tā'* assimilated into the *tā'*. The meaning of the verse is: "and you wished for the caravan and refused to fight the disbelievers."

His words, ﴿and Allah intends﴾ to the end of the verse: the meaning is: Allah intends to make Islam manifest and to raise the call of the law. Abū Ja'far, Shayba and Nāfi' (in a variant reported from them) read *bi-kalimatihi* (with His word) in the singular, which is meant as a plural. The meaning of His words ﴿with His words﴾ is either: by His commands to the angels and the support for everything that makes Islam manifest, or: by His words that preceded in eternity. The meaning is close.

*Al-dābir* is the one who comes behind a people, that is, who comes at their end. So when it is cut off, it has reached their last, on condition that destruction begins with their first. It is an expression for everyone upon whom destruction comes.

The judge Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The implied sense on this interpretation is: they argue with you about the truth with an argument like their aversion to your Lord bringing you out of your house. So on this interpretation the arguing is equivalent to the aversion, and the comparison occurs in meaning in this way. The proponent of this view says that the ones arguing are the believers. The proponent of the first view says that the ones arguing are the polytheists. These are two consistent views, by which the meaning is completed and the arrangement of the wording is good.

Al-Akhfash said: The *kāf* is an adjective (*na't*) of *ḥaqqan* (truly), and the implied sense is: "They are the believers truly, just as He brought you out."

The judge Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The meaning on this interpretation, as you see, is not coherent.

It was also said: The *kāf* is in the nominative position (*raf'*). The implied sense is: "Just as your Lord brought you out, so fear Allah." It is as though it is an inceptive (*ibtidā'*) with a predicate (*khabar*).

The judge Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This meaning was devised by this commentator, and it is not among the words of the verse in its wording or its context.

Abū 'Ubayda said: It is an oath, meaning: "For them are ranks, forgiveness, and generous provision, by He who brought you out." The implied sense is: "And by He who brought you out," so the *kāf* carries the meaning of the particle *wa* (and, by), and *mā* carries the meaning of *alladhī* (the one who).

[p-139] Al-Zajjāj said: The *kāf* is in the accusative position (*naṣb*). The implied sense is: "The spoils belong to you firmly, just as your Lord brought you out."

It was also said: The *kāf* is in the nominative position. The implied sense is: "For them are ranks with their Lord, forgiveness and generous provision. This is a true promise, just as He brought you out."

It was also said: The meaning is: "And set right the matters between you; that is better for you, just as He brought you out," with the *kāf* being an adjective of the predicate of an omitted inceptive. It was also said the implied sense is: "Say: the spoils belong to Allah and the Messenger, just as He brought you out," and this is similar to the first view I mentioned.

'Ikrima said: The implied sense is: "Obey Allah and His Messenger if you are believers, just as your Lord brought you out," meaning: obedience is better for you, just as your going out was better for you.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿from your house﴾ mean: from the city of Yathrib (Madīna). This was said by the majority of the exegetes. Ibn Bakīr said the meaning is: "just as He brought you out of Makkah at the time of the emigration (*hijra*)." 'Abd Allāh ibn Mas'ūd, may Allah be pleased with him, read: "in the truth after it was made clear," with a *ḍamma* on the *bā'* and without a *tā'*. As for the pronoun in His words ﴿they argue with you﴾, it was said it refers to the believers, and it was said it refers to the polytheists. Whoever says it refers to the believers makes "the truth" the fighting against the polytheists of Quraysh, and whoever says it refers to the polytheists makes "the truth" the law of Islam. His words ﴿as though they were being driven to death﴾ mean: in their being driven, on the view that the arguers are the believers, and in their being called to the law, on the view that they are the polytheists. His words ﴿while looking on﴾ are a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) that increases the terror of the driving and indicates the severity of their state.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿And when Allah promised you one of the two groups, that it would be yours﴾, to the end of the verse. In this verse there is a fine narrative which I will abridge, since it is fully recorded in the *Sīra* of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ by Ibn Hishām. Its abridgement is that when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ learned, or it was said that it was revealed to him, that Abū Sufyān ibn Ḥarb had come from Syria with the caravan carrying the trade and wealth of Quraysh, he said to his companions: "The caravan of Quraysh has come upon you; go out to it, perhaps Allah will grant it to you as spoils." He said: So he dispatched those with him who were light and those who were burdened, and some people disliked going out. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ hastened, not turning back for anyone who was excused, nor waiting for anyone who was absent. So he set out with three hundred and thirteen of his companions, among the Emigrants and the Helpers. The people all thought that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ would not meet a battle, so their preparation was not great. Abū Sufyān in the meantime was investigating and being cautious. When he learned of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ's departure, he sent Ḍamḍam ibn 'Amr al-Ghifārī to Makkah to call its people to arms. Ḍamḍam did so, and the people of Makkah came out, a thousand men or about that number. When the news of their coming out reached the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, Allah revealed to him a revelation not recited (*ghayr matlū*) promising him one of the two groups. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ informed his companions of this, and they were pleased and wished that the caravan, which had no fighting with it, would be theirs. When Abū Sufyān learned of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ's nearness, he took the road along the coast, went far away, and escaped. Only the meeting with the people of Makkah remained. Some of the disbelievers advised others to turn back, and they said: "Our caravan has been saved, so let us turn back." But Abū Jahl stirred things up and insisted until the matter of the battle came about. Some of the believers said: "We did not come out for fighting and we did not prepare for it." So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ gathered his companions while he was in a valley called Dhafirān, and said: "Advise me, O people." Abū Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, stood up, spoke well, and urged the meeting with the enemy. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ repeated his request for counsel. 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, stood up and said the same. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ repeated his request for counsel. Then al-Miqdād al-Kindī spoke and said: "We do not say to you, O Messenger of Allah ﷺ, 'Go, you and your Lord, and fight; we are sitting here.' Rather we say: 'We are fighting with you.' By Allah, if you were to lead us to Barak al-Ghimād" (the judge Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: this is a city of Abyssinia) "we would fight with you on the way to it." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was pleased with his words and prayed good for him. Then he said: "Advise me, O people." Sa'd ibn Mu'ādh spoke to him, or it was said Sa'd ibn 'Ubāda.

The judge Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

"It is possible that both of them spoke on that day." He said: "O Messenger of Allah, do you mean us, the group of the Helpers?" The Prophet ﷺ said: "Yes." He said: "We have believed in you and followed you, so proceed with the command of Allah. By Allah, if you were to lead us into this sea, we would plunge into it with you." The Prophet ﷺ said: "Proceed in the blessing of Allah; for I see as though I am looking at the places where the people will fall." Then they met, and it was the battle of Badr. [p-141] Muslima ibn Muḥārib read: "And when He promises you" with the *dāl* jussed (*jazm*), and Abū al-Fatḥ said: this is because of the succession of vowels (*tawālī al-ḥarakāt*). Ibn Muḥaysin read: "And when Allah promises you the one of the two groups," with the hamza of *iḥdā* joined, and the *hā'* joined with the *ḥā'*.

*Al-shawka* is an expression for weapons and sharpness, and from it is the saying of al-A'war: "Indeed the 'arfaj has become sharp." Abū 'Amr, as related by Abū Ḥātim, read "*al-shawka* *tukawn*" with the *tā'* assimilated into the *tā'*. The meaning of the verse is: "and you wished for the caravan and refused to fight the disbelievers."

His words, ﴿and Allah intends﴾ to the end of the verse: the meaning is: Allah intends to make Islam manifest and to raise the call of the law. Abū Ja'far, Shayba and Nāfi' (in a variant reported from them) read *bi-kalimatihi* (with His word) in the singular, which is meant as a plural. The meaning of His words ﴿with His words﴾ is either: by His commands to the angels and the support for everything that makes Islam manifest, or: by His words that preceded in eternity. The meaning is close.

*Al-dābir* is the one who comes behind a people, that is, who comes at their end. So when it is cut off, it has reached their last, on condition that destruction begins with their first. It is an expression for everyone upon whom destruction comes.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 8, verses 8–10:**

The words of the Exalted and Majestic:

﴿That He might establish the truth and nullify falsehood, even though the criminals dislike it.﴾ ﴿When you sought help from your Lord, and He answered you: "I will reinforce you with a thousand of the angels, following one another."﴾ ﴿Allah did not make this except as good news, and so that your hearts might be assured thereby. Victory is only from Allah. Indeed, Allah is Almighty, All-Wise.﴾

[p. 142] ﴿That He might establish the truth﴾ means: that He might make manifest what must be made manifest, which is Islam. ﴿And nullify falsehood﴾ means: disbelief (kufr). ﴿Even though He disliked it﴾ means: their dislike is a fixed reality, so this is a clause in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal).

As for His saying, ﴿When you sought help from your Lord﴾ up to the end of the verse: "idh" (when) is connected to a verb, whose implied form is: "And remember when." This is the first verb that governs it in His saying, ﴿And when He promised you﴾ [al-Anfal: 7]. Al-Tabari said that it is connected to "li-yuhiqqa" and "wa-yubtila."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It is also valid that "yaʿidukum" (He promised you) governs it, since the promise occurred at the time of seeking help. Abu 'Amr read the dhal of idh (ith-dhal) assimilated into the ta' of "tasta'ithuna" (idgham), and Abu Hatim considered this reading good. The meaning of "tasta'ithuna" is: you ask for help. It does not clearly appear from the wording of this verse that the believers knew before the battle that the angels were with them, since "istajaba" (He answered) may occur in the realm of the unseen of Allah, the Exalted. However, it has been narrated that they knew this before the battle, and the purpose of giving comfort and strengthening hearts requires that. Most readers read "annI" with a fatha on the alif. Abu 'Amr, in some of what is narrated from him, and 'Isa ibn 'Umar, in a variant narration from him, read "innI" with a kasra on the alif, meaning: He said, "Indeed I..." "Mumiddukum" means: I will increase you and strengthen you, from amdadtu. Most readers read "bi-alfin" (with a thousand). 'Asim al-Jahdari read "bi-ālufin" (with thousands), on the pattern of fals/afluss, so it is the plural of alf, and the reference by it is to the thousands mentioned in Al 'Imran. 'Asim al-Jahdari also read "bi-ālāfin" (with thousands).

"Murdifin" means: following, and it may be intended that the "murdafin" are the believers, meaning: they were made to follow the angels. In this case, "murdifin" is a circumstantial phrase (hal) from the pronoun in His saying, "mumiddukum." It may also be intended by it: the angels, meaning: some of them followed others. This reading is with a fatha on the dal, the reading of Nafi' and a group of the people of Madina and others. The rest of the Seven, other than Nafi', read it with a kasra on the dal, the reading of al-Hasan and Mujahid, and its meaning is: some of them follow others. It was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father: "Behind every angel is an angel." This is the meaning of successive following. It is said: radifa and ardafa when one follows and comes after something. It may be intended: following the believers. It may also be intended: following one another. Whoever says that "murdifin" means that every angel rode behind another angel is making a weak statement, for no report supports it. A man from the people of Makka, related from him by al-Khalil, read "murad-difin" with a fatha on the ra' and a kasra on the dal with shadda. It is also narrated from al-Khalil that it is with a damma on the ra' like the one before it, and in other places. Some people read with a kasra on the ra', like the two previous readings in other places. Abu 'Amr related this from Sibawayh, and Abu Hatim related it, saying: It seems he intended "murtadifin," so he assimilated (idgham) and made the vowel follow. With this reading, a kasra on the mim is appropriate, though I do not know it as a reading.

Al-Tabari cited as evidence that "ardafa" means "came following" the verse of the poet:

*When al-Jawza' followed al-Thurayya,*
*I suspected the family of Fatima of suspicions.*

Al-Thurayya rises before al-Jawza'.

It is narrated, in the most well-known report, that the angels fought on the day of Badr. Regarding other occasions, there is disagreement about whether they witnessed the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. It was also said: they did not fight on the day of Badr, but only stood by and were present, and this is weak. Al-Tabari related "from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: Jibril descended with a thousand angels upon the right wing of the Prophet ﷺ, and Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, was in it; and Mikail descended with a thousand angels on the left, and I was in it." Ibn 'Abbas said: they were in groups of five hundred and five hundred. Al-Zajjaj said: some of them said the angels were five thousand, and some said nine thousand. Regarding this meaning there are reports which are fully recorded in the books of the biographies (siyar).

As for His saying, ﴿And Allah did not make this﴾ up to the end of the verse: the pronoun in "ja'alahu" (made it) refers to the promise.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This, in my view, is the most suitable of the opinions in terms of meaning. Al-Zajjaj said: "The pronoun refers to the reinforcement (madad), and it may refer to the act of reinforcing (imdad). This is good according to the view of those who say that the angels did not fight, but were only reassured by their presence with the Muslims."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This, in my view, is weak, rejected by the reports that mention the angels fighting, and what the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ saw of that, such as Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, and others.

It may refer to "al-irdaf" (the following), which is the view of al-Tabari. This also follows the same line as the previous opinion. It may refer to "the thousand," and this too is similar, because good news of a thing is only what has not yet occurred. "Bushra" (good news) is a verbal noun from "bashartu." "Tuma'nina" is calm and settledness.

As for His saying, ﴿And victory is only from Allah﴾: this is a statement establishing that the whole affair belongs to Allah, and that a person's striving does not avail if fate does not assist him, although he is still required to strive earnestly, just as the Messenger of Allah ﷺ wore two coats of mail.

This whole story, from the story of the disbelievers and the triumph of the believers over them, is fitting for the attributes of Allah, the Exalted and Majestic, namely might (ʿIzza) and wisdom (Hikma), when this is carefully considered.

This is good according to the view of those who say that the angels did not fight, but were only reassured by their presence with the Muslims."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This, in my view, is weak, rejected by the reports that mention the angels fighting, and what the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ saw of that, such as Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, and others.

It may refer to "al-irdaf" (the following), which is the view of al-Tabari. This also follows the same line as the previous opinion. It may refer to "the thousand," and this too is similar, because good news of a thing is only what has not yet occurred. "Bushra" (good news) is a verbal noun from "bashartu." "Tuma'nina" is calm and settledness.

As for His saying, ﴿And victory is only from Allah﴾: this is a statement establishing that the whole affair belongs to Allah, and that a person's striving does not avail if fate does not assist him, although he is still required to strive earnestly, just as the Messenger of Allah ﷺ wore two coats of mail.

This whole story, from the story of the disbelievers and the triumph of the believers over them, is fitting for the attributes of Allah, the Exalted and Majestic, namely might (ʿIzza) and wisdom (Hikma), when this is carefully considered.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 8, verses 11–12:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿When He covered you with drowsiness as a security from Him, and sent down upon you water from the sky to purify you thereby, and to remove from you the defilement of Satan, and to strengthen your hearts, and to make firm the feet thereby.﴾ ﴿When your Lord inspired the angels: "I am with you, so strengthen those who believe. I will cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieved, so strike above the necks and strike every fingertip of them."﴾

The governing element (al-'amil) in "idh" (when) is the same governing element that operates in His saying: ﴿And when He promised you﴾ [al-Anfal: 7], with its recurrence understood (bi-taqdir takrarihi), because sharing the same first governing element itself can only occur with a conjunction particle (harf 'atf). The purpose is only that He enumerates His blessings, may He be blessed and exalted, upon the believers on the day of Badr, so He says: "And remember when We did such-and-such."

(p-145) Al-Tabari said: the governing element in "idh" is His saying: ﴿and so that your hearts may be at rest﴾ [al-Anfal: 10].

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This, despite its possibility, is weak. Were the governing element of "idh" taken as something close to what precedes it, the better option would be for "idh" to be governed by "Hakim" (All-Wise), because the covering of them with drowsiness and making it a security is a wisdom from Allah, the Exalted and Majestic.

Nafi' recited "yughshikum" with a dammed yā' and a sukun on the ghayn. This is the reading of al-A'raj, Abu Hafs, and Ibn Nassah. 'Asim, Hamzah, Ibn 'Amir, and al-Kisa'i recited "yughashshikum" with a fathah on the ghayn and a shaddah on the shin, with a kasrah; this is the reading of 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr, Abu Raja', al-Hasan, 'Ikrimah, and others. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr recited "yaghshakum" with a fathah on the yā' and an alif after the shin; this is the reading of Mujahid, Ibn Muhaysin, and the people of Makkah. "al-nu'as" is in the nominative case (marfu'). The argument of one who recited "yaghshakum" is the consensus of the reciters on the verse of (Uhud): ﴿He covered a group of you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 154]. The argument of one who recited "yughashshikum" is that the speech coheres with "yunazzil" (He sends down). The meaning of "yughashshikum" is: He covers you with it and pours it upon you, and this is a metaphor (isti'arah).

Al-nu'as is the lightest sleep, the kind that may befall a person while standing or walking. The narratives of this verse make clear that they experienced only a nodding of the heads. The saying of the Prophet ﷺ supports this: "When one of you feels drowsy (na'as) in his prayer..." And the words of the poet confirm it:

A drowsy one whom slumber overtook, and its haze settled over his eyes, yet he is not asleep.

(p-146) His saying: ﴿amanah﴾ is a verbal noun (masdar) from amina al-rajulu, ya'manu, amnan, amanatan, and amanan. The ha' in it marks the feminine form of the verbal noun, as it does in al-masa'ah and al-mashaqqah. Ibn Muhaysin recited "amnatan" with a sukun on the mim. It is related from 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud that he said: "Drowsiness at the time of the onset of battle is a sign of security from the enemy, and it is from Allah; but in prayer it is from Satan."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is a matter whose path is revelation, so it is undoubtedly attributed to it (the Prophet).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He sends down upon you water from the sky﴾ is also an enumeration of this blession, the rain. Some exegetes said—and al-Tabari related it from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, and others, and al-Zajjaj said it—that the disbelievers on the day of Badr got ahead of the believers to the water of Badr and settled upon it, while the believers had no water. Their souls were disturbed, they became thirsty, they became ritually impure (junub), and they prayed in that state. Some of them said among themselves—through Satan's insinuation into them: "We claim that we are the friends of Allah, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is among us, and our condition is this while the polytheists are at the water!" So Allah sent down rain on the night of Badr, the seventeenth of Ramadan, until the valleys flowed. The people drank, purified themselves, and watered their mounts. The sabkhah that lay between them and the polytheists became firm, so that the feet of the Muslims were made steady at the time of fighting, whereas before the rain the feet would sink into it. When the downpour came, it became compacted. They said: "This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿to purify you thereby﴾," that is, (p-147) from major impurity (janabah); ﴿and to remove from you the defilement of Satan﴾, that is, his punishment upon you through his earlier-mentioned whisperings. Rijz means punishment. Abu al-'Aliyah recited "rijs" with a sin, meaning his whisperings which are abhorred and held in disgust. Ibn Muhaysin recited "rijz" with a damma on the ra'. 'Isa ibn 'Umar recited "wa-yudhhib" with a jazm on the ba'. ﴿and to strengthen your hearts﴾, that is, by energizing them, removing laziness from them, and emboldening them against the enemy. From this is the saying: "rabit al-jash," meaning one whose soul is steadfast at the moment of its alarm in war. ﴿and to make firm the feet thereby﴾, that is, on the soft sand-dune where walking was difficult.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The sound view—which is the one in the Sirah of Ibn Ishaq and others—is that the believers got ahead to the water at Badr. In this regard is the speech of Habbab ibn al-Mundhir al-Ansari, "when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ alighted at the first water, and Habbab said to him: 'Is this a revelation, O Messenger of Allah, this place where we have alighted, so that we may neither advance beyond it nor fall behind it, or is it your opinion and strategy?'" The full narration is in the Sirah.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

But the descent of the rain occurred before their arrival at the water. The reason is that a group of the believers were afflicted during their journey with major impurity and lacked water near Badr, so they prayed in that state. This caused disquiet in their souls, and Satan whispered to them about it, along with frightening them with the great number of the enemy and their killing. This was before they saw each other with their eyes. Moreover, between them and the water of Badr lay a long distance of soft, yielding sand (p-148) in which feet sink. They expected that the disbelievers would get ahead of them to the water of Badr, so they urged one another to get ahead to it. Allah sent down that rain, the valleys flowed, they bathed, Allah purified them, and the rijz of Satan departed. The path became smooth and that sand-dune was compacted, so walking upon it became easy and they were able to hasten until they got ahead to the water. It is recorded in the Sirah that the same rain which fell upon the polytheists made their path difficult. So the believers rejoiced and understood from Allah's action toward them that it was an aid for them, and their souls were content, they gathered together and grew courageous. That is the strengthening (rabt) upon their hearts and the making firm of their feet upon the soft sand, so it became possible for them to reach the water before the polytheists.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is one of the possibilities His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and to make firm the feet thereby﴾ may carry. On this reading, the pronoun in "bihi" refers to the water. It is also possible that the pronoun in "bihi" refers to the strengthening of the hearts, so that making the feet firm becomes an expression for victory and aid at the place of war, and it shows that the one whose heart is steadfast also has his foot firm when facing terror.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The descent of the water occurred in time before the covering with drowsiness, and this sequence is not implied in the verse, since its purpose is only the enumeration of blessings. Abu al-Fath related that al-Sha'bi recited "wa-yunazzilu 'alaykum mina al-sama'i ma" with an unvocalised alif, "li-yutahhirakum bihi," and said: it means "alladhi" (that which).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is weak. Ibn al-Musayyab recited "li-yuṭahhirakum" with a sukun on the ta'. As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When your Lord inspired the angels﴾ and the rest of the verse, the governing element of "idh" is the first governing element according to what preceded in the earlier discussion. Were we to estimate it as close, His saying ﴿and to make firm﴾ would be understood with the pronoun returning to the strengthening; but on its return to the water, it is awkward for "wa-yuthabbita" to govern "idh."

The inspiration of Allah to the angels is either by inspiration (ilham) or by sending some of them to others.

'Isa ibn 'Umar recited—with a variant from him—"inni ma'akum" with a kasrah on the alif, as a resumption of narrating the story. The majority of people recited "anni" with a fathah on the alif, as it is governed by "yuhi." The justification for the kasrah is that revelation has the meaning of speech.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so make firm﴾ may mean fighting alongside them, as is related. It may mean being present in their vicinity and giving them companionship through that. It may also mean: make them firm with supportive words that strengthen the heart. It is related in this regard that some of the angels appeared in the form of human beings, and one of them would say to the believer beside him: "It has reached me that the disbelievers said, 'If the Muslims charge against us, we will surely be routed.'" Another would say: "I see nothing but victory and triumph for us." Another would say: "Advance, so-and-so," and similar firm words.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It is also possible that the strengthening commanded is what the angel casts into a person's heart through his inspiration: the illusion of victory and the belittling of the disbelievers, and the thoughts of encouragement that run through him. This interpretation is strengthened by the correspondence with His saying: ﴿I will cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieved﴾, although casting terror corresponds to strengthening in whatever form the strengthening takes, but it is closer to this since they are of one kind.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

On this interpretation, His saying: ﴿I will cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieved﴾ is addressed to the angels. Then His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿so strike above the necks﴾ is in the form of a command but its meaning is a report about the condition of the situation, as when you describe a war to someone you are addressing: "We met the people and defeated them, so strike with your sword wherever you wish, kill, and take your captive"—meaning, this was the state of affairs. (p-150)

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It is also possible that "I will cast" through the end of the verse is a report addressed to the believers about what He will do to the disbelievers in the future, as He did in the past; then He commanded them to strike the necks and fingertips, encouraging them and urging them to support the religion. Al-A'raj recited "al-ru'ub" with a damma on the ayn, while people recite it with a sukun.

People differed concerning His saying: ﴿above the necks﴾. Al-Akhfash said: "fawq" is superfluous (ziyadah). Al-Tabari related from 'Ata' that the meaning is: strike the necks. Others said it means "'ala" (upon). 'Ikrimah, the client of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: it retains its original sense, and he meant the heads, since they are above the necks. Al-Mubarrid said: in this there is permission to strike the disbeliever in the face.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This interpretation is the noblest of them.

In my view, it is also possible that by His saying: ﴿above the necks﴾ He means describing the most forceful and effective blows to the neck, namely the blow that lands above the bone of the neck and below the bone of the head, at the joint.

This meaning is alluded to in the saying of Duraid ibn al-Simmah al-Jushami to Ibn al-Dughunnah al-Sulami when he said to him: "Take my sword, and raise it away from the bone, and lower it away from the brain, for thus I used to strike the necks of heroes." A similar saying is the verse of the poet:

I placed the sword between his neck and... and between the soft cheeks of his face, a sideburn.

On this reading, "fawq al-a'naq" is firmly fitting. Ibn Qutaybah said: "fawq" in this verse means "dun" (below). This is a clear error; the confusion arose from His saying: ﴿a gnat or what is above it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 26], meaning "what is below it."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

"Fawq" here does not mean "dun." Rather, the intended meaning is: "what is above it in smallness and tininess," so the meaning approximates "dun." As for "al-banan," one group said: it is the joints wherever they are among the limbs; the meaning on this view is: "strike them in every place." Another group said: al-banan is the fingers, and this is the correct view. On this interpretation—though striking in every place is permissible—the most effective target is intended, because a fighter whose fingertips are cut off is disabled and cannot benefit from any of his limbs in confrontation and combat.

﴿That is because they opposed (shaqqū) Allah and His Messenger; and whoever opposes Allah and His Messenger, then indeed Allah is severe in punishment.﴾ ﴿That, so taste it; and that for the disbelievers is the punishment of the Fire.﴾ ﴿O you who have believed, when you meet those who have disbelieved advancing (zaḥfan), do not turn your backs to them.﴾ ﴿And whoever turns his back to them on that day—except one who withdraws for (the purpose of) battle or one who retreats to a company—then he has returned with anger from Allah, and his refuge is Hell, and wretched is the destination.﴾

This address is to the Prophet ﷺ, and the believers are included in it by meaning. The pronoun in "bi-annahum" refers to those who disbelieved. The word ﴿shāqqū﴾ means: they opposed, defied and severed. It is derived from al-shiqq (the split), which is cutting and separating between two things. This is a form of mufā'ala (reciprocal form). So it is as if Allah, when He legislated a law and commanded commands, and they denied and obstructed, what was between them became distant, separated and split apart. It is derived from this, because (p-152) together with its other side they moved apart and separated. The exegetes have explained His the Exalted's saying ﴿shāqqū﴾ as: they came to be in a split other than His split.

Al-Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Although this meaning is correct, the precise derivation is what we have mentioned, and the first example is al-shaqq with a fatḥah on the shīn. They agreed on idghām (assimilation) in "yushāqiq" following the orthography of the muṣḥaf. His saying: ﴿Indeed Allah is severe in punishment﴾ is the response of the conditional clause, containing a warning and threat.

His the Exalted's saying: ﴿That, so taste it﴾ is addressed to the disbelievers, meaning: that is the striking and killing and what Allah inflicted upon them on the Day of Badr. It is as if He said: The matter is that, so taste it. Sibawayh also explained it this way. Some said: it is possible that ﴿Dhālikum fadhūqūhu﴾ is in the place of an accusative, like the saying: "Zaydan fa-ḍribhu" (Zayd, so strike him). The majority of readers read "wa-anna" with a fatḥah on the alif. It is either on the estimate "wa-ḥatmun anna" (and it is a decree that...), so it is estimated as a deleted inceptive with "anna" as its predicate, or on the estimate "wa-'lamū anna" (and know that...), in which case it is—according to this—in the place of an accusative. Sulaymān narrated from al-Ḥasan ibn Abī al-Ḥasan: "wa-inna" with a kasrah, as a fresh resumption (qaṭ' wa-istiʾnāf).

His the Exalted's saying: ﴿O you who have believed, when you meet those who have disbelieved advancing (zaḥfan)﴾ the verse. "Zaḥfan" is intended to mean: facing one another in rows and persons, i.e., some advance toward others. The origin of zaḥf is advancing while sliding on the buttocks; then every walker toward another in war, slowly, was called zāḥif, since in his gait there is the slowness and sluggishness found in the gait of one who crawls. From zaḥf, which is advancing, is the saying of people about the fire of ʿarfaj and what is similar to it in swiftness of kindling: "nār al-zaḥfatayn" (the fire of the two zaḥfs). From slowness in walking is the saying of the poet: (p-153)

"As if they, in the hands of the people in distress, are birds unveiled from a dark-colored (cloud) that is drawn out."

From it is the saying of al-Farazdaq:

"Upon our turbans they are cast, and our feet... upon crawling (zawāḥif) ones we drive them, exhausted."

From it is the saying of another:

"For whom are these litters, whose going is a zaḥaff..."

From zaḥaf in the sense of pushing against one another is the saying of al-Hudhalī: (p-154)

"As if the zaḥāfif of the snakes in it, before the dawn, are the traces of whips."

In this verse Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, commanded that the believers not turn their backs before the disbelievers. This command is restricted by the condition stated regarding the two-to-one ratio of believers. If a group of believers meets a group that is double the number of the believing group from the polytheists, then the obligation is that they not flee before them. Fleeing there is a destructive major sin, by the apparent meaning of the Qur'an and ḥadīth and the consensus of the majority of the Ummah. The number is taken into account according to what is in the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic; this is the view of the majority of the Ummah. A sect, among them Ibn al-Mājishūn in al-Wāḍiḥa, said: strength, weakness and equipment are also taken into account. So it is permissible, according to their view, that a hundred horsemen flee if they know that the polytheists have twice what they have in equipment, valor and boldness, and they face fewer or more according to that. As for the view of the majority, the fleeing of a hundred is not lawful except before more than two hundred.

The expression "bi-l-dubur" (with the backs) in this verse is of eloquent refinement, because it is shameful to the fleeing one and condemns him. The majority read "dubarahu" with a ḍammah on the bā'; al-Ḥasan ibn Abī al-Ḥasan read "dubrahu" with a sukūn on the bā'.

The interpreters differed regarding what is indicated by His saying "yawma'idhin" (on that day). One group said: the reference is to the Day of Badr and what followed it; on that day the threat of anger was made against those who fled, and after that the ruling of the verse was abrogated by the verse of weakness (al-ḍaʿf), and fleeing from the battlefield remained not a major sin. People fled on the Day of Uhud, and Allah pardoned them, and He said about them on the Day of Ḥunayn: ﴿Then you turned back retreating﴾ [al-Tawbah: 25], and there was no rebuke upon that.

Al-Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The majority of the Ummah said: the reference of "yawma'idhin" is to the day of the encounter which is contained in His saying: (p-155) ﴿when you meet﴾, and the ruling of the verse remains until the Day of Resurrection with the condition of the two-to-one ratio which Allah, the Exalted, explained in another verse. There is no abrogation in the verse. As for the Day of Uhud, the people fled from more than twice their number, and despite that they were rebuked because the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was among them and because of their fleeing from him. As for the Day of Ḥunayn, likewise, whoever fled only fled before the multitude. It is possible that Allah's pardon of those who fled on the Day of Uhud was a pardon for a major sin.

"Mutaḥarrifan li-qitāl" (one who withdraws for battle)

It is intended: one who sees that his doing so is more damaging to the enemy and more beneficial to himself in harm; it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl), and likewise the accusative of "mutaḥayyizan". As for the exception, it is from those who turn back, which "man" contains. Some people said: the exception is from the types of turning back.

Al-Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

If that were so, it would necessarily be: "illā taḥarrufan wa-taḥayyuzan" (except by withdrawing and retreating).

"Al-fi'ah" here: the group of people present for the battle. This is according to the view of the majority that fleeing from the zaḥf is a major sin. As for the other view, "al-fi'ah" is the city, the imam and the community of the Muslims wherever they are. This view has been narrated from ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "I am your fi'ah, O Muslims."

Al-Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This was from him as a measure of caution for the believers, since in that time they would stand firm against their multiples many times. In the Musnad of Ibn Abī Shaybah, through the chain of ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar: "that the Prophet ﷺ said to a group that fled in one of his expeditions, when they came to him: 'I am the fi'ah of the Muslims.'" And in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, from (p-156) the ḥadīth of Abū Hurayrah, he said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: "Avoid the seven destructive matters," and he enumerated among them fleeing from the zaḥf.

"Bā'a" in the sense of "nahaḍa" (rose) bearing the weight mentioned in the speech, whether it is anger or the like. Anger is among the attributes of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic; when it is taken in the sense of will, it is an attribute of essence (ṣifat dhāt), and when it is taken in the sense of manifesting the actions of one who is angry toward the servant, it is an attribute of action (ṣifat fi'l). This latter meaning is closer to this verse. And "al-ma'wā" is the place to which a person retreats.
