The exegetes have explained His the Exalted's saying ﴿shāqqū﴾ as: they came to be in a split other than His split.

Al-Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Although this meaning is correct, the precise derivation is what we have mentioned, and the first example is al-shaqq with a fatḥah on the shīn. They agreed on idghām (assimilation) in "yushāqiq" following the orthography of the muṣḥaf. His saying: ﴿Indeed Allah is severe in punishment﴾ is the response of the conditional clause, containing a warning and threat.

His the Exalted's saying: ﴿That, so taste it﴾ is addressed to the disbelievers, meaning: that is the striking and killing and what Allah inflicted upon them on the Day of Badr. It is as if He said: The matter is that, so taste it. Sibawayh also explained it this way. Some said: it is possible that ﴿Dhālikum fadhūqūhu﴾ is in the place of an accusative, like the saying: "Zaydan fa-ḍribhu" (Zayd, so strike him). The majority of readers read "wa-anna" with a fatḥah on the alif. It is either on the estimate "wa-ḥatmun anna" (and it is a decree that...), so it is estimated as a deleted inceptive with "anna" as its predicate, or on the estimate "wa-'lamū anna" (and know that...), in which case it is—according to this—in the place of an accusative. Sulaymān narrated from al-Ḥasan ibn Abī al-Ḥasan: "wa-inna" with a kasrah, as a fresh resumption (qaṭ' wa-istiʾnāf).

His the Exalted's saying: ﴿O you who have believed, when you meet those who have disbelieved advancing (zaḥfan)﴾ the verse. "Zaḥfan" is intended to mean: facing one another in rows and persons, i.e., some advance toward others. The origin of zaḥf is advancing while sliding on the buttocks; then every walker toward another in war, slowly, was called zāḥif, since in his gait there is the slowness and sluggishness found in the gait of one who crawls. From zaḥf, which is advancing, is the saying of people about the fire of ʿarfaj and what is similar to it in swiftness of kindling: "nār al-zaḥfatayn" (the fire of the two zaḥfs). From slowness in walking is the saying of the poet: (p-153)

"As if they, in the hands of the people in distress, are birds unveiled from a dark-colored (cloud) that is drawn out."

From it is the saying of al-Farazdaq:

"Upon our turbans they are cast, and our feet... upon crawling (zawāḥif) ones we drive them, exhausted."

From it is the saying of another:

"For whom are these litters, whose going is a zaḥaff..."

From zaḥaf in the sense of pushing against one another is the saying of al-Hudhalī: (p-154)

"As if the zaḥāfif of the snakes in it, before the dawn, are the traces of whips."

In this verse Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, commanded that the believers not turn their backs before the disbelievers. This command is restricted by the condition stated regarding the two-to-one ratio of believers. If a group of believers meets a group that is double the number of the believing group from the polytheists, then the obligation is that they not flee before them. Fleeing there is a destructive major sin, by the apparent meaning of the Qur'an and ḥadīth and the consensus of the majority of the Ummah. The number is taken into account according to what is in the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic; this is the view of the majority of the Ummah. A sect, among them Ibn al-Mājishūn in al-Wāḍiḥa, said: strength, weakness and equipment are also taken into account. So it is permissible, according to their view, that a hundred horsemen flee if they know that the polytheists have twice what they have in equipment, valor and boldness, and they face fewer or more according to that. As for the view of the majority, the fleeing of a hundred is not lawful except before more than two hundred.

The expression "bi-l-dubur" (with the backs) in this verse is of eloquent refinement, because it is shameful to the fleeing one and condemns him. The majority read "dubarahu" with a ḍammah on the bā'; al-Ḥasan ibn Abī al-Ḥasan read "dubrahu" with a sukūn on the bā'.

The interpreters differed regarding what is indicated by His saying "yawma'idhin" (on that day). One group said: the reference is to the Day of Badr and what followed it; on that day the threat of anger was made against those who fled, and after that the ruling of the verse was abrogated by the verse of weakness (al-ḍaʿf), and fleeing from the battlefield remained not a major sin. People fled on the Day of Uhud, and Allah pardoned them, and He said about them on the Day of Ḥunayn: ﴿Then you turned back retreating﴾ [al-Tawbah: 25], and there was no rebuke upon that.

Al-Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The majority of the Ummah said: the reference of "yawma'idhin" is to the day of the encounter which is contained in His saying: (p-155) ﴿when you meet﴾, and the ruling of the verse remains until the Day of Resurrection with the condition of the two-to-one ratio which Allah, the Exalted, explained in another verse. There is no abrogation in the verse. As for the Day of Uhud, the people fled from more than twice their number, and despite that they were rebuked because the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was among them and because of their fleeing from him. As for the Day of Ḥunayn, likewise, whoever fled only fled before the multitude. It is possible that Allah's pardon of those who fled on the Day of Uhud was a pardon for a major sin.

"Mutaḥarrifan li-qitāl" (one who withdraws for battle)

It is intended: one who sees that his doing so is more damaging to the enemy and more beneficial to himself in harm; it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl), and likewise the accusative of "mutaḥayyizan". As for the exception, it is from those who turn back, which "man" contains. Some people said: the exception is from the types of turning back.

Al-Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

If that were so, it would necessarily be: "illā taḥarrufan wa-taḥayyuzan" (except by withdrawing and retreating).

"Al-fi'ah" here: the group of people present for the battle. This is according to the view of the majority that fleeing from the zaḥf is a major sin. As for the other view, "al-fi'ah" is the city, the imam and the community of the Muslims wherever they are. This view has been narrated from ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "I am your fi'ah, O Muslims."

Al-Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This was from him as a measure of caution for the believers, since in that time they would stand firm against their multiples many times. In the Musnad of Ibn Abī Shaybah, through the chain of ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar: "that the Prophet ﷺ said to a group that fled in one of his expeditions, when they came to him: 'I am the fi'ah of the Muslims.'" And in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, from (p-156) the ḥadīth of Abū Hurayrah, he said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: "Avoid the seven destructive matters," and he enumerated among them fleeing from the zaḥf.

"Bā'a" in the sense of "nahaḍa" (rose) bearing the weight mentioned in the speech, whether it is anger or the like. Anger is among the attributes of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic; when it is taken in the sense of will, it is an attribute of essence (ṣifat dhāt), and when it is taken in the sense of manifesting the actions of one who is angry toward the servant, it is an attribute of action (ṣifat fi'l). This latter meaning is closer to this verse. And "al-ma'wā" is the place to which a person retreats.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 8, verse 17–18:

His, may He be Exalted and Glorified, saying:

﴿So you did not kill them, but it was Allah who killed them. And you did not throw when you threw, but it was Allah who threw, and that He might test the believers with a good test from Him. Indeed, Allah is Hearing and Knowing.﴾ ﴿That is so; and that Allah weakens the plot of the disbelievers.﴾

This is an address to the believers, by which Allah informs them that the killers among the believers were not independent in killing through being empowered to it. Creation and bringing into existence in all the states of the killer belong only to Allah the Exalted; the killer has no share in them. He merely participates through his acquisition (kasb) and intention (qasd). These words refute those who say that the actions of servants are their own creation.

The occasion of this verse, as it is related, is that when the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) returned from Badr, each one of them mentioned what he had done. One said: "I killed such-and-such, and I did such-and-such," so there arose from this boasting and the like, and the verse was revealed.

His, may He be Exalted, saying: ﴿And you did not throw when you threw﴾ is intended to refer to what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did on that day. He took handfuls of pebbles and dust and threw them into the faces of the people and in front of them three times, and they were routed at the last throw. It is also related that he said on the day of Badr: "Ugly be the faces" (shāhat al-wujūh). This act also occurred on the day of Hunayn without dispute. It is related that the dust he threw did not remain without some of it entering the eyes of every disbeliever. It is also related that he threw three stones, and the defeat came with the third stone.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The saying of Allah, ﴿And you did not throw when you threw, but it was Allah who threw﴾ may bear the same meaning as what we stated concerning His saying: ﴿So you did not kill them, but it was Allah who killed them﴾. This is explicitly stated in al-Tabari and others. It comes out in the speech of the Arabs with the meaning: "And you did not throw the sufficient throw when you threw," similar to the saying of al-'Abbas ibn Mirdas:

"…………… *** So I was not given anything, nor was I prevented."

That is: "I will not be given anything satisfactory."

It may also be intended: "And you did not cast terror into their hearts when you threw your pebbles, but Allah cast it." This too is explicitly stated in al-Mahdawi and others.

It may also be intended: "And you did not suffice when you threw your pebbles, but Allah threw," meaning: He helped you and granted you victory. The Arabs say in supplication: "May Allah throw for you," meaning: may He help you and act on your behalf. Abu 'Ubayda related this in the book Al-Majaz. A group read: "wa-lakinna Allaha ramā" with a shadda on the nūn, and a group read: "wa-lakin Allahu ramā" with its lightening and raising of the hā' of "Allah."

And ﴿wa-liyubliya﴾ means: that He might afflict them with a good trial. The apparent description of it as "good" implies that He intended spoils, victory, and honour. It has been said that He intended martyrdom for those who were martyred on the day of Badr, who were fourteen, among them 'Ubayda ibn al-Harith ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, Mahja' the freedman of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, Mu'adh and 'Amr, the two sons of 'Afra', and others.

﴿Indeed, Allah is Hearing﴾ of your supplication ﴿Knowing﴾ of the wisdom in all His actions. There is no god but Him.

al-Tabari related that the intended meaning of His, may He be Exalted, saying: ﴿And you did not throw when you threw﴾ is the throw by the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) of the spear at Ubayy ibn Khalaf on the day of Uhud.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is weak, because the verse was revealed right after Badr, and on this view it would be unrelated to what precedes and follows it, and that is far-fetched. It is also related that the intended meaning is the arrow that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) shot at the fortress of Khaybar, which flew through the air until it struck Ibn Abi al-Huqayq and killed him while he was on his bed. This is corrupt, since the conquest of Khaybar was much later than Uhud, and the correct account of the killing of Ibn Abi al-Huqayq is other than this. These two opinions are therefore weak for the reasons we have mentioned.

His, may He be Exalted, saying: ﴿That is so﴾ refers to what preceded: the killing of Allah and His throwing of them. The position of "dhalikum" in grammar is in the nominative case. Sibawayh said: the implied sense is "the matter is that." Some grammarians said it may be in the accusative case with an implied verb, with "wa-anna" conjoined to "dhalikum," and it may also be the predicate of an implied subject, its implied sense being: "and it is a decree, established and fixed," or similar. A group read "wa-inna" with a kasra on the hamza, as a resumption and new sentence. ﴿Muwhinu﴾ means: weakening and nullifying. It is said: "wahana al-shay'" (wahn), like "wa'ada ya'idu"; and it is said: "wahina," like "wali yali." It was read "fa-ma wahanu li-ma asabahum" with a kasra on the hā'. Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Ibn 'Amir, and Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim read: "Muwhinu kaydi" from awhana. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', and Abu 'Amr read: "Muwahhinu kaydi" from wahhana. Hafs on the authority of 'Asim read: "Muwhini kaydi" with a kasra on the dal and the idafa. Al-Zajjaj mentioned that there are four modes in it: he mentioned these three readings, and added "Muwahhini kaydi" with a shadda on the hā' and the idafa, though he did not state that it is a reading.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 8, verse 19–21:

Allah the Mighty and Majestic said:

﴿If you seek a judgment, then the judgment has indeed come to you. And if you desist, it is better for you. And if you return, We will return. And your company will not avail you anything, even if it is numerous. And indeed, Allah is with the believers.﴾ ﴿O you who have believed, obey Allah and His Messenger, and do not turn away from him while you hear.﴾ ﴿And do not be like those who said, "We hear," while they do not hear.﴾

Some of the interpreters (mutawwilun) said: this verse is addressed to the believers present at Badr. Allah said to them: ﴿If you seek a judgment, then the judgment has indeed come to you﴾, and it is the decision between you and the disbelievers; so it has come to you, and Allah has decided in your favour. ﴿And if you desist﴾ from what you did of speech concerning the matter of the spoils and what disputes arose among you regarding them, and from your boasting of your deeds, such as killing and other things, ﴿it is better for you. And if you return﴾ to these deeds, ﴿We will return﴾ to rebuke you. Then He informed them that the company (fi'ah), which is the group, does not avail, even if it is numerous, except by Allah's help and support. Then He comforted them with His saying and His obligation that He is with the believers.

Most of the interpreters said: this verse is addressed to the disbelievers of Makkah. This is because it is narrated that Abu Jahl used to supplicate constantly in the assemblies of Quraysh, saying: "O Allah, whichever of us is more severed from kinship and has brought what we do not know, destroy him and make him the vanquished," meaning Muhammad (ﷺ) and themselves. It is also narrated that when Quraysh resolved to go out to protect the caravan, they clung to the curtains of the Ka'bah and sought victory (istaftahu). It is narrated that Abu Jahl said on the morning of the Battle of Badr: "O Allah, support the dearer of the two groups to You, and manifest the better of the two religions in Your sight. O Allah, whoever is more severed from kinship, destroy him tomorrow morning," and similar things. So Allah said to them: if you seek victory, it has come to you as you see it upon yourselves, not for you.

(p-160) The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

In this there is rebuke. Then He said to them: ﴿And if you desist﴾ from your disbelief and error, ﴿it is better for you﴾. Then He informed them that if they returned to seeking victory, the like of the blow of the day of Badr would return upon them. Then He informed them that their company does not avail anything, even if it is large. Then He informed them that He is with the believers.

A group of the interpreters said: the saying of the Exalted: ﴿If you seek a judgment, then the judgment has indeed come to you﴾ is addressed to the believers, and the rest of the verse is addressed to the polytheists, as if He said: "And you, the disbelievers, (if you desist, it is better for you)."

Ibn Kathir, 'Asim in the narration of Abu Bakr, Abu 'Amr, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "wa-inna Allah" with a kasra on the hamza, as a new sentence (al-qat'). Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, and 'Asim in the narration of Hafs read "wa-anna" with a fatha on the alif. Then it is either in the position of nominative as the predicate of an elided subject, or in the position of accusative by an implied verb. What al-Tabari mentioned, that the estimate is: "because of its multitude and because Allah is with the believers," is a possible meaning. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "and even if they are numerous, and Allah is with the believers," and this strengthens the reading of the one who put a kasra on the alif of "inna."

As for the saying of the Exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, obey Allah and His Messenger﴾, the address is to the believers who affirm, He renewed the command to them to obey Allah and the Messenger, and they were forbidden to turn away from him. This is the view of the majority. This is consistent with the view of those who say: "the address in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And if you desist﴾ is to the believers," so the speech comes in one pattern in its meaning. But according to the view of those who say: "the address in 'if you desist' is to the disbelievers," they hold that this verse was revealed because of their disputing over the spoils, their argument about the truth, their hatred of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) going out, and their boasting of killing the disbelievers and inflicting harm upon them. A group said: the address in this verse is only to the hypocrites, and the meaning is: "O you who have believed with their tongues only."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This, although it is possible, is very far-fetched and very weak, because Allah described those addressed in this verse with faith, and faith is affirmation (tasdiq), and the hypocrites do not possess any affirmation (p-161) of anything. It was also said that the address is to the Children of Israel, and this is foreign to the verse.

And ﴿tawallaw﴾ originally is: tatawallaw, because the prefix ta of the present tense was joined by the ta of the second person, so one of them was deleted; the deleted one is the ta of "tafa'ala," and the remaining one is the ta of the sign (of the second person plural), because the need for it here is more pressing, so that the verb remains in the future sense. His saying: ﴿while you hear﴾ means: His calling you with the Qur'an, the admonitions, and the signs.

His saying: ﴿like those who said﴾ means: the disbelievers, either from Quraysh, because of their saying: ﴿We have heard. If we wished, we could say the like of this﴾ [al-Anfal: 31], or the disbelievers in general who say: "We have heard the Qur'an, and we know that it is sorcery, or poetry, or fables," according to their differing views. Then Allah informed about them a report by which He negated that they had heard, that is, understood and comprehended, because there is no disagreement that they were hearing the recitation with their ears, but their hearts were sealed and Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, did not open them to receive the meanings of the Qur'an and belief in it.

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿Indeed, the worst of beasts in the sight of Allah are the deaf and the dumb who do not reason.﴾ ﴿And if Allah had known any good in them, He would have made them hear. And even if He had made them hear, they would have turned away while being averse.﴾ ﴿O you who believe, respond to Allah and to the Messenger when he calls you to that which gives you life. And know that Allah intervenes between a man and his heart, and that to Him you will be gathered.﴾

The purpose of this verse is to make clear that this wicked group of disbelievers is the worst of people in the sight of Allah, the Exalted and Majestic, and that they are the lowest of stations before Him. He expressed it with "beasts" in order to emphasize their condemnation, and to give preference over them to the rabid dog, the pig, and similar among the predatory beasts and the five vermin (al-fawasiq) and others. "Dawabb" (beasts): everything that crawls, which encompasses animals in their entirety. His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿the deaf and the dumb﴾ is an expression for what is in their hearts, the scarcity of the expansion of their breasts and the perception of their minds; therefore He described them as deaf and dumb and stripped them of reason. It is related that this verse was revealed concerning a group from the Banu 'Abd al-Dar, and its apparent meaning is general regarding them and regarding others who are characterized by these attributes. Then the Exalted informed that their lack of hearing and guidance is only due to what Allah knew of them and what preceded from His decree concerning them. This came in an eloquent expression of their condemnation in His, the Glorified, saying: ﴿And if Allah had known any good in them, He would have made them hear﴾, and what is meant is: He would have made them hear with the hearing of understanding and guidance. Then the Exalted began the report about them with what they are upon of His decree against them of disbelief, saying: ﴿And even if He had made them hear﴾, i.e., even if He had made them understand, ﴿they would have turned away﴾ by the judgment of the preceding decree concerning them, and they would have turned away from the guidance that had become clear to them. His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿O you who believe, respond to Allah and to the Messenger﴾, the verse. This is an address to the believers who affirm, without disagreement. ﴿Istajibu﴾ means ajibu (respond), but the customary usage of speech is that "istajaba" is transitive with the preposition "li," while "ajaba" is transitive without a preposition; and it may occur that "istajaba" is transitive without "li." The evidence is the poet's saying:

"And a caller who called, 'O you who answers to the call,' so no answerer answered him at that time."

His saying: ﴿to that which gives you life﴾. Mujahid and the majority said: the meaning is: for obedience and what the Qur'an includes of commands and prohibitions. This is a metaphorical life, since it is from the death of disbelief and ignorance. It was said: Islam. This is close to the first, but it is weak because one who has already believed is not told: enter into Islam. It was also said: ﴿to that which gives you life﴾ means: for war and jihad against the enemy, and it gives life through honor, dominance, and victory; so that is called life, as you say: "the condition of so-and-so has come to life" when it is elevated. The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is the connection between the life of this world and the life of the Hereafter.

This interpretation is consistent with His saying: ﴿and that to Him you will be gathered﴾, i.e., so hasten to acts of obedience and provision for them for the Day of Gathering. Among them: that by His saying: ﴿And know that Allah intervenes between a man and his heart﴾ He intends to inform them that the power of Allah, His encompassing and His knowledge, stand as a barrier between a man and his heart, a barrier between him and his heart.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

So it is as if He said to the believers in this other passage: respond to Allah and to the Messenger, and do not feel secure, if you do so, that there will befall you what befell the disbelievers of the barrier between them and their hearts; thus He alerted them to what happened to the disbelievers with the most eloquent expression and the most gripping to the soul.

Among them: that the meaning is a hope given to them that Allah will transform the fear in their hearts from the multitude of the enemy into boldness and strength, while the disbelievers receive the opposite, for Allah is the Turner of hearts, as was the oath of the Prophet ﷺ. Some people said: from this is: "There is no power and no strength except with Allah," i.e., no power to refrain from disobedience and no strength to obey except with Allah.

Commentators said various things about this, which are foreign to the wording of the verse, related by al-Tabari, among them that Allah intervenes between the believer and the disbeliever, and between the disbeliever and faith, and similar.

Ibn Abi Ishaq read "bayna al-mir'" with a kasra on the mim, mentioned by Abu Hatim. Abu al-Fath said: al-Hasan and al-Zubaydi read "bayna al-marr" with a fatha on the mim and a shadda on the kasra-marked ra.

﴿Tuhsharun﴾ means you will be resurrected on the Day of Resurrection. It is related through the chain of Malik ibn Anas and al-Nasa'i that "the Messenger of Allah ﷺ called Ubayy ibn Ka'b while he was in prayer, and he did not respond, and he hastened through the rest of his prayer. When he came to him, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to him: Did you not hear what was revealed to me: ﴿O you who believe, respond to Allah and to the Messenger when he calls you to that which gives you life﴾? Ubayy said: Indeed, O Messenger of Allah, you will never call me except that I will answer you," the hadith in full with variations in wording. In al-Bukhari and Muslim it is that this occurred with Abu Sa'id ibn al-Mu'alla, and it is related that something similar occurred with Hudhayfa ibn al-Yaman during the Battle of the Trench.

[p. 165]

His saying, Mighty and Majestic:

﴿And beware of a trial which will not strike exclusively those of you who have done wrong. And know that Allah is severe in punishment.﴾ ﴿And remember when you were few and oppressed in the land, fearing that people would snatch you away, so He sheltered you, strengthened you with His help, and provided you with good things, that you might be grateful.﴾

This verse admits several interpretations (*ta'wilat*). The one that first comes to mind is that Allah intends to warn all the believers against a trial which, if it strikes, will not be limited to the wrongdoers but will strike everyone, wrongdoer and innocent alike. This is the interpretation that al-Zubayr ibn al-'Awwam, may Allah be pleased with him, adopted, for he said on the Day of the Camel: "I did not know that we were meant by this verse until today, and I did not think it was addressed to anyone except those it addressed at that time." Likewise al-Hasan al-Basri interpreted it, saying: "This verse concerns 'Ali, 'Ammar, Talha and al-Zubayr." Likewise Ibn 'Abbas interpreted it, saying: "Allah commanded the believers in this verse not to tolerate wrongdoing among them, lest punishment overtake them all." Al-Qutabi explained it, as reported from him by Makki, with a thorough explanation.

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

On this interpretation, His saying ﴿لا تُصِيبَنَّ﴾ (*lā tuṣībanna*, "will not strike") is a description of the trial. Given this, the wording should have been *lā tuṣību* (without the emphatic ending), but it was softened to allow the heavy nūn (*al-nūn al-thaqīla*, the emphatic nūn) to enter a statement about the trial. Al-Zajjaj said: Some grammarians claimed that the speech is a conditional (*jazā'*) with a form of prohibition in it. He said: A similar example is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿ادْخُلُوا مَساكِنَكم لا يَحْطِمَنَّكُمْ﴾ (Enter your dwellings, lest they crush you) [al-Naml: 18]. The meaning is: if you enter, it will not crush you. Likewise here: if you are wary (*in tattaqū*), it will not strike (*lā tuṣībanna*). Others said: it is a statement with the meaning of a conditional, which is why the nūn could enter. Al-Mahdawi said: It was also said that it is the answer to an implied oath, its assumed form being: "And beware of a trial, by Allah, it will not strike," and the nūn entered with *lā* by analogy with its entering with the lām alone.

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad said:

In this view there is some awkwardness, because when the answer to an oath is negated or contains *lā*, the nūn does not enter; when it is affirmative, the lām and the heavy nūn enter, as in your saying: "By Allah, Zayd will not stand," and "By Allah, Zayd will certainly stand." This is the rule of the subject. Yet the meaning of this verse fits with the awkwardness we have mentioned.

The other interpretation of the verse is that His saying ﴿واتَّقُوا فِتْنَةً﴾ (And beware of a trial) is a general address to all the believers, standing on its own; the speech is complete at that point. Then a new prohibition begins, aimed specifically at wrongdoers, against exposing themselves to wrong, so that the trial strikes them in particular. The prohibition is expressed in the form of addressing the trial itself, so it is a transferred prohibition (*nahy maḥwwal*). The Arabs do this, as they say: "لا أرَيْنَّكَ هاهُنا" (*lā arayannaka hāhunā*, "I should not see you here"), meaning: do not stand here, so that I see you; they did not mean to forbid the one doing the seeing. Likewise, the meaning in the verse is: let no wrong proceed from your wrongdoers, so that the trial does not strike them. This was the view of al-Zajjaj and is the opinion of Abu al-'Abbas al-Mubarrad; al-Naqqash related it from al-Farra'. The prohibition of wrongdoers here is expressed in the form of addressing a group, as you say to a people: "Let your fools not do such and such," while you only mean the fools.

﴿خاصَّةً﴾ (*khāṣṣatan*, "specifically") is an adjective (*na't*) of an omitted verbal noun (*maṣdar*), whose assumed form is إصابَةً خاصَّةً (*iṣābatan khāṣṣatan*, "a striking specific to them"). It is therefore in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*), since the verbal noun has been omitted, and the state is from the pronoun in ﴿تُصِيبَنَّ﴾, with this verb being the operative. It is possible that ﴿خاصَّةً﴾ is a state from the pronoun in ﴿ظَلَمُوا﴾ (who have done wrong), in which case no omitted verbal noun is needed. The first is more apt in meaning.

ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, Zayd ibn Thabit, Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn 'Ali, al-Rabi' ibn Anas, Abu al-'Aliya and Ibn Jammaz read ﴿لَتُصِيبَنَّ﴾ (*latuṣībanna*) with the lām, as an answer to an oath. On this reading the meaning is a warning to the wrongdoers only. Abu al-Fath said: It may be that by this reading the intended form is *lā tuṣībanna*, with the alif of *lā* dropped for lightness and the vowel left to suffice, as they say *am wallāhi*. It may also be that by the reading of the majority, *lā tuṣībanna* is intended as *latuṣībanna*, the vowel of the lām being prolonged so that an alif arose from it.

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad said: This is an over-elaborate forcing of analysis. Al-Naqqash related this reading from al-Zubayr ibn al-'Awwam, and this contradicts what al-Tabari and others related of al-Zubayr's interpretation of the verse. Al-Naqqash related from Ibn Mas'ud that he read: "واتَّقَوْا فِتْنَةً أنْ تُصِيبَ" (And beware of a trial that it strike...).

His saying ﴿واعْلَمُوا أنَّ اللهَ شَدِيدُ العِقابِ﴾ (And know that Allah is severe in punishment) is a warning that fits well with the interpretations of al-Zubayr and al-Hasan, and fits the other interpretations in various ways.

It is related from 'Ali ibn Sulayman al-Akhfash that His saying ﴿لا تُصِيبَنَّ﴾ is in the sense of supplication (*du'a'*), as reported by al-Zahrawi.

His saying ﴿واذْكُرُوا إذْ أنْتُمْ قَلِيلٌ﴾ (And remember when you were few) and the rest of the verse: this verse contains an enumeration of Allah's blessings upon the believers. ﴿إذْ﴾ (*idh*, "when") is an adverb of time (*ẓarf*) governed by the object of ﴿واذْكُرُوا﴾ (remember). Its assumed form is: "remember your state which was or which was established, when you were few." It is not permissible for ﴿إذْ﴾ to be an adverb of time for the remembering itself; rather the remembering governs ﴿إذْ﴾ only if we take it as an object (*maf'ūl*).

People differed about the state referred to in this verse. A group, which is the majority, said: it is the state of Makkah at the beginning of Islam. The people whose snatching was feared are the unbelievers of Makkah. The sheltering (*ma'wā*), on this interpretation, is Madina and the Ansar. The strengthening with help is the Battle of Badr and what was accomplished with it in its time. The good things are the spoils and what else Allah granted them. Another group said: the state referred to is the state of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his companions at the Battle of Badr. The people whose snatching was feared, on this view, are the army of Makkah and the other tribes neighbouring it, for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) feared some of them. The sheltering and the strengthening with help are the reinforcement with angels and victory over the enemy. The good things are the booty.

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad said: These two views suit the time of the revelation, since the verse was revealed right after Badr. Wahb ibn Munabbih and Qatada said: The state referred to is the state of the Arabs as a whole, for they were the most destitute of people in body, the hungriest in stomach, and the fewest in men and livestock. The people whose snatching was feared, on this interpretation, are Persia and Rome. The sheltering is prophethood and the law. The strengthening with help is the conquest of lands and the overcoming of kings. The good things are the blessings of food, drink and clothing.

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad said: This interpretation is refuted by the fact that the Arabs at the time this verse was revealed were unbelievers, apart from a few, and the conditions this interpreter mentioned had not come about. The Arabs could only have been addressed with this verse at the end of the time of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him. If someone applies this verse to the condition of the Arabs, his application is valid; but that the condition of the Arabs was the cause of the revelation is far-fetched, for the reason we have mentioned.

His saying ﴿لَعَلَّكم تَشْكُرُونَ﴾ (that you may be grateful) is an expectation in human terms, connected to His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿واذْكُرُوا﴾ (and remember).

**Ibn 'Atiyya's commentary (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 8, verses 27–30:**

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿O you who have believed, do not betray Allah and the Messenger or betray your trusts while you know.﴾ ﴿And know that your wealth and your children are a trial, and that with Allah is a great reward.﴾ ﴿O you who have believed, if you fear Allah, He will grant you a criterion (furqan) and will remove from you your misdeeds and forgive you. And Allah is the possessor of great bounty.﴾ ﴿And [recall] when those who disbelieved plotted against you to restrain you, or kill you, or expel you. They plot, and Allah plots, and Allah is the best of plotters.﴾

This is an address to all believers until the Day of Resurrection, and it encompasses all kinds of betrayal, small and great. Al-Zahrawi said: the meaning is, do not betray through misappropriation (ghulul) of the spoils. Al-Zahrawi and Abdullah ibn Abi Qatada said: the occasion of its revelation was the affair of Abu Lubaba. He gestured to the Banu Qurayza, when he went to them, toward his throat, intending to inform them that the only thing left for them from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was slaughter, i.e., do not come down. Then he regretted it and tied himself to one of the pillars of the mosque until Allah accepted his repentance. This is the well-known hadith. Al-Tabari related that he remained for seven days without tasting anything until he was forgiven. It is also related that Abu Lubaba had property and children with them, and for this reason the verse ﴿And know that your wealth and your children are a trial﴾ was revealed.

Ata' ibn Abi Rabah related from Jabir ibn Abdullah: its occasion was that a man from the hypocrites wrote to Abu Sufyan ibn Harb with news of the affairs of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and so the verse was revealed. His saying, glorified is He, ﴿O you who have believed﴾ means: manifest faith. It may also be that it addresses those who truly believe, that they should not do the like of that hypocrite's act.

Al-Tabari related from al-Mughira ibn Shu'ba that he said: this verse was revealed concerning the killing of Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

It is likely that the verse is given as an example of the killing of Uthman, may Allah have mercy on him, for it was a betrayal of Allah, of the Messenger, and of the trusts. Betrayal (khiyana) is the diminishing of a thing by concealment. It is used for a person doing what is contrary to what should be done in guarding a matter, whether it is property, a secret, or otherwise. Betrayal of Allah, Exalted is He, is the diminishing of His commands in secret. Betrayal of the Messenger is the diminishing of what was entrusted to him, and betrayal of trusts (amanat) is their diminishing and their abandonment. A trust (amana) is a state of a person by which he is trusted with what he has been entrusted with; he has been entrusted with his religion, his worship, and the rights of others. It has been said: the meaning is ﴿and betray those who hold your trusts﴾, and I think al-Farisi, Abu Ali, related it. ﴿While you know﴾ means that the betrayal is not harmful to one except when it is done deliberately.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿fitna﴾ means a trial, a test, and an affliction, so that He may see how you act in all of that. His saying ﴿and that with Allah is a great reward﴾ means the success of the Hereafter. So do not leave your share of it out of concern for guarding your wealth and your children, for what is stored up for the Hereafter is greater in worth than the gains of this world.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿and betray﴾: al-Tabari said: it may be within the prohibition, as if He said: "Do not betray Allah and the Messenger, and do not betray your trusts." In this case its position is jussive (majzum). It may also be that the meaning is: "Do not betray Allah and the Messenger, for that is a betrayal of your trusts," in which case its position is accusative (nasb), with the sense of "and that you betray your trusts." The poet said:

*Do not forbid a trait while doing its like;*
*Shame upon you is great when you do it.*

Mujahid and Abu Amr ibn al-'Ala', as also related from him, read ﴿wa-takhunu amanatakum﴾ with the singular "amana."

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿O you who have believed, if you fear Allah﴾ and the verse that follows, is a promise to believers on condition of God-consciousness and obedience to Him. ﴿He will grant you a criterion (furqan)﴾ means: a distinction between your truth and the falsehood of those who dispute with you, that is, by victory and support over them. Furqan is a verbal noun from "faraqa bayna al-shay'ayn," when he separates the two or opposes their judgment, and from it is His saying: ﴿the Day of the Criterion﴾ [al-Anfal: 41]. Qatada and some exegetes rendered furqan here as deliverance. Al-Suddi and Mujahid said: its meaning is a way out, and similar to this, which is included in what we have mentioned. The Arabs do use furqan in the sense the exegetes mentioned. Among that is the saying of Mizrad ibn Dirar:

*The horizon hastened to set, but when*
*the night grew dark, it found no furqan.*

Another said:

*What remedy do you have against long grief?*
*Since the dwellers departed and went away.*

Another said:

*How can I hope for eternity when death pursues me,*
*and I have no furqan from the cup of death?*

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And [recall] when those who disbelieved plotted against you﴾ and the verse that follows: it is likely that His saying "wa-idh" is coordinated with His saying "idh antum qalil" (when you were few), and this is a reminder of the condition of Makkah and its narrowness with the disbelievers, and of Allah's beautiful handling in gathering them. It may also be that it begins a new statement. All of this is on the basis that the verse is Medinan like the rest of the surah, and this is the correct view. Al-Tabari related from Ikrima and Mujahid that this verse is Makkan, and it is related from Ibn Zayd that it was revealed after Allah sufficed His Messenger against the mockers by what He brought upon each one of them, the well-known hadith. In my view, the statement of Ikrima and Mujahid that it is Makkan may be understood as referring to the story, not to the verse.

Makr (plotting) is subtle deception and cunning. You say, "So-and-so plots against so-and-so" when he lures him and drives him toward a pit, while showing good intentions and concealing what he intends. It is said: the root of makr is twisting (fatl), as Ibn Fawrak said, so the one who plots against a person is as if he twists with him until he brings him down. From makr in the sense of twisting comes their saying of a girl of moderate flesh: mamkurah (well-twisted). So the plotting of Quraysh against the Prophet (ﷺ) was their scheming for what would grieve him, their effort to corrupt his condition and extinguish his light. The plotting of Quraysh against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in these three forms had been ongoing from the beginning of his appearance, but their open declarations are not called makr; what they concealed is makr. Al-Tabari mentioned that Abu Talib said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "O Muhammad, what are your people plotting concerning you?" He said: "They want me to be killed, imprisoned, or expelled." Al-Zahrawi and Abdullah ibn Abi Qatada said: the occasion of its revelation was the affair of Abu Lubaba. He gestured to the Banu Qurayza, when he went to them, toward his throat, intending to inform them that the only thing left for them from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was slaughter, i.e., do not come down. Then he regretted it and tied himself to one of the pillars of the mosque until Allah accepted his repentance. This is the well-known hadith. Al-Tabari related that he remained for seven days without tasting anything until he was forgiven. It is also related that Abu Lubaba had property and children with them, and for this reason the verse ﴿And know that your wealth and your children are a trial﴾ was revealed.

Ata' ibn Abi Rabah related from Jabir ibn Abdullah: its occasion was that a man from the hypocrites wrote to Abu Sufyan ibn Harb with news of the affairs of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and so the verse was revealed. His saying, glorified is He, ﴿O you who have believed﴾ means: manifest faith. It may also be that it addresses those who truly believe, that they should not do the like of that hypocrite's act.

Al-Tabari related from al-Mughira ibn Shu'ba that he said: this verse was revealed concerning the killing of Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

It is likely that the verse is given as an example of the killing of Uthman, may Allah have mercy on him, for it was a betrayal of Allah, of the Messenger, and of the trusts. Betrayal (khiyana) is the diminishing of a thing by concealment. It is used for a person doing what is contrary to what should be done in guarding a matter, whether it is property, a secret, or otherwise. Betrayal of Allah, Exalted is He, is the diminishing of His commands in secret. Betrayal of the Messenger is the diminishing of what was entrusted to him, and betrayal of trusts (amanat) is their diminishing and their abandonment. A trust (amana) is a state of a person by which he is trusted with what he has been entrusted with; he has been entrusted with his religion, his worship, and the rights of others. It has been said: the meaning is ﴿and betray those who hold your trusts﴾, and I think al-Farisi, Abu Ali, related it. ﴿While you know﴾ means that the betrayal is not harmful to one except when it is done deliberately.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿fitna﴾ means a trial, a test, and an affliction, so that He may see how you act in all of that. His saying ﴿and that with Allah is a great reward﴾ means the success of the Hereafter. So do not leave your share of it out of concern for guarding your wealth and your children, for what is stored up for the Hereafter is greater in worth than the gains of this world.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿and betray﴾: al-Tabari said: it may be within the prohibition, as if He said: "Do not betray Allah and the Messenger, and do not betray your trusts." In this case its position is jussive (majzum). It may also be that the meaning is: "Do not betray Allah and the Messenger, for that is a betrayal of your trusts," in which case its position is accusative (nasb), with the sense of "and that you betray your trusts." The poet said:

*Do not forbid a trait while doing its like;*
*Shame upon you is great when you do it.*

Mujahid and Abu Amr ibn al-'Ala', as also related from him, read ﴿wa-takhunu amanatakum﴾ with the singular "amana."

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿O you who have believed, if you fear Allah﴾ and the verse that follows, is a promise to believers on condition of God-consciousness and obedience to Him. ﴿He will grant you a criterion (furqan)﴾ means: a distinction between your truth and the falsehood of those who dispute with you, that is, by victory and support over them. Furqan is a verbal noun from "faraqa bayna al-shay'ayn," when he separates the two or opposes their judgment, and from it is His saying: ﴿the Day of the Criterion﴾ [al-Anfal: 41]. Qatada and some exegetes rendered furqan here as deliverance. Al-Suddi and Mujahid said: its meaning is a way out, and similar to this, which is included in what we have mentioned. The Arabs do use furqan in the sense the exegetes mentioned. Among that is the saying of Mizrad ibn Dirar:

*The horizon hastened to set, but when*
*the night grew dark, it found no furqan.*

Another said:

*What remedy do you have against long grief?*
*Since the dwellers departed and went away.*

Another said:

*How can I hope for eternity when death pursues me,*
*and I have no furqan from the cup of death?*

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And [recall] when those who disbelieved plotted against you﴾ and the verse that follows: it is likely that His saying "wa-idh" is coordinated with His saying "idh antum qalil" (when you were few), and this is a reminder of the condition of Makkah and its narrowness with the disbelievers, and of Allah's beautiful handling in gathering them. It may also be that it begins a new statement. All of this is on the basis that the verse is Medinan like the rest of the surah, and this is the correct view. Al-Tabari related from Ikrima and Mujahid that this verse is Makkan, and it is related from Ibn Zayd that it was revealed after Allah sufficed His Messenger against the mockers by what He brought upon each one of them, the well-known hadith. In my view, the statement of Ikrima and Mujahid that it is Makkan may be understood as referring to the story, not to the verse.

Makr (plotting) is subtle deception and cunning. You say, "So-and-so plots against so-and-so" when he lures him and drives him toward a pit, while showing good intentions and concealing what he intends. It is said: the root of makr is twisting (fatl), as Ibn Fawrak said, so the one who plots against a person is as if he twists with him until he brings him down. From makr in the sense of twisting comes their saying of a girl of moderate flesh: mamkurah (well-twisted). So the plotting of Quraysh against the Prophet (ﷺ) was their scheming for what would grieve him, their effort to corrupt his condition and extinguish his light. The plotting of Quraysh against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in these three forms had been ongoing from the beginning of his appearance, but their open declarations are not called makr; what they concealed is makr. Al-Tabari mentioned that Abu Talib said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "O Muhammad, what are your people plotting concerning you?" He said: "They want me to be killed, imprisoned, or expelled." Abu Talib said: "Who informed you of this?" He said: "My Lord." He said: "Your Lord is indeed a Lord of truth, so ask Him to be good to you." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Rather, O uncle, He is the one who asks good of me."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

This plotting that Allah mentioned in this verse is, by the consensus (ijma') of the exegetes, a reference to the gathering of Quraysh in Dar al-Nadwa in the presence of Iblis in the form of an old man from Najd, as Ibn Ishaq stated in his Sira, the hadith in its full length. This is the event for which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) left Makkah. There is no disagreement that this was after the death of Abu Talib. In the story, Abu Jahl said: "The opinion is that we take from every clan of Quraysh a strong, vigorous youth, and they gather, then each one takes a sword and they come to Muhammad in his bed and strike him with the blow of one man. Then the Banu Hashim will not be able to fight all of Quraysh, so they will accept blood money, and we will be rid of him." The Najdi said: "The young man is right; I see no other opinion." So they dispersed on that. Allah informed His Prophet (ﷺ) of this and permitted him to leave for Madinah. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) left that very night and said to Ali ibn Abi Talib: "Wrap yourself in my Hadrami cloak and lie down in my bed, for nothing will harm you." Ali did so. The young men of Quraysh came and began to watch the figure and wait for him to rise, so they could attack him. When he rose, they saw Ali and said to him: "Where is your companion?" He said: "I do not know." In the biographies it is related that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out before them while they were on his path, and Allah blinded their eyes to him, and placed dust on the head of each of them, and he went on his way. A man came to them and said: "What are you waiting for?" They said: "Muhammad." He said: "I saw him just now coming from your direction, and he certainly placed dust on your heads." So each of them put his hand to his head, and they came to the Prophet's (ﷺ) bed and found Ali. Then they mounted and pursued him, every swift and tame mount, while he was in the cave.

The meaning of ﴿to restrain you (liyuthbitukа)﴾ is to imprison you so that you remain confined. This was said by al-Suddi, Ata', and Ibn Abi Kathir. Ibn Abbas and Mujahid said: its meaning is to bind you. Al-Tabari said: others said the meaning is to bewitch you.

Yahya ibn Wathhab, as mentioned by Abu Amr al-Dani, read "liyuthabbitukа" (with doubled tha'), and this is likewise a transitive form by intensification. al-Naqqash related from Yahya ibn Wathhab that he read "liyubayyitukа" from the verb bayt (to attack at night). This means taking him captive together with killing, so it is weaker in this respect. Abu Hatim said: the meaning of ﴿liyuthbitukа﴾ is by wounding, as one says "the wound fixed him in place (athbatat-hu al-jirahah)." al-Naqqash related this from the people of linguistics without naming anyone.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And Allah plots﴾ means: He does acts, among which is punishment for them, and among which is nullifying their plotting, repelling it, and pushing it back so that it does not succeed. All of this is named by the name of the offense for which it came. Nothing suits this meaning except this. As for attributing makr to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, in the sense understood in the language, it is not permissible to say it. Ibn Fawrak mentioned in this regard something close to what we have rejected. Our statement "And Allah plots" is like when you say of a man who insulted the emir and the emir killed him: "This is the insult," naming the punishment by the name of the offense. His saying, glorified is He, ﴿the best of plotters﴾ means: the most capable of them and the most powerful in standing.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

In this respect, I mean capability and power, comparison occurs, because the disbelievers' plotting has some capability, so the comparative form is used because they share in it. As for the aspect of goodness that is in what Allah, Exalted is He, knows, there is no sharing of goodness with the disbelievers, so comparison is impossible according to the position of Sibawayh and the Basrans, except as we have explained regarding general terms such as "good," "most beloved," and similar, since there is no one free from some sharing, even if only in a belief of a sect or of an individual.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 8, verse 31–32:

(p-174) His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿When Our verses are recited to them, they say, "We have heard. If we willed, we could say the like of this. This is nothing but the myths of the ancients."﴾ ﴿And when they said, "O Allah, if this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky, or bring us a painful punishment."﴾

The pronoun in "ʿalayhim" (upon them) refers to the disbelievers, and "the verses" (al-āyāt) here specifically means the verses of the Qur'an, by the indication of His saying "are recited" (tutlā). And "qad samiʿnā" (we have indeed heard) means: "We have indeed heard this recited material; if we willed, we could say the like of it, and we have heard its equivalent." This is in line with what is related: that al-Naḍr (al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith) heard the tales of the people of al-Ḥīra from the ʿIbād, so he said, "If we willed, we could say the like of it, of stories and prophets, for these are only the myths of those who came before, that is, their written and inscribed narratives." "Asāṭīr" (myths) is the plural of "usṭūra" (a tale). It may also be the plural of "asṭār", and it is not the plural of "asṭur" as al-Ṭabarī said, because the plural would then have come as "asāṭir" without a yāʾ; this is the general rule of this pattern, though something has deviated from it, such as "ṣayraf", whose plural they said is "ṣayārif".

What is widely transmitted through reports from Ibn Jurayj, al-Suddī, and Ibn Jubayr is that the one who uttered this statement was al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith. That is because he frequently travelled to Persia and al-Ḥīra, and he had heard the stories of the monks and the Gospels, and had heard the accounts of Rustam and Isfandiyar. When he heard the Qur'an and saw in it the reports of the prophets and the nations, he said, "If I wished, I could say the like of this." Al-Naḍr was among the rebellious leaders of Quraysh who harmed the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and verses of the Book of Allah were revealed concerning him. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ had him executed by patient killing (ṣabran) at al-Ṣafrāʾ, on his return from Badr, at a place called al-Uthayl. He had been captured by al-Miqdād. "When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ ordered his neck to be struck, al-Miqdād said, 'My captive, O Messenger of Allah!' (p-175) The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, 'He used to speak in the Book of Allah what you know.' Then al-Miqdād repeated his plea until the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, 'O Allah, enrich al-Miqdād from Your bounty.' Al-Miqdād said, 'This is what I wanted,' and he struck the neck of al-Naḍr."

Al-Ṭabarī related from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr that "the Messenger of Allah ﷺ killed three men by patient killing on the day of Badr: al-Muṭʿim ibn ʿAdī, al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith, and ʿUqba ibn Abī Muʿayṭ."

The author, Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is a great error regarding the report about al-Muṭʿim, for he had died before the day of Badr, and about him the Prophet ﷺ said: "If al-Muṭʿim had been alive and had spoken to me about these stinking ones [meaning the captives of Badr], I would have left them to him."

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when they said, "O Allah, if this is indeed the truth from You"﴾ and the rest of the verse, it is related from Mujāhid, Ibn Jubayr, ʿAṭāʾ, and al-Suddī that the one who uttered this statement was al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith mentioned above, and concerning him this verse was revealed.

The author, Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It follows that al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith made a statement and the Qur'an attributes it to all of them, because al-Naḍr was among them marked with intelligence and understanding, and they relied upon his opinion. When he said a statement, many of them said it with him and followed him in it, as people always do with their scholars and jurists. The one indicated by "this" (hādhā) is the Qur'an (p-176) and the law of Muḥammad ﷺ. What moved them to this statement was envy, for they found it implausible that Allah would bestow this honour upon Muḥammad ﷺ over them, and their insight was blinded from guidance. They insisted that this was not the truth, so they said this statement, just as a person says, regarding a matter he believes has not come to pass, "If such-and-such is the case, then may Allah do such-and-such to me." Ibn Fawrak related that this statement came out in the manner of obstinacy while they knew it to be true. Likewise some people of Yemen challenged Muʿāwiya ibn Abī Sufyān with the well-known story in the chapter on answers, and al-Ṭabarī related it from Muḥammad ibn Qays and Yazīd ibn Rūmān.

The author, Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This interpretation is far-fetched, and no sane person would say this in obstinacy. It is permissible in Arabic to read "al-ḥaqq" (the truth) in the nominative, as the predicate of "huwa", with the whole clause being the predicate of "kāna". Al-Zajjāj said: "I do not know of anyone who recited with this permissible reading; the recitation of the people is only with the accusative "al-ḥaqqa", as the predicate of "kāna", with "huwa" being a separating pronoun (faṣl). In that case it is a noun, and it carries the sense of informing that what follows it is a predicate and not an adjective." "Fa-amṭir" (then rain down) is used only for what is disliked, whereas "maṭara" is used for mercy; so said Abū ʿUbayda.

The author, Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is contradicted by His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿This is a cloud bringing us rain﴾ [al-Aḥqāf: 24], for they thought it was a cloud of mercy. And their saying "from the sky" (min al-samāʾ) is an exaggeration and an excess.

These two kinds of punishment which they demanded are the ones that befell the earlier nations. May Allah keep us safe, pardon us, and not let us go astray by His favour and His blessing.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 8, verse 33–34:

(p-177) The Most High said:

﴿And Allah would not punish them while you are among them, nor would Allah punish them while they seek forgiveness.﴾ ﴿And what is [the matter] with them that Allah should not punish them, while they bar [people] from the Sacred Mosque, and they were not its guardians? Its guardians are only the God-fearing, but most of them do not know.﴾

A group said: this whole verse was revealed in Mecca. Another group said: all of it was revealed after the Battle of Badr, as a narration of what had passed. Ibn Abza said: His saying, ﴿And Allah would not punish them while you are among them﴾, was revealed in Mecca following their saying, ﴿Or bring us a painful punishment﴾ [al-Anfal: 32]. His saying, ﴿nor would Allah punish them while they seek forgiveness﴾, was revealed when the Prophet ﷺ left Mecca on his way to Medina, while believers who were seeking forgiveness remained in Mecca. And His saying, ﴿And what is [the matter] with them﴾, to the end of the verse, was revealed after Badr when the punishment appeared upon them.

The judge Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

The commentators (al-mutaʾawwilun) agreed that the meaning of His saying, ﴿And Allah would not punish them while you are among them﴾, is that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, never punished a nation while its prophet was among them. So He would not punish this [nation] while you are among them; rather, your honour with Him is greater. He said, (I think it is narrated from Abu Zayd): I heard from the Arabs one who says, "ma kana Allahu liyuʿadhdhibahum" with a fatha on the lam, but this is a dialect that is neither well known nor used in the Qur'an.

They differed concerning the meaning of His saying, ﴿nor would Allah punish them while they seek forgiveness﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father), Ibn Abza, Abu Malik, and al-Dahhak said what it implies: the pronoun in His saying "muʿadhdhibahum" refers to the disbelievers of Mecca, and the pronoun in His saying "wa-hum" refers to the believers who remained in Mecca after the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, meaning: Allah would not punish the disbelievers while among them there are believers seeking forgiveness. (p-178)

The judge Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

This view is refuted at its outset, because the believers to whom the pronoun is returned have not been previously mentioned. Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father) also said, in what implies: both pronouns refer to the disbelievers, because they used to say in their supplication, "Ghufranaka" (Your forgiveness), and "Labbayka, la sharika laka" (Here I am, You have no partner), and similar things which are supplication and seeking forgiveness, so Allah made this a safeguard from the punishment of this world. On this basis the saying of Abu Musa al-Ashʿari and Ibn ʿAbbas is constructed: Allah placed two safeguards against the punishment of this world, the presence of the Messenger ﷺ among the people, and seeking forgiveness. The first was lifted, and seeking forgiveness remained until the Day of Resurrection. Qatada said: the pronoun refers to the disbelievers.

His saying, the Exalted, ﴿and they seek forgiveness﴾, is a clause in the position of a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl), if it were [so]. The meaning is: Allah would not punish them while they are in a state of repentance and seeking forgiveness for their disbelief, if that were to occur from them. Al-Tabari chose this view. Then, after this, the rebuke and the warning became fitting with His saying, ﴿And what is [the matter] with them that Allah should not punish them﴾.

Al-Zajjaj said in substance: the pronoun in His saying "wa-hum" refers to the disbelievers, and what is meant is whoever it had already been decreed in Allah's knowledge would embrace Islam and seek forgiveness. So the meaning is: Allah would not punish the disbelievers while among them is one who seeks forgiveness and believes in a later state. Al-Tabari related this from Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father).

Mujahid said in the book of al-Zahrawi: what is meant by His saying, ﴿and they seek forgiveness﴾, is the offspring of the polytheists on that day, who had been decreed in Allah's knowledge to become believers. So the meaning is: Allah would not punish them while their offspring seek forgiveness and believe, and the seeking of forgiveness is attributed to them because their offspring are of them. Makki mentioned it without attributing it.

In al-Tabari, from a group, the meaning of ﴿yastaghfirun﴾ is: they pray, and from another group: they submit to Islam, and similar sayings which come close to the saying of Qatada.

(p-179) His saying, the Mighty and Majestic, ﴿And what is [the matter] with them that Allah should not punish them﴾, is a threat of the punishment of this world. Its estimate is: "wa-ma yuʿlimuhum aw yudrihim" and similar verbs which require that "an" be in the accusative position. Al-Tabari said: its estimate is: "wa-ma yamnaʿuhum min an yuʿadhdhabu" (what prevents them from being punished). The apparent sense of "wa-ma" is that it is an interrogative, in the manner of affirmation, rebuke and questioning, and this is more eloquent in speech and more decisive against them in argument. It is also valid that "ma" be negating, and the statement be informative, meaning: "And it is not for them that they should not be punished while they bar [others]."

His saying:

﴿wa-hum yaṣuddūn﴾

On both interpretations it is a clause in the position of a circumstantial phrase. And ﴿yaṣuddūn﴾ in this place means: they prevent others, so it is transitive, as in the saying:

"You (f.) turned the cup away from us, Umm ʿAmr..."

And "ṣadda" may come intransitive, as Abu ʿAli recited:

"Khulayda turned away from us, she does not speak to us..."

The pronoun in His, the Glorified, saying ﴿awliyāʾahu﴾ refers back to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, from His saying ﴿Allah punish them﴾, or to the Sacred Mosque. All of this is sound, and the latter was narrated from al-Hasan, and the other pronoun follows the first.

His, the Most High, saying ﴿but most of them do not know﴾ means: they do not know that they are not His guardians, rather they think that they are His guardians. (p-180) As for His saying "aktharuhum" (most of them), and we find all of them with this description, it is an expression that is either: you may say that it is a word of specific application intended in a general sense, and this is common in the speech of the Arabs; from it Sibawayh related their saying, "Say, who says that?" while they mean: no one says it. Or you may say that by His saying "aktharuhum" He intended that [the Prophet] should know and be aware that among them and within them are people who had inclined toward faith and had attained knowledge, even if their outward appearance was disbelief, so He excluded them from the whole by His saying "aktharuhum." Such was the condition of Mecca and its people, for among them were al-ʿAbbas, Umm al-Fadl, and others.

Al-Tabari related from ʿIkrima: al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: His saying, ﴿And what is [the matter] with them that Allah should not punish them﴾, abrogates His saying, ﴿And Allah would not punish them while they seek forgiveness﴾.

The judge Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

In this there is room for scrutiny, because it is a report, and a report is not subject to abrogation.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 8, verse 33–34:

(p-177) The Most High said:

﴿And Allah would not punish them while you are among them, nor would Allah punish them while they seek forgiveness.﴾ ﴿And what is [the matter] with them that Allah should not punish them, while they bar [people] from the Sacred Mosque, and they were not its guardians? Its guardians are only the God-fearing, but most of them do not know.﴾

A group said: this whole verse was revealed in Mecca. Another group said: all of it was revealed after the Battle of Badr, as a narration of what had passed. Ibn Abza said: His saying, ﴿And Allah would not punish them while you are among them﴾, was revealed in Mecca following their saying, ﴿Or bring us a painful punishment﴾ [al-Anfal: 32]. His saying, ﴿nor would Allah punish them while they seek forgiveness﴾, was revealed when the Prophet ﷺ left Mecca on his way to Medina, while believers who were seeking forgiveness remained in Mecca. And His saying, ﴿And what is [the matter] with them﴾, to the end of the verse, was revealed after Badr when the punishment appeared upon them.

The judge Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

The commentators (al-mutaʾawwilun) agreed that the meaning of His saying, ﴿And Allah would not punish them while you are among them﴾, is that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, never punished a nation while its prophet was among them. So He would not punish this [nation] while you are among them; rather, your honour with Him is greater. He said, (I think it is narrated from Abu Zayd): I heard from the Arabs one who says, "ma kana Allahu liyuʿadhdhibahum" with a fatha on the lam, but this is a dialect that is neither well known nor used in the Qur'an.

They differed concerning the meaning of His saying, ﴿nor would Allah punish them while they seek forgiveness﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father), Ibn Abza, Abu Malik, and al-Dahhak said what it implies: the pronoun in His saying "muʿadhdhibahum" refers to the disbelievers of Mecca, and the pronoun in His saying "wa-hum" refers to the believers who remained in Mecca after the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, meaning: Allah would not punish the disbelievers while among them there are believers seeking forgiveness. (p-178)

The judge Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

This view is refuted at its outset, because the believers to whom the pronoun is returned have not been previously mentioned. Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father) also said, in what implies: both pronouns refer to the disbelievers, because they used to say in their supplication, "Ghufranaka" (Your forgiveness), and "Labbayka, la sharika laka" (Here I am, You have no partner), and similar things which are supplication and seeking forgiveness, so Allah made this a safeguard from the punishment of this world. On this basis the saying of Abu Musa al-Ashʿari and Ibn ʿAbbas is constructed: Allah placed two safeguards against the punishment of this world, the presence of the Messenger ﷺ among the people, and seeking forgiveness. The first was lifted, and seeking forgiveness remained until the Day of Resurrection. Qatada said: the pronoun refers to the disbelievers.

His saying, the Exalted, ﴿and they seek forgiveness﴾, is a clause in the position of a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl), if it were [so]. The meaning is: Allah would not punish them while they are in a state of repentance and seeking forgiveness for their disbelief, if that were to occur from them. Al-Tabari chose this view. Then, after this, the rebuke and the warning became fitting with His saying, ﴿And what is [the matter] with them that Allah should not punish them﴾.

Al-Zajjaj said in substance: the pronoun in His saying "wa-hum" refers to the disbelievers, and what is meant is whoever it had already been decreed in Allah's knowledge would embrace Islam and seek forgiveness. So the meaning is: Allah would not punish the disbelievers while among them is one who seeks forgiveness and believes in a later state. Al-Tabari related this from Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father).

Mujahid said in the book of al-Zahrawi: what is meant by His saying, ﴿and they seek forgiveness﴾, is the offspring of the polytheists on that day, who had been decreed in Allah's knowledge to become believers. So the meaning is: Allah would not punish them while their offspring seek forgiveness and believe, and the seeking of forgiveness is attributed to them because their offspring are of them. Makki mentioned it without attributing it.

In al-Tabari, from a group, the meaning of ﴿yastaghfirun﴾ is: they pray, and from another group: they submit to Islam, and similar sayings which come close to the saying of Qatada.

(p-179) His saying, the Mighty and Majestic, ﴿And what is [the matter] with them that Allah should not punish them﴾, is a threat of the punishment of this world. Its estimate is: "wa-ma yuʿlimuhum aw yudrihim" and similar verbs which require that "an" be in the accusative position. The apparent sense of "wa-ma" is that it is an interrogative, in the manner of affirmation, rebuke and questioning, and this is more eloquent in speech and more decisive against them in argument. It is also valid that "ma" be negating, and the statement be informative, meaning: "And it is not for them that they should not be punished while they bar [others]."

His saying:

﴿wa-hum yaṣuddūn﴾

On both interpretations it is a clause in the position of a circumstantial phrase. And ﴿yaṣuddūn﴾ in this place means: they prevent others, so it is transitive, as in the saying:

"You (f.) turned the cup away from us, Umm ʿAmr..."

And "ṣadda" may come intransitive, as Abu ʿAli recited:

"Khulayda turned away from us, she does not speak to us..."

(p-180) As for His saying "aktharuhum" (most of them), and we find all of them with this description, it is an expression that is either: you may say that it is a word of specific application intended in a general sense, and this is common in the speech of the Arabs; from it Sibawayh related their saying, "Say, who says that?" while they mean: no one says it.
