The judge Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

In this there is room for scrutiny, because it is a report, and a report is not subject to abrogation.

The commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya on surah 8, verse 35:

Allah the Mighty and Majestic says:

﴿Their prayer at the House was nothing but whistling and clapping. So taste the punishment because you used to disbelieve.﴾

The majority of readers (al-jumhur) read "wa-ma kana ṣalātuhum" with a nominative (raf') ending on ṣalātuhum, and "ʿinda al-bayti illā mukāʾan" with an accusative (naṣb) ending on mukāʾan, and "wa-taṣdiyatan" likewise in the accusative. It is related from ʿĀṣim that he read "ṣalātahum" in the accusative and "illā mukāʾun wa-taṣdiyatun" in the nominative. It is also related from Sulaymān al-Aʿmash, with a variant from him, as Abū Ḥātim reported. Abū ʿAlī reported from al-Aʿmash that he said, regarding ʿĀṣim's reading: "If ʿĀṣim makes a grammatical error, do you make one?" Abū al-Fatḥ said: this letter has also been related in this way from Abān ibn Taghlib. Some people said: this reading is an error, because it makes the subject indefinite (nakira) and the predicate definite (maʿrifa). Abū Ḥātim said: if it is said that "al-mukāʾa and al-taṣdiyata" (p-181) are a noun of genus (ism jins), and the noun of genus, whether definite or indefinite, is one in definiteness, it is replied: its use in this way is not permissible except in the necessity of poetry, as Ḥassān said:

"As if a wine from the house of Ras, whose mixture is honey and water."

This is not to be analogized upon.

As for Abū al-Fatḥ, he justified this reading by what we have mentioned about the definiteness of the noun of genus, and after that he preferred the reading of the people.

Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī said: those who went to this reading did so only because they saw that the verb is feminine, since "al-ṣalāh" is feminine, and they saw that the predicate attached to it has no feminine marker, so they wanted to attach it to a masculine noun, namely "al-mukāʾ". In this they erred, for the Arabs attach a verb that has no marker to a feminine noun. From this is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And the Blast seized those who did wrong﴾ (Hud 67), and His saying, glorified is He: ﴿So see how was the outcome of their plot﴾ (al-Naml 51), and "how was the outcome of the corrupters" (kayfa kāna ʿāqibata al-mufsidīn), and similar to this, where the verb is attributed without a marker to a feminine noun.

Al-mukāʾ, on the pattern fiʿāl, is whistling. This is said by Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, and the majority. It may be with the mouth, and it may be with the fingers and the palm in the mouth. Mujāhid and Abū Salama ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān said: the nose may also take part. It is said: makā yamkū, when one whistles. From this is the saying of ʿAntara:

"And the husband of a lady of beauty, I left him stretched out, whose wind-pipe whistles like the cheek of the one with a cleft lip."

From this is the saying of the poet:

"As if he whistles with a white-footed, wise (wild ass)..." (a line describing a man to whom an animal fled).

From this is the saying of al-Ṭirimmāḥ:

"So he turned toward the first of them with a thrust of one on guard, whose sides whistle from the streams."

And the anus of the animal whistled (makat istu al-dābba) when it made a sound; it is said: "and nothing whistles except an uncovered anus." From this the word "makwa" is said for the anus. Abū ʿAlī said: the hamza in mukāʾ is changed from a waw.

The judge Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

From this the bird is called al-mukkāʾ, because it whistles (yamkū), that is, it makes a sound in its warbling. Its pattern is fuʿʿāl with a doubled ʿayn, like khuṭṭāf. Sounds for the most part come in the pattern fuʿāl with a light ʿayn, like al-bukāʾ, al-ṣurākh, al-duʿāʾ, al-juʾār, al-nubāḥ and similar. It is related from Qatāda that al-mukāʾ is the sound of hands, but this is weak. It is related from Abū ʿAmr that he read "illā makā" with a shortened vowel.

As for "al-taṣdiya", most people explained it as clapping (al-taṣfīq). Qatāda explained it as clamour and shouting. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr explained it as obstruction and prevention. Those who said it is clapping said: it was only to prevent remembrance of Allah and to oppose the recitation of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) of the Qur'an. The word taṣdiya may be from ṣadā yaṣdā, when it makes a sound, and al-ṣadā is sound. From this is the saying of al-Ṭirimmāḥ describing the wild cow:

"For her, whenever she is startled, an echo and a stillness, in Miṣrān, above the two peaks of Shamām al-Bawāʾin."

According to this derivation, the saying of the one who said it is clapping, and the saying of the one who said it is clamour, come together. The saying of the one who said it is obstruction and prevention does not come together with it, unless it is said that vocalizing is only intended for prevention, so the word is explained by its intended purpose and not by what is specific to its meaning.

It is possible that "al-taṣdiya" is from ṣadda yaṣuddu, the verb used doubled for intensity and multiplication and not to make it transitive, so it is said ṣaddada. This is because a verb that is transitive, when doubled, is doubled for multiplication, since transitivity is already present before doubling. This is like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and she bolted the doors﴾ (Yusuf 23). What is doubled to make it transitive is like their saying ʿallama and gharrama. So when we say of ṣadda: ṣaddada, the regular verb's verbal noun (maṣdar) comes in most cases in the pattern tafʿīl, and in fewer cases in the pattern tafʿila, like kammala takmīlan and takmila, and other such. Unlike the defective verb, which in most cases comes in the pattern tafʿila, like ʿazzā taʿziyatan, and in rare cases in the pattern tafʿīl, like the saying of the poet:

"He spent the night pulling his bucket in a pulling..."

When a verb in the regular form has two identical radicals, the pattern tafʿila is dropped for it, like our saying taṣdiya, and it is changed to tafʿīl so that the yā' separates the two identical letters, as in takhfīf and tashdīd. So when they took the verbal noun of ṣaddada the dropped way, it was corrected by changing one of the two identical letters into yā', as they did in tazannantu and similar, and so it came as taṣdiya. On this derivation, the saying of the one who said: al-taṣdiya is preventing from the House and obstruction, comes together.

It is possible also that taṣdiya is from ṣadda yaṣiddu (with a kasra on the sad in the imperfect), when it cries out, and in this case too one of the two identical letters is changed. Among this is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿when your people from it turn away﴾ (al-Zukhruf 57) with a kasra on the sad, mentioned by al-Naḥḥās.

Most exegetes went to the view that al-mukāʾ and al-taṣdiya were introduced by the disbelievers at the time of the sending of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), in order to cut off his recitation and the prayer of him and the believers, and to confuse them. So when a believer stood to recite, there would be gathered around him from the disbelievers, on his right and left, those who whistled and clapped until his recitation was confused. (p-185) So when Allah negated their guardianship over the House, it was possible for an objector to say: "How then are we not its guardians, when we dwell in it and pray at it?" So Allah cut off this objection by saying: "Their prayer was nothing but whistling and clapping." This is like a man saying: "I do good," and it is said to him: "Your doing good is only that you drink wine and kill," that is, this is your habit and your end.

The judge Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

What has reached me of the affairs of the Arabs, outside what is recorded, is that al-mukāʾ and al-taṣdiya were practices of the Arabs in ancient times before Islam, as a way of seeking nearness (to their gods) and making it a religious practice. I have seen it reported from some of the strong Arabs that he would whistle on al-Ṣafā, and it would be heard from the mountain of Ḥirāʾ, and between them is a distance of four miles. On this basis their reproach and disparagement is correct, that their law, their prayer and their worship were not out of awe nor out of desire, but were only whistling and clapping, of the kind of play. Yet they would multiply these during the time of the Prophet (ﷺ) in order to occupy him and his community from the recitation and the prayer.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So taste the punishment because you used to disbelieve﴾ is an indication of their punishment at Badr by the sword, as said by Ibn Jurayj, al-Ḥasan and al-Ḍaḥḥāk. From this it follows that this last verse was revealed after Badr, certainly.

The judge Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The more probable view is that all of it was revealed after Badr, as a narration of what had passed. And Allah is the Guardian of success, by His mercy.

(p-186) The Exalted said:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve spend their wealth to averted from the way of Allah. They will spend it, then it will become a regret for them, then they will be overcome. And those who disbelieve will be gathered to Hell.﴾

Some narrators, among them Ibn Abza, Ibn Jubayr, al-Suddi and Mujahid, said: The occasion of the revelation of this verse was that Abu Sufyan spent forty ounces of gold, or about that, on the Ahabish (the confederate tribes) and others during the Battle of Uhud, and the verse was revealed concerning that.

Ibn Shihab, Muhammad ibn Yahya ibn Hayyan, Asim ibn Umar ibn Qatada, and al-Husayn ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Amr ibn Sa'd ibn Mu'adh said: When those who were killed at Badr were killed, their sons and relatives gathered and said to those whose wealth had been saved in the caravan: "Muhammad has inflicted upon us what you see. But help us with this wealth which was the cause of the event, so that perhaps we may obtain vengeance from him." So they did, and the verse was revealed concerning that.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

On both accounts, the wealth was spent at the Battle of Uhud. In this verse, Allah the Exalted informs of a report whose wording is general concerning the disbelievers, while the reference is to particular people: that they spend their wealth intending thereby to averted from the way of Allah and to repel (Islam) in the early days of Islam. Then He informed of a report that specifically concerns those referred to: that they will spend it, then it will become a regret for them, since their intention will not be accomplished and the wealth will go to waste. Al-hasra (regret) is grief over what has been lost. It is possible that the regret will be on the Day of Resurrection, but the first is more apparent, although the regret of the Resurrection will be constant upon them. This is from the Qur'an's reports of the unseen, for it informed of what would happen before it happened, and so it was as it informed. Ibn Salam said: Allah the Mighty and Majestic made clear that they would be overcome a year before they fought. This was related by al-Zahrawi.

Then Allah the Exalted informed concerning the disbelievers that they will be gathered (yuhsharun) to Hell. Al-hashr is the gathering of people and beasts and other things that are gathered and brought forth. From it is the saying of the Blessed and Exalted: ﴿And We gathered upon them every thing in front of them﴾ [al-An'am: 111]. And from it, in the exegesis, is that the quail (al-salwa) is a bird which the south wind used to gather (tahshuruhu) for the Children of Israel. The people whom Abu Sufyan brought and on whom he spent the wealth were the Ahabish from Kinana. Concerning them Ka'b ibn Malik said:(p-187)

"We came to a wave of the sea, in its midst
The Ahabish, some of them bareheaded and some helmeted.
Three thousand, and we are a small band,
Three hundred, or four if we are more."

Al-Dahhak and others said: This verse was revealed concerning the expenditure of the polytheists who went out to Badr, who used to slaughter ten camels one day and nine the next. Al-Naqqash related something similar to this.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 8, verses 37–40:**

His Exalted and Majestic Lord said:

﴿That Allah may distinguish the wicked from the good, and place the wicked on top of one another, heap them all together, and put them into Hell. Those are the losers.﴾ ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: If they desist, what has passed will be forgiven them; but if they return, the precedent of the former peoples has already gone before.﴾ ﴿And fight them until there is no more fitnah and religion is entirely for Allah. But if they desist, then indeed Allah is Seeing of what they do.﴾ ﴿And if they turn away, know that Allah is your Protector; an excellent Protector and an excellent Helper.﴾

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', 'Asim, Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir recited "liyamiza" (لِيَمِيزَ) with a fatha on the yā' and a kasra on the mīm. This is the reading of al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far, Shayba ibn Nisah, Shibl, Abu 'Abd al-Rahman, al-Hasan, 'Ikrima and Malik ibn Dinar. One says mistu al-shay' (مِزْتُ الشَيْءَ, "I separated the thing"), and the Arabs say mistuhu fa-lam yatamayyaz li (مِزْتُهُ فَلَمْ يَتَمَيَّزْ لِي, "I separated it but it did not become distinct to me"). This is reported by Ya'qub. In the irregular (shādhdh) readings there is "wa-inmazu al-yawm" (وانْمازُوا اليَوْمَ, "and separate yourselves today"). Abu Zayd recited:

> When Allah turned from me the evil of his enemy,
> I separated, neither causing terror nor fearful.

Its form is the intransitive (muṭāwi') of māza (مازَ).

Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited "liyumayyiza" (لِيُمَيِّزَ) with a ḍamma on the yā', a fatha on the mīm and a shadda on the yā'. This is the reading of Qatada, Talha ibn Musarrif, al-A'mash, also al-Hasan, and 'Isa al-Basri. One says mayyaztu uməyyizu (مَيَّزْتُ أُمَيِّزُ) when you separate two things or more. In the Qur'an: ﴿tamayyazu min al-ghayz﴾ ("it almost bursts with rage") [al-Mulk: 8]. It is the intransitive of mayyaza (مَيَّزَ), and its meaning is "to be separated" (تَنْفَصِلُ). Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, and al-Suddi said: "The wicked" (al-khabīth) refers to the disbelievers, and "the good" (al-ṭayyib) refers to the believers.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

On this interpretation, the lām in "liyamiza" (لِيَمِيزَ) is connected to "yuhsharun" (يُحْشَرُونَ) [al-Anfal: 36]. The meaning is that Allah gathers the disbelievers to Hell in order to separate the disbelievers from the believers, by bringing the disbelievers together and casting them into Hell.

Then He informed of them that they are "the losers" (al-khāsirūn), meaning those whose efforts have failed, whose hands have perished, and who have gone to the Fire. Ibn Salam and al-Zajjaj said: "The wicked" refers to the wealth that the polytheists spent in barring from the path of Allah, and "the good" is what the believers spent in the path of Allah.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

On this interpretation, the lām in "liyamiza" is connected to "yughlabun" (يُغْلَبُونَ) [al-Anfal: 36]. The meaning is that the disbelievers spend their wealth, and it becomes a regret for them, then they are overcome along with its expenditure. This happens so that Allah may distinguish the difference between the wicked and the good, abandoning the people of wickedness and granting victory to the people of goodness. His words, on this interpretation, ﴿and place the wicked on top of one another﴾ up to ﴿into Hell﴾ are a consequence of what has been narrated from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "Allah, the Exalted, will bring out on the Day of Resurrection the wealth that was given in charity or for the sake of nearness to Allah, then He will command the rest of that wealth and it will be cast into the Fire." Al-Zahrawi reported from al-Hasan that the disbelievers will be punished with that wealth, and this is like His saying: ﴿so their foreheads, their sides and their backs will be branded with it﴾ [al-Tawbah: 35]. Al-Zajjaj also said this. On both interpretations, His saying ﴿and place the wicked on top of one another, heap them all together﴾ is simply an expression for gathering that, collecting it, and compacting its scattered parts into a dense mass by bringing them together.

"Yarkumuhu" (يَرْكُمُهُ) in the language of the Arabs means "to make it dense" (يُكَثِّفُهُ). From this comes ﴿a heaped-up cloud﴾ [al-Tur: 44] and rukām (رُكامٌ, "heaped sand"). From it is also the verse of Dhu al-Rummah:

> ................... Drive with the reins, and the night's bulk is heaped up.

His saying ﴿and place the wicked﴾ (وَيَجْعَلَ الخَبِيثَ) means "cast" (يُلْقِي), as Abu 'Ali said. Then Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿But if they desist﴾, meaning from disbelief, then indeed Allah is Seeing of their deeds, recompensing them for it. With Him is its reward and the gracious requital for it. Ya'qub ibn Ishaq and Salam ibn Sulayman recited "bi-mā taʿmalūna" (بِما تَعْمَلُونَ) with the letter tā' (you), meaning: in your fighting, your striving and your battling in defence of His religion.

His saying ﴿And if they turn away﴾ and the rest of the verse is parallel to His saying ﴿But if they desist﴾. The meaning is: if they desist from disbelief, then Allah will recompense them, or will recompense you according to the reading "taʿmalūna." And if they turn away, know that Allah will grant you victory over them. This is a pure promise of help and triumph, meaning: so strive.

Here "al-mawlā" (المَوْلى) means "the one who befriends and helps." Among the various meanings of al-mawlā in the language, this is the one that fits this place. The mawlā in the sense of "master" (al-sayyid) who is joined to the slave is general, encompassing both believers and polytheists.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 8, verses 37–40:**

His Exalted and Majestic Lord said:

﴿That Allah may distinguish the wicked from the good, and place the wicked on top of one another, heap them all together, and put them into Hell. Those are the losers.﴾ ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: If they desist, what has passed will be forgiven them; but if they return, the precedent of the former peoples has already gone before.﴾ ﴿And fight them until there is no more fitnah and religion is entirely for Allah. But if they desist, then indeed Allah is Seeing of what they do.﴾ ﴿And if they turn away, know that Allah is your Protector; an excellent Protector and an excellent Helper.﴾

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', 'Asim, Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir recited "liyamiza" (لِيَمِيزَ) with a fatha on the yā' and a kasra on the mīm. This is the reading of al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far, Shayba ibn Nisah, Shibl, Abu 'Abd al-Rahman, al-Hasan, 'Ikrima and Malik ibn Dinar. One says mistu al-shay' (مِزْتُ الشَيْءَ, "I separated the thing"), and the Arabs say mistuhu fa-lam yatamayyaz li (مِزْتُهُ فَلَمْ يَتَمَيَّزْ لِي, "I separated it but it did not become distinct to me"). This is reported by Ya'qub. In the irregular (shādhdh) readings there is "wa-inmazu al-yawm" (وانْمازُوا اليَوْمَ, "and separate yourselves today"). Abu Zayd recited:

> When Allah turned from me the evil of his enemy,
> I separated, neither causing terror nor fearful.

Its form is the intransitive (muṭāwi') of māza (مازَ).

Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited "liyumayyiza" (لِيُمَيِّزَ) with a ḍamma on the yā', a fatha on the mīm and a shadda on the yā'. This is the reading of Qatada, Talha ibn Musarrif, al-A'mash, also al-Hasan, and 'Isa al-Basri. One says mayyaztu uməyyizu (مَيَّزْتُ أُمَيِّزُ) when you separate two things or more. In the Qur'an: ﴿tamayyazu min al-ghayz﴾ ("it almost bursts with rage") [al-Mulk: 8]. It is the intransitive of mayyaza (مَيَّزَ), and its meaning is "to be separated" (تَنْفَصِلُ). Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, and al-Suddi said: "The wicked" (al-khabīth) refers to the disbelievers, and "the good" (al-ṭayyib) refers to the believers.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

On this interpretation, the lām in "liyamiza" (لِيَمِيزَ) is connected to "yuhsharun" (يُحْشَرُونَ) [al-Anfal: 36]. The meaning is that Allah gathers the disbelievers to Hell in order to separate the disbelievers from the believers, by bringing the disbelievers together and casting them into Hell.

Then He informed of them that they are "the losers" (al-khāsirūn), meaning those whose efforts have failed, whose hands have perished, and who have gone to the Fire. Ibn Salam and al-Zajjaj said: "The wicked" refers to the wealth that the polytheists spent in barring from the path of Allah, and "the good" is what the believers spent in the path of Allah.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

On this interpretation, the lām in "liyamiza" is connected to "yughlabun" (يُغْلَبُونَ) [al-Anfal: 36]. The meaning is that the disbelievers spend their wealth, and it becomes a regret for them, then they are overcome along with its expenditure. This happens so that Allah may distinguish the difference between the wicked and the good, abandoning the people of wickedness and granting victory to the people of goodness. His words, on this interpretation, ﴿and place the wicked on top of one another﴾ up to ﴿into Hell﴾ are a consequence of what has been narrated from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "Allah, the Exalted, will bring out on the Day of Resurrection the wealth that was given in charity or for the sake of nearness to Allah, then He will command the rest of that wealth and it will be cast into the Fire." Al-Zahrawi reported from al-Hasan that the disbelievers will be punished with that wealth, and this is like His saying: ﴿so their foreheads, their sides and their backs will be branded with it﴾ [al-Tawbah: 35]. Al-Zajjaj also said this. On both interpretations, His saying ﴿and place the wicked on top of one another, heap them all together﴾ is simply an expression for gathering that, collecting it, and compacting its scattered parts into a dense mass by bringing them together.

"Yarkumuhu" (يَرْكُمُهُ) in the language of the Arabs means "to make it dense" (يُكَثِّفُهُ). From this comes ﴿a heaped-up cloud﴾ [al-Tur: 44] and rukām (رُكامٌ, "heaped sand"). From it is also the verse of Dhu al-Rummah:

> ................... Drive with the reins, and the night's bulk is heaped up.

His saying ﴿and place the wicked﴾ (وَيَجْعَلَ الخَبِيثَ) means "cast" (يُلْقِي), as Abu 'Ali said. And ﴿those are the losers﴾ (أُولَئِكَ هُمُ الخاسِرُونَ), on this interpretation, refers to the hypocrites among the disbelievers, and the word "loss" (al-khasārah) is fitting for them in respect of wealth and in other respects.

His saying ﴿Say to those who disbelieve﴾ and the rest of the verse is a command from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, to His Prophet ﷺ to say to the disbelievers this meaning, which is contained in the words ﴿if they desist, what has passed will be forgiven them﴾. It makes no difference whether the Prophet ﷺ said it in this phrasing or another. Even if the wording were as al-Kisa'i mentioned, that in the codex of Ibn Mas'ud it reads: "Say to those who disbelieve: If they desist, what has passed will be forgiven you," the message would only have been fulfilled with those exact words. This is according to what the wording requires. His saying ﴿if they desist﴾ means desisting from disbelief, without doubt. What necessitates this is the answer of the condition: ﴿what has passed will be forgiven them﴾, and forgiveness of what has passed is only for one who has desisted from disbelief. His saying ﴿but if they return﴾ ("in āda") means "return" to fighting, because the word "ʿāda yaʿūdu" (عادَ يَعُودُ), when used without qualification, implies a return to a state in which the person was before and from which he then moved away. We find in this verse no state for these disbelievers resembling what we have mentioned, except fighting. It is not valid to interpret it as "if they return to disbelief," because they had not separated from it. We said "when unqualified" because the word ʿāda may occur in the language of the Arabs governing a subject and predicate, in the sense of "ṣāra" (صارَ, "became"). This is like your saying: "ʿĀda Zayd malikan" (عادَ زَيْدٌ مَلِكًا), meaning "Zayd became a king." From it is the verse of Abu al-Salt:

> Those are noble deeds, not two bowls of milk
> Mixed with water, then they became urine.

This does not imply a return to a state the one returning had been in before, but it is restricted by its predicate, which cannot be omitted, so its ruling is that of "ṣāra."

His saying ﴿then the precedent of the former peoples has already gone before﴾ combines the threat, the warning, and the example of the nations that perished in ancient times by the punishment of Allah when they turned away from the face of His Prophet, and of those who perished on the day of Badr by the sword of Islam and the Law. The meaning is: "You have seen and heard about the nations what befell them."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The warning to them by the story of Badr is more severe, because it is the nearest to them and the thing they witnessed directly. Ibn Ishaq and al-Suddi stated this explicitly.

His saying ﴿And fight them until there is no more fitnah﴾ and the rest of the verse is a command from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, by which it became obligatory upon the believers to fight the disbelievers. As for "fitnah" (الفِتْنَةُ): Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, and others said its meaning is shirk (polytheism). Ibn Ishaq said its meaning is: until no one is tempted away from his religion, as the Quraysh used to do in Makkah to those who embraced Islam, such as Bilal and others. This is what is implied by the answer of 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr to 'Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan when he asked him about the emigration of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ from Makkah.

His saying ﴿and religion is entirely for Allah﴾ means: no idol or false god is associated with Him, and nothing else is worshipped. Qatada said: until the word of sincerity, "There is no god but Allah," becomes widespread.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

All these meanings are mutually implicative. Al-Hasan said: until there is no trial (balā'). On this interpretation, fighting is required against the rebellious faction (al-fi'ah al-bāghiyah) in the strife among the Muslims. On all the other sayings we have mentioned, the one who withdraws is in a state of ease. This is also the view expressed by the saying of 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him: "As for us, we fought until there was no fitnah, but as for you and your companions, you want us to fight until there is fitnah."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The view of 'Umar is that fitnah in this verse is shirk, and this is the apparent meaning. The saying of the Prophet ﷺ explains this verse: "I have been commanded to fight the people until they say: There is no god but Allah. When they say it, they have protected their blood and their wealth from me, except by its right, and their reckoning is with Allah." As for the one who said the meaning is "until there is no shirk," the verse, in his view, refers to a specific group, namely those from whom the jizyah (poll-tax) is not accepted. Ibn Salam said: it concerns the polytheists of the Arabs.

Then Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿But if they desist﴾, meaning from disbelief, then indeed Allah is Seeing of their deeds, recompensing them for it. With Him is its reward and the gracious requital for it. Ya'qub ibn Ishaq and Salam ibn Sulayman recited "bi-mā taʿmalūna" (بِما تَعْمَلُونَ) with the letter tā' (you), meaning: in your fighting, your striving and your battling in defence of His religion.

His saying ﴿And if they turn away﴾ and the rest of the verse is parallel to His saying ﴿But if they desist﴾. The meaning is: if they desist from disbelief, then Allah will recompense them, or will recompense you according to the reading "taʿmalūna." And if they turn away, know that Allah will grant you victory over them. This is a pure promise of help and triumph, meaning: so strive.

Here "al-mawlā" (المَوْلى) means "the one who befriends and helps." Among the various meanings of al-mawlā in the language, this is the one that fits this place. The mawlā in the sense of "master" (al-sayyid) who is joined to the slave is general, encompassing both believers and polytheists.

(p-192) His saying, may He be exalted:

﴿And know that whatever you obtain as spoils of war, a fifth of it belongs to God, and to the Messenger, and to the near relatives, and the orphans, and the needy, and the wayfarer, if you have believed in God and in what We sent down to Our servant on the Day of the Criterion, the day the two hosts met. And God is over all things competent.﴾

The position of the second "anna" (that) is in the nominative case. The implied phrase is "so its ruling is that," and it stands in the position of the predicate of the inchoative (mubtada'). The ghanima (spoils) linguistically means what a man or a group obtains through effort. From this is the verse of the poet:

"I have traversed the horizons until I was content with the spoils of returning."

Another poet said:

"The one who feeds on spoils, on the day of spoils, his food is his, wherever he goes, and the one deprived is deprived."

From the same root is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning the pledge: "Its gain is for him, and its risk is upon him." And his saying: "Fasting in winter is the cold spoils." So whatever the Muslims obtain from their enemy through effort and by pressing horses and camels is ghanima, and this name became attached to this meaning until it became its customary usage.

The fay' (booty acquired without battle) is derived from "faa'a yafee'u," meaning he returned. It is everything that comes to the Muslims without war or pressing, such as the kharaj (land tax) of the land, the jizya (poll tax) of the heads, the fifth of the ghanima, and the like.

[p-193] Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

The zakat is also a separate wealth with its own rulings, distinct from the rulings of these two. Sufyan al-Thawri and 'Ata' ibn al-Sa'ib said: "The ghanima is what is taken by force, and the fay' is what is taken by agreement." This is close to what we have explained. Qatada said: "The fay' and the ghanima are one thing, and in both is the fifth." He also said: this verse in al-Anfal abrogates (naskh) His saying in Surat al-Hashr: ﴿What God has returned to His Messenger from the people of the towns﴾ [al-Hashr: 7]. That is because the ruling in that verse was first, then God gave its people only the fifth, and placed the four-fifths for the fighters.

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This is a weak opinion, which the scholars have explicitly declared weak, and it has no basis from several aspects. Among them: this surah was revealed before Surat al-Hashr; this one concerns Badr, and that one concerns the Banu al-Nadir and the villages of 'Urayna. Also, the two verses agree, and the ruling of the fifth and the ruling of that verse are one, because it was revealed concerning the Banu al-Nadir when they went into exile and fled, and the people of Fadak when they were invited to a settlement, and the Muslims obtained what was theirs without pressing. Ibn al-Mundhir related from al-Shafi'i that in the fay' there is a fifth, and that this occurred in the villages of 'Urayna during the time of the Prophet (ﷺ), and that four-fifths of them were for the Messenger of God (ﷺ) alone, to the exclusion of the Muslims, to place wherever he willed.

Abu 'Ubayda said: this verse abrogates His saying, exalted is He, at the beginning of the surah: ﴿Say: the spoils belong to God and the Messenger﴾ [al-Anfal: 1], and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) did not take a fifth of the spoils of Badr, so his ruling regarding not taking the fifth was abrogated by this verse.

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

What appears from the words of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him, in al-Bukhari: "I had a she-camel from my share of the booty at Badr, and another she-camel that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) gave me from the fifth at that time," indicates that the spoils of Badr were divided into fifths. If this is so, Abu 'Ubayda's view is invalid. It is possible that the fifth that 'Ali ibn Abi Talib mentioned was from one of the expeditions between Badr and Uhud. There were the expedition of Banu Sulaym, the expedition of al-Sawiq, the expedition of Dhi Amr, and the expedition of Bahran, in which no fighting is recorded, but it is possible that spoils were taken. And God knows best.

His saying, exalted is He, in this verse: ﴿from anything﴾ — its apparent meaning is general, but its intended meaning is specific. As for cash, goods, children, women, and animals whose meat is not eaten and which may be lawfully owned, the imam has no right in all of that, whether much or little, such as thread and sewn garments, except that he takes the fifth and divides the rest among the army. As for land, Malik said: the imam divides it if he sees that as correct, as the Prophet (ﷺ) did with Khaybar, and does not divide it if his judgment leads him not to, as 'Umar, may God be pleased with him, did with the land of Egypt and the fertile land of Kufa.

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

Because the action of 'Umar, may God be pleased with him, does not contradict the action of the Prophet (ﷺ), since the circumstance was not one and the same, given the differing conditions of the two periods, the needs and the small numbers of the Companions. All of this was reversed in the time of 'Umar, may God be pleased with him. As for the men and the boys who have approached puberty, the imam, according to Malik and the majority of scholars, has the choice regarding them in five ways. Among them: killing, which is recommended for those of courage and effective strength; ransom (fida'), which is recommended for one of high station who is not brave and whose opinion or scheming is not feared, in order that the Muslims benefit from the wealth taken from him; release without ransom (mann), which is recommended for one who is hoped to show kindness toward Muslim captives and similar circumstances; enslavement; and imposing the jizya and leaving him in protected status (dhimma). As for food, sheep, and the like, which are eaten, they are permitted in the land of the enemy, and people eat them; what remains is part of the booty.

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

As for the four-fifths of what is seized, the imam divides it among the army. The mention of the division does not belong specifically to this verse, so I shall abridge it here. As for the fifth, the scholars have differed about it.

Malik, may God have mercy on him, said: the matter concerning it is for the imam; he places it in the fay' treasury, and gives from that treasury to the relatives of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) whatever he sees fit, just as he gives from it to the orphans, the needy, and others. The reason that the one who mentioned them did so was to draw attention to them, since they are among the most important recipients. Al-Zajjaj, arguing in support of Malik, said: God, exalted is He, said: ﴿They ask you what they should spend. Say: whatever good you spend is for the parents and the near relatives, the orphans, the needy, and the wayfarer﴾ [al-Baqara: 215]. And the imam, by consensus (ijma'), may spend on other categories than these when he sees fit.

A group said: the fifth was divided into six portions: a portion for God, which is returned to the poor Muslims or to the House of God; a portion for the Prophet (ﷺ); a portion for his relatives; and a portion for the rest of those named. Mundhir ibn Sa'id related this view and it was refuted. Abu al-'Aliya al-Riyahi said: the Prophet (ﷺ) would take a handful from the fifth of the spoils and place it for the Ka'ba, and that is for God; then he divided the rest into five: a portion for himself, and a portion for the rest of those named.

Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad, Ibn 'Abbas, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, Qatada, and al-Shafi'i said: His saying, ﴿that for God is its fifth﴾, is the opening of a statement, as a man says to his slave: "God has freed you, and I have freed you," for the sake of blessing and magnifying the matter. The whole world belongs to God, and the portion of God and the portion of the Messenger are one, and the Messenger, peace be upon him, divided the fifth into five portions, as has been mentioned.

Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, also said, as al-Tabari transmitted from him: the fifth is divided into four portions, and the Messenger of God's portion is for his relatives; there is nothing for God or for the Messenger.

A group said: after the death of the Messenger (ﷺ), his portion is returned to the people of the fifth, the relatives and others. Another group said: it is returned to the army, the companions of the four-fifths. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him, said: the imam takes from them the portion of God and His Messenger. Another group said: it is held in reserve for purchasing weapons and horses in the cause of God.

Ibrahim al-Nakha'i said: this is what Abu Bakr and 'Umar, may God be pleased with them both, chose regarding it.

The People of Opinion (ahl al-ra'y) said: after the Prophet (ﷺ), the fifth is divided into three portions: a portion for the orphans, a portion for the needy, and a portion for the wayfarer. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) did not leave an inheritance, so his portion and the portion of the near relatives lapsed. Their evidence for this is that Abu Bakr, 'Umar, and 'Uthman, may God be pleased with them, withheld it from the near relatives.

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

The withholding has not been established. Rather, the Banu Hashim objected that the Quraysh are also relatives. It was also said: during the period of Abu Bakr, may God be pleased with him, there was no booty.

Al-Shafi'i said: the fifth must be given to its recipients in every case, and the imam gives preference to those in need, but he must not completely deprive any of its categories. Malik, may God have mercy on him, said: the imam may give to the most needy even if he deprives the others.

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was specially privileged in the booty in three respects: he had a fifth of the fifth; he had a man's share in the remaining four-fifths; and he had the safiyy (the choice portion), which he took before the division: a mount, or a sword, or a slave girl. No one after him has a safiyy by consensus, except what Abu Thawr said, that the safiyy remains for the imam, but this is an opinion counted among the anomalous views.

As for dhawu al-qurba (the near relatives), they are the relatives of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). 'Ali ibn al-Husayn, 'Abdullah ibn al-Hasan, and 'Abdullah ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them, said: "They are the Banu Hashim only." Mujahid said: the family of Muhammad (ﷺ) were not permitted to receive charity, so they were given the fifth of the fifth. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, said: "But our people refused this for us, and they said: 'All of Quraysh are relatives.'" Al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, said: "They are the Banu Hashim and the Banu al-Muttalib only," and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to 'Uthman ibn 'Affan and Jubayr ibn Mut'im, at the time of the division of the portion of the near relatives from Khaybar among the Banu Hashim and the Banu [p-197] al-Muttalib: "The Banu Hashim and the Banu al-Muttalib are one thing; they have not separated from us in the Jahiliyya or in Islam."

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

They were with the Banu Hashim in the valley (al-Sh'ib).

Another group said: all of Quraysh are relatives. It was narrated from 'Ali ibn al-Husayn and 'Abdullah ibn Muhammad ibn 'Ali, may God be pleased with them, that they both said: "The whole verse concerns Quraysh," and the meaning is: the orphans of Quraysh and its needy.

Another group said: the portion of the relatives after the Prophet (ﷺ) is held for his relatives. 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz sent it to the Banu Hashim and the Banu al-Muttalib only. Another group said: it is for the relatives of the reigning imam who is in charge of the affair. Qatada said: the portion of the near relatives was a provision (tu'ma) for the Messenger of God (ﷺ) as long as he lived; when he died, it was assigned to the one in charge of the affair after him. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan al-Basri said the same. Al-Tabari also transmitted from al-Hasan that he said: "People differed about these two portions after the death of the Prophet (ﷺ). Some said: the Prophet's portion is for the caliph. Some said: the Prophet's portion is for the Prophet's relatives. Some said: the portion of the relatives is for the caliph's relatives. Their opinion then agreed to place these two portions in horses and equipment, and it remained so during the period of Abu Bakr, may God be pleased with him." Others besides al-Hasan added: "and 'Umar."

The orphans (al-yatama) are the young children who have lost their fathers. Orphanhood among the children of Adam is through the fathers, and among animals it is through the mothers. The needy (al-miskin) are those who have nothing; the word is derived from sukun (stillness) and little movement. The wayfarer (ibn al-sabil) is the traveler who passes through and has become in need during a journey, and whether he is wealthy in his own land or poor, he is ibn al-sabil. He is named so either because the road brings him forth, as if it gave birth to him, or because he clings to the road, as they say: "son of water" and "brother of travel." From this is His saying, peace be upon him: "The son of adultery will not enter Paradise," which has been mentioned previously.

[p-198] Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

I have summarized the jurisprudence (fiqh) of this verse as far as brevity allows, and God is the One sought for help.

The "ma" in His saying, exalted is He, "ma ghanimtum" (whatever you obtained), means "alladhi" (that which), and in His saying "ghanimtum" there is a pronoun referring back to it. It is reported from al-Farra' that he permitted "ma" to be conditional, with the implied meaning "innahu ma" (indeed whatever). Omitting this pronoun is not permitted according to Sibawayh except in poetry, and from it is the verse:

"Indeed whoever enters the church one day..."

Al-Jumhur read "fa-anna lillah" with an open hamza. Al-Ju'fi from Abu Bakr from 'Asim, and Husayn from Abu 'Amr, read "fa-inna" with a kasra on the hamza. Al-Hasan read "khumsahu" with the mim sukun.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 8, verse 41 (part 2 of 2):

And His saying, the Exalted: ﴿If you have believed in Allah﴾ [and the verse], al-Zajjaj said, on the authority of a group: the meaning is: "Know that Allah is your Protector, if you are [believers]." So "in" (if) is connected to this promise. He also said, on the authority of another group, that it is connected to His saying: ﴿And know that whatever you gained﴾.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
This is the correct view, because His saying "and know" (wa-'lamu) includes the command to submit and yield to Allah's command regarding the spoils. So "in" is connected to "and know" with this meaning, i.e.: if you are believers in Allah, then submit and yield to Allah's command concerning what He has informed you of regarding the division of the spoils. His saying ﴿and what We sent down﴾ is coordinated (ʿatf) with His saying "in Allah," and what is indicated by "mā" is the victory and triumph which Allah, Blessed and Exalted, sent down on the day of Badr upon His Prophet and his Companions. That is: if you are believers in Allah and in these signs and the dazzling great matters that were sent down on the day of Badr. It is also possible that the reference is to a Qur'an that was revealed on the day of Badr, or to the story of the day of Badr, though this last interpretation is strained.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
It is also possible that the meaning is: "And know that whatever you gained on the day of the Criterion (al-Furqan), the day the two hosts met, its fifth is for such-and-such, if you have believed," i.e., submit to that and yield. This is a good interpretation in meaning, but it faces the objection of separating the adverbial phrase from what is connected to it by this lengthy stretch of speech.

﴿The day of the Criterion﴾ means: the day of distinction between truth and falsehood, through the strengthening of Islam and the humbling of polytheism. Al-Furqan is a verbal noun from faraqa, yafruqu. "The two hosts" refers to the host of the Muslims and the host of the disbelievers, and it is the day of the encounter in which the chieftains of Quraysh were killed at Badr. There is no disagreement on this, and Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Miqsam, al-Hasan ibn 'Ali, Qatada and others explicitly stated it. It was on Friday, the seventeenth of Ramadan in the second year after the Hijra. This is the view of the majority of people. Abu Salih said it was the nineteenth, and 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr expressed doubt about this, saying: "the nineteenth or the seventeenth." The correct view is that of the majority.

And His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And Allah is over all things Competent﴾ supports the view that His saying ﴿and what We sent down upon Our servant﴾ refers to victory and triumph, i.e., the signs and great matters, namely the overcoming of the few over the many, and this is by the power of Allah, the Exalted, who is over all things Competent.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 8, verse 42:**

His words, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿When you were on the nearer side of the valley, and they were on the farther side, and the caravan was below you. Had you made an appointment together, you would have differed about the appointment. But (it happened so) that Allah might accomplish a matter that was to be done, so that whoever perished might perish upon clear proof, and whoever lived might live upon clear proof. Indeed, Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.﴾

The governing element (al-'amil) in "idh" (when) is His saying "met" (iltaqa). The 'udwa is the edge of the valley and its lip, where walking becomes difficult, like the rim of a well (rahā al-bi'r), because it "prevents" ('adat) whatever water and the like is in the valley from passing beyond the valley, that is, it stops it. From this is the saying of the poet:

"The enemies ('adawi) prevented me from visiting you,
and a fierce war (harb zabun) came between us and it."

It is also called 'udwa because it is what lies beyond (ma 'ada) the valley, that is, it passes over it. The bank and the open land running alongside the valley are called 'udwa by way of adjacency, and this is the 'udwa mentioned in the verse.

Nafi', 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "bil-'udwati" with a damma on the 'ayn. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read "bil-'idwati" with a kasra on the 'ayn. Both are dialectal forms. al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan, Qatada and 'Amr read "bil-'adwati" with a fatha on the 'ayn, and it is possible that this is a verbal noun used as a name. Abu al-Fath (Ibn Jinni) said: what this indicates is that it is a third dialect, like their saying for milk: ra'wa, ru'wa, ri'wa. al-Kisa'i related: "I spoke to him in the presence (bi-hadrati) of so-and-so, and in his presence (hadratihi), and in his presence (hudratihi)," and he cited many similar examples from Abu al-Fath.

His saying "al-dunya" and "al-quswa" (the nearer and the farther) is relative only to Madina. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud it is: "idh antum bil-'udwati al-'ulya wa-hum bil-'udwati al-sufla" (when you were on the upper side of the valley and they were on the lower side). The valley of Badr runs between the east and the qibla, bending toward the sea which is near that region. Madina, relative to the valley from the place of the battle, lies to the east, and between them are two stages of travel. My father told me that he saw these places as I have described them. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "Badr lies between Makka and Madina." "Al-dunya" is from "dunuww" (nearness), and "al-quswa" is from "qasw", which means distance. The analogical form would have been "al-quṣyā", but it is irregular. al-Khalil said in al-'Ayn: "Two words are anomalous: al-quswa and al-fatwa, whose analogical form would have been with a yā' like al-dunya and al-'ulya."

"Al-rakb" (the caravan) is by consensus of the exegetes, except for Abu Sufyan. "Rakb" is only said of the riding camels, and it is a collective noun. "Rakib" (rider) may be pluralised as "rakb" like sahib/sahb and tajir/tajr. "Rakb" is not said of large collective groups. al-Qutabi said: "Al-rakb: ten or so." This is not sound, because the Prophet ﷺ said: "And three is a rakb." His saying "asfala" is in the position of a genitive, the implied sense being "in a place lower (fi makanin asfala)"; so said Sibawayh. Abu Hatim said: "Asfala" is in the accusative as an adverb of place (zarf). It is also permissible to read "al-rakbu asfala", meaning: "and the position of the caravan was lower," or "the caravan being situated lower."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The caravan and the one managing its affair, Abu Sufyan, had veered away from Badr when he sensed the Prophet ﷺ, and took the coastal route (sayf al-bahr), so it was lower relative to the upper part of the valley from where they would come. Mujahid said in the book of al-Tabari: Abu Sufyan and his companions came from Syria as merchants, unaware of the companions at Badr, and the companions of (Muhammad ﷺ) were unaware of the Quraysh disbelievers, nor were the Quraysh disbelievers aware of Muhammad ﷺ and his companions, until they met at the water at Badr, each one wanting to water his own, so they fought, and the companions of Muhammad ﷺ overcame them and took them captive.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

In this there is a point of criticism, and among these groups there was clear awareness from having a full grasp of the story in its entirety.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And had you made an appointment together, you would have differed about the appointment﴾. al-Tabari and others said: Had you agreed upon meeting, then you had known their number and your own fewness, you would have differed and would not have gathered with them. al-Mahdawi (p-202) said: the meaning is: you would have differed through the obstacles and impediments that cut between people.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is the more noble and sounder view. Its clarification is that the purpose of the verse is to show the blessing of Allah, may He be blessed and exalted, and His power in the story of Badr, and His facilitating what He facilitated of it. The meaning is: when Allah prepared this state for you, had you arranged for it yourselves you would have differed, except with the facilitation of Him who completed that. This is like when you say to your companion about a matter that Allah has arranged without much toil: "Had we built upon this and striven for it, it would not have been completed in this way."

Then He, exalted is He, explained that this came about only through the subtle grace of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, "so that He might accomplish a matter," that is, so that He might execute and manifest a matter which He had decreed from eternity to be done by you, on the condition of your existence at the time of your existence; and all of that is non-existent to Him.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so that whoever perished might perish upon clear proof﴾ to the end of the verse. al-Tabari said: The meaning is: that whoever among the Quraysh disbelievers and others was killed, would be killed upon a clear proof from Allah and a warning through the message; and whoever lived would also live upon a clear proof from Him and a warning, with no argument against him. Thus, according to this interpretation, death and life are both literal.

Ibn Ishaq and others said: The meaning of "li-yahlika" (that he might perish) is "li-yakfura" (that he might disbelieve), and "wa-yahya" (and might live) is "li-yu'mina" (that he might believe). Thus, according to this, death and life are metaphorical. The meaning is that Allah, exalted is He, made the story of Badr a lesson and a sign, so that whoever believed would believe upon clarity and manifest proof, and whoever disbelieved would likewise disbelieve upon the same kind of proof.

The people read "li-yahlika" with a kasra on the second lam. al-A'mash read "li-yahlaka" with a fatha on the lam, and 'Ismah related it from Abu Bakr from 'Asim.

"Bayyina" is a descriptive attribute: a clear matter (qadiyya bayyina). The first lam in His saying "li-yahlika" corresponds to the lam in His saying "li-yaqdiya."

Ibn Kathir, in the narration of Qunbul, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and 'Asim, in the narration of Hafs, read "man hayya" with a single doubled yā'. Nafi', Ibn Kathir in the narration of al-Bazzi, and 'Asim in the narration of Abu Bakr read "man hayiya" with both yā's pronounced, the first kasra and the second fatha. Whoever reads "hayya" says: because the yā' has been bound to a vowel, so the verb, through the binding of the vowel to it, has become like a sound (sahih) verb, such as 'abba and shamma and the like. Do you not see that the deletion of the yā' in "jiwar" in the genitive and nominative does not hold in the accusative, when you say "ra'aytu jawari," because of its resemblance by vowel to the other sound letters? From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nay, when it reaches the collarbones﴾ [al-Qiyama: 26]. In the manner of "hayya" came the saying of the poet:

"They were incapable (ayyu) in their affair, as the dove was incapable with its egg."

And from it is the saying of Labid:

"My neighbour asked me about my people, and when one of sound mind is incapable (ayya), he asks."

And the saying of al-Mutalammis:

"So this is the time of the review, its flies alive (hayy dhubabuhu), its wasps and the blue-eyed one, al-Mutalammis."

It is also narrated: "junna dhubabuhu" (its flies went mad).

Abu 'Ali and others said: This shows that wherever the vowel is bound to a yā' in the imperfect, idgham (assimilation) in its perfect is permissible. Do you not see that His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Is He not able to give life to the dead?﴾ [al-Qiyama: 40] does not allow idgham in it, because the vowel of the accusative is not binding? Do you not see that it disappears in the nominative and is dropped in the jussive? Nor should one pay attention to what some of them recited, because it is an unknown verse:

"And as if she, among the women, were an ingot, walking at the threshold of her house, becoming tired (fata'iyya)."

Abu 'Ali said: As for the reading of the one who reads "hayiya," it is clear and there is no idgham, for Sibawayh said: Yunus informed us of this dialect, and he said: "We heard some Arabs say: 'ahyiya'." Abu Hatim said: The reading is to pronounce both yā's, and idgham is good; recite as you were taught, for both dialects are well known in Arabic speech, and in the script there is one yā'.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

In this word Abu 'Ali exhausted the discussion of what derives from "hayiya," including "al-hayy," which is its verbal noun, and other forms.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 8, verses 43–44:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, words:

﴿When Allah showed them to you in your dream as few. And had He shown them to you as many, you would have lost heart and disputed about the matter, but Allah saved [you]. Indeed, He is Knowing of what is within the breasts.﴾ ﴿And when He showed them to you, when you met, as few in your eyes, and made you seem few in their eyes, that Allah might accomplish a matter that was [already] to be done. And to Allah are [all] matters returned.﴾

Al-Mahdawi said: "Idh" (when) is in the accusative, by the implied verb: "and remember."

(p-205) Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Or it is a substitute (badal) for the preceding "idh," and this is the better view.

The reports are consistent that this verse was revealed concerning a vision that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ saw, in which he saw the number of the disbelievers as few. He informed his Companions of this, so their souls were strengthened and they were urged to engage in battle. This is the meaning of Allah's words: ﴿in your dream﴾, i.e., in your sleep, as said by Mujahid and others.

It is related from al-Hasan that the meaning of His words ﴿in your dream﴾ is "in your eye," since the eye is the place of sleep; and according to this interpretation the seeing would be while awake.

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This view is weak, and al-Naqqash interpreted it this way and attributed it to al-Mazini.

The pronoun in ﴿showed them﴾, under both interpretations, refers to the disbelievers of Makkah. What weakens what is related from al-Hasan is that the meaning of this verse is repeated in the one that follows, because the Prophet ﷺ is addressed in the second as well. And it is well established in reports that the Prophet ﷺ woke up and said to his Companions: "Rejoice, for I have seen the places where the people will fall," and similar words. He had already known that they were between nine hundred and a thousand; how then would he see them with his eyes contrary to what he knew? The apparent meaning is that he saw them in his sleep as few in their worth, their condition, and their might, defeated and struck down. It is also possible that he saw them as few in number, and the interpretation of his vision was their defeat. Thus "few" and "many," taken literally, are used figuratively for something other than number, as they say: "A man is many by his brother," and other examples of this kind. Al-fashal (losing heart) is weakness regarding the matter, either after engaging in it or after resolving to engage in it. ﴿And you would have disputed﴾ means you would have disagreed, and ﴿about the matter﴾ means about the encounter and the fighting. ﴿Saved﴾ is a term that covers every fear that attaches to the matter or arises in its path, so Allah saved them from all of that. Some people expressed it as "He saved your affair for you" and similar phrases, which fall within what we have mentioned. His words ﴿Indeed, He is Knowing of what is within the breasts﴾ mean: of your faith and your disbelief, and He will recompense accordingly.

(p-206) The majority of readers recited "wa-lakinna Allah sallama" with the nun doubled and the written word in the accusative. A group recited "wa-lakin Allah" with the written word in the nominative.

As for His words, ﴿And when He showed them to you, when you met﴾, the verse continues: "wa-idh" is coordinated with the first. This seeing was while awake, by consensus, and it is the seeing that occurred when they met and eye met eye. The meaning is that when Allah, desiring to carry out His decree to support and manifest Islam, made each group seem few in the eyes of the other, an error occurred in the estimation and guessing that people use in this kind of spying, each group upon the other, and the causes of war were set in motion. It is related on the authority of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud that he said: "I said that day to a man beside me: Do you think they are seventy? He said: Rather, they are a hundred. Then when we defeated them, we captured a man from among them and we asked him: How many were you? He said: A thousand."

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This meaning of diminishment is refuted by what is related: "When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ asked about how many they slaughtered each day, he was informed that one day they slaughtered ten and another day nine. He said: They are between nine hundred and a thousand." Either 'Abdullah and those who share his view did not know the statement of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, or we must take the diminishment mentioned in the verse to be diminishment of worth, awe, and standing in valor. Something similar occurred in His words: ﴿that Allah might accomplish a matter that was [already] to be done﴾, and the "matter to be done" mentioned in both verses refers to the whole story. Some people held that the two verses denote two of the meanings of the story, but the general sense is preferable.

His words, ﴿And to Allah are [all] matters returned﴾, are a reminder that all power belongs entirely to Allah, Blessed and Exalted, and that every matter belongs to Him and returns to Him. Al-Hasan, 'Isa ibn 'Umar, and al-A'mash recited "tarji'" with a fatha on the ta' and a kasra on the jim; Abu Hatim said this is the recitation of the common people. Al-A'raj, Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Nafi' and others recited "turja'" with a damma on the ta' and a fatha on the jim.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 8, verse 45–47:

(p-207) His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿O you who believe, when you encounter a company, stand firm and remember Allah much, that you may succeed.﴾ ﴿And obey Allah and His Messenger, and do not dispute, lest you lose courage and your strength depart; and be patient. Indeed, Allah is with the patient.﴾ ﴿And do not be like those who went out from their homes insolent and to be seen by people, and who averted [others] from the way of Allah. And Allah is encompassing of what they do.﴾

This is a command containing the impetus of victory and the cause of might. It is a precept from Allah directed according to the restriction in the verse of weakness (ḍaʿf). In line with the meaning of the verse is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Do not wish for an encounter with the enemy; ask Allah for well-being. But when you do meet them, then stand firm."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

Thus it is fitting that the Muslim, in the office of leadership and judgeship, does not seek it or wish for it; and if he is tested with it, he should be patient in establishing the truth.

And "al-fiʾah" (company): the group. Its origin is fiʾwah, and it is from fa'att, meaning "I gathered."

Then Allah, exalted, commanded the abundant remembrance of Him in that situation, for it is the protection of the one who seeks help and the refuge of the one who seeks aid. Qatadah said: Allah made His remembrance obligatory at the time when they are most preoccupied, at the striking of swords.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

This is a silent remembrance, because raising voices in the place of battle is reprehensible and disliked when it is mere shouting. (p-208) However, if it comes from all together at the charge, it is good, striking fear into the arm of the enemy. Qays ibn ʿAbbad said: The companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) disliked raising the voice at three times: during the recitation of the Qur'an, at funerals, and in battle. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Seek the answering of supplication at the time of battle, at the establishing of prayer, and at the descent of rain." Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: Covering the face (talaththum) is disliked during battle.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

For this reason—and Allah knows best—the fighters on the frontier are customarily to remove it in battle, out of their attachment to it.

And ﴿tufliḥūn﴾: you attain your aim and reach your hopes. This is like the saying of Labid:

Prosper by whatever you wish, for the weak may reach it, and the shrewd may be deceived.

As for His saying, exalted: ﴿And obey Allah and His Messenger﴾ to the end of the verse, it is a continuation of the admonition and of holding their hands to account regarding their disagreement over the matter of Badr and their dispute. ﴿Fatafshalū﴾ is in the accusative by the fāʾ in answer to the prohibition. Abu Hatim said in the book of "Ibrahim": "fatafshalū" with a kasra on the shin, and this is not well known. The majority of readers recited "watadhhaba" with the taʾ on top and the bāʾ in the accusative; Hubayra from Hafs from ʿAsim recited "watadhhab" with the taʾ and the bāʾ jussive; ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar recited "wayadhhab" with the yāʾ below and "yadhhab" jussive; Abu Hayawa recited "wayadhhaba" with the yāʾ below and the bāʾ in the accusative, and it was narrated by Aban and ʿIsmah from ʿAsim. The majority hold that "rīḥ" here is metaphorical (p-208) and that what is meant by it is victory and strength, as you say: "The wind is for so-and-so" when he is prevailing in a matter. From this meaning is the saying of the poet, who is ʿUbayd ibn al-Abras:

As We protected you on the day of al-Naʿf from the Shaṭib...
and the superiority belongs to the people through wind and through number.

Mujahid said: "rīḥ" is victory and strength, and the wind of the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ) departed when they disputed with him on the day of Uhud. Zayd ibn ʿAli said: ﴿and your wind departs﴾ means: the terror in the hearts of your enemy.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

This is good on the condition that the enemy knows of the dispute; and if the enemy does not know, then what departs is the strength of those disputing, so they are routed. The poet of the Ansar said:

Their swords have accustomed them that the wind of battle and the spoils of those who met them belong to them.

And from the metaphorical use of "wind" is the saying of another:

When your winds blow, seize them, for every gust has a calm.

This is common and widely used. Ibn Zayd and others said: "rīḥ" is in its literal sense. It is narrated that victory never occurred except by a wind that blows and strikes the faces of the disbelievers, and some of them relied for this view on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "I have been given victory by the east wind (al-ṣabā)." Al-Hakam said: ﴿and your wind departs﴾ means: the east wind, for by it was the victory of Muhammad (ﷺ) and his community.

(p-210) The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

This was specifically at the Battle of the Trench. His saying ﴿and be patient﴾ to the end of the verse is a completion of the admonition and a comforting promise. His saying, exalted: ﴿And do not be like those who went out from their homes﴾ to the end of the verse is a verse that contains criticism of those indicated, who are the disbelievers of Quraysh, and this came in the form of a prohibition against following their path. The indication is to the disbelievers of Quraysh by consensus. "Baṭar" means: arrogance, ingratitude for blessings, and being occupied with exultation in them so as to turn away from thanking them. "Riʾāʾ" means: showing off and affecting what another sees; it is a form from rāʾā yurāʾī, its hamza having been eased. It is narrated that when Abu Sufyan perceived that his caravan had passed beyond the fear of the Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions, he sent to Quraysh saying: "Indeed Allah has delivered your caravan, which you went out to support; so return safely, for you have achieved your aim." **Ibn 'Atiyya's commentary on Surah al-Anfal (8), verses 48–49:**

Allah the Mighty and Majestic says:

﴿And when Satan made their deeds seem fair to them and said, "No one among the people can overcome you today, and I am your protector." But when the two hosts sighted each other, he turned back on his heels and said, "Indeed, I am free of you. Indeed, I see what you do not see. Indeed, I fear Allah, and Allah is severe in punishment."﴾ ﴿When the hypocrites and those in whose hearts is a disease say, "Their religion has deluded these people." But whoever puts his trust in Allah, then indeed Allah is Mighty and Wise.﴾

The implied sense is: "Remember when..." The pronoun in "lahum" refers to the disbelievers. "Al-Shaytan" is Iblis himself. Al-Mahdawi and others report that the "making fair" (tazyin) in this verse and what follows is by whispering (waswasa) and inner conversation within the souls.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This view is weakened by the fact that His words, "And I am your protector," are not the kind of thing cast by whispering. The majority of scholars hold, based on what has been transmitted and widely reported, that Iblis came to the disbelievers of Quraysh. In Ibn Hisham's Sirah (biography of the Prophet), it is said that he came to them in Makkah, and in other accounts that he came to them while they were on their way to Badr. They feared the Banu Bakr and Kinana because of wars that had occurred between them. Iblis came to them in the form of Suraqa ibn Malik ibn Ju'sham, who was one of their chiefs, and said to them, "I am your protector. You will not fear my people, who are your helpers in achieving your aim, and no one will overcome you." They were delighted at this and proceeded on their course. He also said to them, "You are fighting for the religion of your fathers, and you will not be deprived of victory." It is narrated that when the two hosts met, his hand was in the hand of al-Harith ibn Hisham. When he saw the angels, he turned back on his heels. Al-Harith said to him, "Are you fleeing, O Suraqa?" but he did not look back. It is also reported that he said to him what the verse contains. It is further reported that 'Umayr ibn Wahb (or al-Harith ibn Hisham) said to him, "Where are you going, O Suraqa?" but he did not turn, and he pushed against al-Harith's chest and departed, and then the defeat occurred. It was reported that Suraqa had fled with the people, and this reached Suraqa ibn Malik (p-212), so he came to Makkah and said to them, "By Allah, I knew nothing of your affair until your defeat reached me, and I did not see you, nor was I with you." Al-Tabari transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: "On the day of Badr, Iblis came with a host of devils with him. I saw him in the form of a man from Banu Mudlij, and he said, '﴿No one among the people can overcome you today﴾,'" and so on, to the end of the verse.

"Al-yawm" (today) is an adverbial of time, and the governing element in it is the meaning of the negation of overcoming. It is also possible that the governing element is the complement of "lakum" (for you), while "ghalib" cannot govern it, because that would require the form "la ghaliban" (not overcoming).

His words, "And I am your protector," mean: "So you are under my protection and safeguard."

"Taraat" is from the verb "tafa'ala" (to see one another) derived from "ru'ya" (sight), meaning each party saw the other. Al-A'mash and 'Isa ibn 'Umar read it as "tara'at" with a short vowel. Abu Hatim reported from al-A'mash that he pronounced the alif with inclination while the ra was thinned, and then he retracted from this.

His words, "He turned back on his heels," mean: he returned from where he had come. The original meaning of "nukus" (recoil) in the language is returning backward. Zuhayr said:

They strike the sword-edges when they meet, and they do not recoil when they are dealt blows, and they stand firm.

This is how al-Tabari recited it, but in the version of al-Asma'i it is "istalǎmu" (when they are clad in armour). Al-Tabari explained this verse accordingly, but that is far-fetched. Rather, his turning back in this verse is a figurative comparison to genuine recoiling. The lexicographers said: "Nukus" is holding back from something. One says: "He intended a matter, then recoiled from it." Ta'abbata Sharran said:

Turning back on one's heels is no nobility, for true nobility is advancing upon the spear.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

There is no backward walking here; rather it is flight. Mu'arrij said: "Nakasa" means "raja'a" (returned) in the dialect of Sulaym.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

His words, "on his heels," clarify that he intended only flight and retreat, the opposite of his advance. His words, "Indeed, I am free of you," mean his abandonment of them and his separation from them. His words, "Indeed, I see what you do not see," refer to the angels. He, the wicked one, had only stipulated that no one among the people would overcome them. When he saw the angels and the breaking of the customary order, he feared and fled. In the Muwatta' (the hadith collection of Imam Malik) and others, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Satan has never been seen on any day smaller, more contemptible, or more humiliated than on the Day of 'Arafah, because of what he sees of the descent of mercy, except what he saw on the Day of Badr." It was said: "And what did he see, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "He saw the angels, and Jibril (peace be upon him) was apparently leading them." Al-Hasan said: "Iblis saw Jibril, peace be upon him, leading his horse before the Prophet (ﷺ), wrapped in a striped cloak, with the bridle in his hand."

His words, "Indeed, I fear Allah," it has been said: "This is a false excuse, and fear never reached him at all." This was said by Qatada and Ibn al-Kalbi. Al-Zajjaj and others said: "Rather, he feared what he saw of the matter and its terror, and that it was the day to which he had been given respite." This is strengthened by the fact that he saw the breaking of the customary order and the descent of the angels for battle.

Al-Tabari, with his chain of transmission, reported that when the polytheists were routed on the Day of Badr, after the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) threw a handful of dust into the faces of the disbelievers, Jibril (peace be upon him) approached Iblis. When Iblis saw him, and his hand was in the hand of a man from among the polytheists, he snatched his hand away and turned around in flight. The man said to him, "O Suraqa, do you claim that you are our protector?" He said, "Indeed, I see what you do not see," and so on, to the end of the verse. Then he departed.

His words, the Exalted: "When the hypocrites and those in whose hearts is a disease say..." to the end of the verse. The governing element of "idh" (when) is "zayyana" (made fair) or "nakasa" (turned back), because that situation was the time frame for all these events. The exegetes said: Those described with hypocrisy and disease of the heart were from among the army of the disbelievers. When they came in sight of the Muslims and saw their small number and few troops, they said, pointing to the Muslims, "Their religion has deluded these people," meaning: they were deceived, so they cast themselves into what they had no capacity to bear.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Hypocrisy is more specific than disease of the heart, because disease of the heart is applied to the disbeliever, to one who has been struck by doubt, and to one who is between these two. The heart is used as a metaphor for beliefs, since the heart is their seat. It is reported in a similar interpretation from al-Sha'bi that some people, in whose hearts Islam had not entered, went out with the polytheists to Badr. Some of them were compelled, and some of them flattered and dissembled. When they came in sight of the Muslims and saw their small number, they doubted and believed that they would be overcome, so they said, "Their religion has deluded these people." Mujahid said: Among them were Qays ibn al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, Abu Qays ibn al-Fakih ibn al-Mughira, al-Harith ibn Zam'a ibn al-Aswad, 'Ali ibn Umayya ibn Khalaf, and al-'As ibn Umayya ibn al-Hajjaj.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

No one among those who fought at Badr is mentioned as a hypocrite, except for what became apparent afterward concerning Mu'attib ibn Qushayr, brother of 'Amr ibn 'Awf, for he is the one who said on the day of Uhud: ﴿If we had any say in the affair, we would not have been slain here﴾ [Al 'Imran: 154]. It is also possible that the hypocrites of Madinah, when news reached them of Quraysh's departure with great strength, said this about the Muslims, and Allah informed His Prophet of it in this verse.

Then Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, informed that whoever puts his trust in Allah and leans upon Him, then indeed the might and wisdom of Allah, Blessed and Exalted, are sufficient to grant him victory and strengthen his support. This meaning was expressed in the most concise and eloquent wording.
