"Taraat" is from the verb "tafa'ala" (to see one another) derived from "ru'ya" (sight), meaning each party saw the other. Al-A'mash and 'Isa ibn 'Umar read it as "tara'at" with a short vowel. Abu Hatim reported from al-A'mash that he pronounced the alif with inclination while the ra was thinned, and then he retracted from this.

His words, "He turned back on his heels," mean: he returned from where he had come. The original meaning of "nukus" (recoil) in the language is returning backward. Zuhayr said:

They strike the sword-edges when they meet, and they do not recoil when they are dealt blows, and they stand firm.

This is how al-Tabari recited it, but in the version of al-Asma'i it is "istalǎmu" (when they are clad in armour). Al-Tabari explained this verse accordingly, but that is far-fetched. Rather, his turning back in this verse is a figurative comparison to genuine recoiling. The lexicographers said: "Nukus" is holding back from something. One says: "He intended a matter, then recoiled from it." Ta'abbata Sharran said:

Turning back on one's heels is no nobility, for true nobility is advancing upon the spear.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

There is no backward walking here; rather it is flight. Mu'arrij said: "Nakasa" means "raja'a" (returned) in the dialect of Sulaym.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

His words, "on his heels," clarify that he intended only flight and retreat, the opposite of his advance. His words, "Indeed, I am free of you," mean his abandonment of them and his separation from them. His words, "Indeed, I see what you do not see," refer to the angels. He, the wicked one, had only stipulated that no one among the people would overcome them. When he saw the angels and the breaking of the customary order, he feared and fled. In the Muwatta' (the hadith collection of Imam Malik) and others, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Satan has never been seen on any day smaller, more contemptible, or more humiliated than on the Day of 'Arafah, because of what he sees of the descent of mercy, except what he saw on the Day of Badr." It was said: "And what did he see, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "He saw the angels, and Jibril (peace be upon him) was apparently leading them." Al-Hasan said: "Iblis saw Jibril, peace be upon him, leading his horse before the Prophet (ﷺ), wrapped in a striped cloak, with the bridle in his hand."

His words, "Indeed, I fear Allah," it has been said: "This is a false excuse, and fear never reached him at all." This was said by Qatada and Ibn al-Kalbi. Al-Zajjaj and others said: "Rather, he feared what he saw of the matter and its terror, and that it was the day to which he had been given respite." This is strengthened by the fact that he saw the breaking of the customary order and the descent of the angels for battle.

Al-Tabari, with his chain of transmission, reported that when the polytheists were routed on the Day of Badr, after the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) threw a handful of dust into the faces of the disbelievers, Jibril (peace be upon him) approached Iblis. When Iblis saw him, and his hand was in the hand of a man from among the polytheists, he snatched his hand away and turned around in flight. The man said to him, "O Suraqa, do you claim that you are our protector?" He said, "Indeed, I see what you do not see," and so on, to the end of the verse. Then he departed.

His words, the Exalted: "When the hypocrites and those in whose hearts is a disease say..." to the end of the verse. The governing element of "idh" (when) is "zayyana" (made fair) or "nakasa" (turned back), because that situation was the time frame for all these events. The exegetes said: Those described with hypocrisy and disease of the heart were from among the army of the disbelievers. When they came in sight of the Muslims and saw their small number and few troops, they said, pointing to the Muslims, "Their religion has deluded these people," meaning: they were deceived, so they cast themselves into what they had no capacity to bear.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Hypocrisy is more specific than disease of the heart, because disease of the heart is applied to the disbeliever, to one who has been struck by doubt, and to one who is between these two. The heart is used as a metaphor for beliefs, since the heart is their seat. It is reported in a similar interpretation from al-Sha'bi that some people, in whose hearts Islam had not entered, went out with the polytheists to Badr. Some of them were compelled, and some of them flattered and dissembled. When they came in sight of the Muslims and saw their small number, they doubted and believed that they would be overcome, so they said, "Their religion has deluded these people." Mujahid said: Among them were Qays ibn al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, Abu Qays ibn al-Fakih ibn al-Mughira, al-Harith ibn Zam'a ibn al-Aswad, 'Ali ibn Umayya ibn Khalaf, and al-'As ibn Umayya ibn al-Hajjaj.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

No one among those who fought at Badr is mentioned as a hypocrite, except for what became apparent afterward concerning Mu'attib ibn Qushayr, brother of 'Amr ibn 'Awf, for he is the one who said on the day of Uhud: ﴿If we had any say in the affair, we would not have been slain here﴾ [Al 'Imran: 154]. It is also possible that the hypocrites of Madinah, when news reached them of Quraysh's departure with great strength, said this about the Muslims, and Allah informed His Prophet of it in this verse.

Then Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, informed that whoever puts his trust in Allah and leans upon Him, then indeed the might and wisdom of Allah, Blessed and Exalted, are sufficient to grant him victory and strengthen his support. This meaning was expressed in the most concise and eloquent wording.

(p-٢١٥) His, may He be exalted and glorified, saying:

﴿If only you could see when the angels take the lives of those who disbelieve, striking their faces and their backs, [saying], "Taste the punishment of the burning." That is for what your hands have sent forward, and because Allah is not unjust to the servants.﴾ ﴿[They are] like the custom of the people of Pharaoh and those before them, who disbelieved in the signs of Allah, so Allah seized them for their sins. Indeed, Allah is Strong, Severe in punishment.﴾

This verse expresses wonder at what befell the disbelievers on the day of Badr. This is the view of Mujahid and others. It also contains a warning to those among them who remained. The omission of the answer to "law" (if only) is an eloquent expression of vagueness (ibhām).

The majority of the Seven Readers and the common readers recite *yatawaffā* with the *yā'* (ي). Here a verb bearing the masculine marker is attributed to a feminine noun in form, and this is permissible because the feminine here is not real (ḥaqīqī). *al-Malā'ika* ("the angels") is the subject (marfū') of *yatawaffā*. Some of those who read this way said that the meaning is: "when Allah takes the lives of those who disbelieve," and *al-malā'ika* is the subject of an inchoative sentence (mubtada'), with *yaḍribūna* as its predicate (khabar), and the whole clause is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This interpretation is weakened by the absence of the conjunctive *wāw* of the circumstantial clause, since it is usually obligatory in such a construction. Ibn 'Amir of the Seven Readers, and al-A'raj, recite *tatawaffā* with the *tā'* (ت), attributing the verb to the form of the word "angels," and *yaḍribūna* is then in the position of a circumstantial phrase.

As for His saying: ﴿and their backs﴾, the majority of the exegetes (mufassirūn) said: it means their posteriors (asti'a), but Allah is Generous and uses euphemism. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: it means their backs and what was turned away of them. The meaning of this is that the angels would overtake them while they were fleeing and strike their backs. As for while they were facing forward, the striking of the faces is clearly firmly established.

Al-Hasan narrated that "a man said: O Messenger of Allah, I saw on the back of Abu Jahl something like a strap (shirāk). The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'That is the striking of the angels.'" He expressed it with the plural "angels," though the Angel of Death is one, since he has helpers among the angels in this task.

As for His saying: ﴿Taste the punishment of the burning﴾, it was said: the disbelievers were being told this phrase at that time, and "saying" (yaqūlūna) was omitted for brevity. It was also said: its meaning is that their condition on the Day of Resurrection will be that this is said to them. *al-Ḥarīq* is on the pattern *faʿīl* from *al-ḥarq* (burning).

Makki and al-Zahrawi said: it may also be in the position of the accusative (naṣb) with the removal of the preposition *bā'*, the presumed form being *bi-anna* (because that). When the *bā'* is removed, it comes to be in the accusative position.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is neither well-founded nor clear, unless it is put in the accusative by means of an implied verb.

As for His saying: ﴿Like the custom of the people of Pharaoh﴾ and the rest of the verse: *al-da'b* means habit (ʿāda) in the speech of the Arabs, and from it is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*Like your custom with Umm al-Huwayrith before her,*
*and her neighbour Umm al-Rabab at Ma'sil.*

It is also transmitted as *ka-dīnika* (like your religion/way). And from it is the saying of Khirash ibn Zuhayr al-'Amiri:

*That custom continued until Hawazin abandoned [its allies], and Sulaym and 'Amir scattered.*

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 8, verses 53–56:**

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿That is because Allah never changes a blessing He has bestowed upon a people until they change what is in themselves, and indeed Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.﴾ ﴿Like the custom of the people of Pharaoh and those before them: they denied the signs of their Lord, so We destroyed them for their sins and drowned the people of Pharaoh, and they were all wrongdoers.﴾ ﴿Indeed, the worst of living creatures in the sight of Allah are those who disbelieve, so they will not believe.﴾ ﴿Those with whom you made a treaty, and then they break their treaty every time, and they do not fear Allah.﴾

"ذَلِكَ" (dhalika, "that") is in the nominative position as the predicate of an inchoative (mubtada'). Its implied estimate, according to Sibawayh, is: "the matter is that" (al-amr dhalika). It may also be estimated as: "it is required that" (wajaba dhalika), and the "ba'" (باء) is the ba' of causation (باء السببية).

His saying ﴿لَمْ يَكُ مُغَيِّرًا﴾ (lam yaku mughayyiran, "never changing") is a jussive form after "lam," and its jussive marking is by deleting the nun. The original is "yakunu." When "lam" enters, it becomes "lam yakun." Then they said "lam yaku," as though they intended lightness, imagining the entry of "lam" upon "yakun," so the nun was deleted for the jussive. This was acceptable in it because of its resemblance to the vowel-letters (حروف اللين) that are deleted for the jussive, as they said "lam ubali" (لم أُبالِ), and then they said "lam ubli" (لم أُبْلِ), imagining the entry of "lam" upon "ubali."

The meaning of this verse is the information that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, when He bestows a blessing upon a people, does not, out of His kindness and mercy, begin to change it or make it turbid until that comes from them by their changing their own condition which is desired and good. When they do that and engage in earning sins or disbelief that necessitates their punishment, Allah changes His blessing upon them into His vengeance upon them. An example of this: Allah's blessing upon Quraysh through Muhammad (ﷺ), and they disbelieved what they ought to have been upon, so Allah changed that blessing by transferring it to others, the Ansar, and brought down His punishment upon them.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿وَأنَّ﴾ (wa-anna, "and that indeed") is conjoined to the first (clause). ﴿سَمِيعٌ عَلِيمٌ﴾ (samee'un 'aleem) means: He hears everything and knows everything that occurs from people in changing what is in themselves; nothing of that is hidden from Him, whether secret or open.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿كَدَأْبِ آلِ فِرْعَوْنَ﴾ (ka-da'bi Al Fir'awn, "like the custom of the people of Pharaoh") and the rest of the verse: the kaf (ك) in "ka-da'b" in this verse is connected to His saying ﴿حَتّى يُغَيِّرُوا﴾ (until they change). This repetition is for a meaning other than the first, since the first is the custom of their being destroyed when they disbelieved, while this second is the custom of their blessing not being changed until they changed what was in themselves. We have already mentioned the connections of the kaf in the first verse. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 8, verses 57–59:

The words of the Most High:

﴿So if you overpower them in war, then make of them a deterrent for those behind them, that they may take heed.﴾ ﴿And if you fear treachery from a people, then throw back to them [their treaty] on equal terms. Indeed, Allah does not love the treacherous.﴾ ﴿And let not those who disbelieve think that they have escaped. Indeed, they cannot cause [Allah] to fail.﴾

The nun (nūn) entered with "fa-immā" for emphasis, and to distinguish it from "immā," which is a disjunctive particle, as in your saying: "There came to me either (immā) Zayd or (wa-immā) 'Amr." "Tuthaqqifahum" (and you overpower them) means: you capture them and bring them under your control (thiqāf), or you meet them in a state of weakness in which you have power over them and overcome them. This is necessarily implied by the wording, given His saying: ﴿in the war﴾. It has also been said: thaqifa means "he seized swiftly," and from this comes their saying: "a man who is thaqif and laqif" (quick and adept).

Some people said: its meaning is "tuṣādifannahum" (you encounter them), and other such statements that do not connect with the meaning, since one who encounters an enemy may prevail, and may not prevail, so making a deterrent of him is not certain. The thiqāf in the language is that with which a spear-shaft and the like is bound, and from this is the poet's saying:

"Indeed my spear is a firm cane that the biting of the thiqāf does not weaken, nor oil, nor fire."

And another said:

"You call Qu'ayn, while the iron has bitten them, with the biting of the thiqāf upon the solid joints (of the spear)."

The words of the Most High: ﴿fa-sharrid﴾ mean: drive away, frighten, and remove them far from doing the like of their deed. The "sharīd" is one exiled from his homeland or the like. The meaning is: by an action you take against them, such as killing or the like, which serves as a frightening for those behind them, that is, for those who come after them with the like of what they did, whether they are contemporaries of theirs or not.

Whatever precedes a thing is "bayna yadayhi" (before it), and whatever comes after it is "khalfahu" (behind it). So the meaning of the verse is: if you take captive these violators in your war against them, then do to them of retribution that which will be a deterrent for whoever comes after them in their way. The pronoun in "la'allahum" refers to the dispersed group. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him both, said: the meaning is: make an example of those behind them. A group said: "sharrid bihim" means: make them a warning (sammi' bihim), related by al-Zahrawi from Abu 'Ubayda; and the meaning is close, because making them a warning is included in what we explained first. In the codex of 'Abd Allah it reads "fa-sharridh" with a dotted dhāl, which is the reading of al-A'mash. "Sharridh" is not attested in the language of the Arabs, and there is no justification for it except that the dotted dhāl is substituted for the dāl, as they said: laḥmun kharādīl and kharādhīl (loose flesh).

Abu Haywa read—and al-Mahdawi related it from al-A'mash with a variant from him—"min khalfihim" with a kasra on the mīm of "man" and a kasra on the fā' of "khalfahum." The expectation in His saying "la'allahum" is according to human reckoning. And "yadhdhakkarūn" means: they take admonition.

The words of the Most High: ﴿And if you fear treachery﴾ and the verse. Most of the compilers of tafsir said: this verse concerns the Banu Qurayza, and al-Tabari related it from Mujahid. What appears from the wording of the Qur'an is that the matter of the Banu Qurayza was concluded at His saying: ﴿so make of them a deterrent for those behind them﴾. Then, blessed and exalted is He, began in this verse (p-221) by commanding what is to be done in the future with whoever one fears treachery from, until the end of time. The Banu Qurayza were not within the category of those whose treachery is feared, so that this verse would be applied to them; rather their treachery was manifest and notorious. So this verse, in my view, concerns whoever's future state is anticipated among the rest of mankind other than the Banu Qurayza. The fear of treachery is when the sparks of evil appear from the side of the covenanted parties, statements are heard from them, and the beginnings of deceit are sensed from them. Those beginnings are known, while the treachery which is their aim is feared, not certain. Then one throws back to them on equal terms: if they keep to peace as is required, well and good; otherwise they are to be fought. The Banu Qurayza broke the covenant twice. Yahya ibn Salam said: "takhāf" (you fear) in this verse means: "ta'lam" (you know).

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is not so. His saying: ﴿treachery﴾ requires that a covenant has come into being, because one who has no covenant between you and him, his fighting against you is not treachery. Al-Farra' mentioned that the meaning is: throw back to them with moderation and equality of the matter, that is, make it clear to them according to the measure of what appeared from them; do not exceed, and do not surprise them with war, but do to them the like of what they did to you.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

That is, reciprocity and comparison. His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not love the treacherous﴾ may be understood as a censure of the treacherous among those with whom the Prophet ﷺ made a covenant. It may also be understood as meaning: throw back to them on equal terms until you are far from treachery, for Allah does not love the treacherous; so the repudiation, on this interpretation, is for the reason that Allah does not love the treacherous.

In the speech of the Arabs, "sawā'" may mean justice and equity, and from it is His saying: ﴿to a word that is equal between us and you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 64], and from it is the saying of the rajaz poet:

"So strike the faces of the treacherous enemies until they come to you in equity."

It may also mean the middle, and from it is His saying: ﴿in the midst of the blazing Hellfire﴾ [al-Saffat: 55]. (p-223) And from it is the saying of Hassan ibn Thabit:

"Woe to the helpers of the Prophet and his kin, after the concealment in the midst of the grave."

The words of the Most High: ﴿And let not those who disbelieve think that they have escaped﴾. Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, and al-Kisa'i read: "wa-lā taḥsibanna" with a ta' addressing the Prophet ﷺ, and with a kasra on the sin (except 'Asim, who read it with a fatha). "Alladhina kafaru" is the first object, and "sabaqu" is the second object, and the meaning is: they escaped with themselves and saved them. "Innahum lā yu'jizūn" with a kasra on the alif of "inna," on the basis of a fresh beginning. "Yu'jizūn" means: they slip away and make their pursuer unable (to catch them). It is transitive to "'ajaza" with the hamza; you say: "'ajaza Zayd" and "a'jazahu ghayruhu" and "'ajjazahu" also. Suwayd said:

"Abu Layla Tufayl, healthy of skin, from the traces of weapons, made us unable (to catch him)."

It is related that the verse was revealed concerning those of the disbelievers who escaped in the war of the Prophet ﷺ, such as the Quraysh at Badr and others. So the meaning is: do not think them saved; rather they will be overtaken. It has also been said: its meaning is: they will not be unable in this world. It has been said: the intended meaning is in the Hereafter. Abu Hatim said: Mujahid, Ibn Kathir, and Shibl read: "wa-lā tiḥsibanna" with a kasra on the ta'. Al-A'raj, 'Asim, and Khalid ibn Ilyas read: "taḥsabanna" with a fatha on the ta' from above and a fatha on the sin. Al-A'mash read: "wa-lā yaḥsabu" with a fatha on the sin and the ya' from below and deletion of the nun. Abu Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qa', Abu 'Abd al-Rahman, Ibn Muhaysin, and 'Isa read: "wa-lā yaḥsibanna" with a ya' from below, a kasra on the sin, and a shaddated nun. Hafs from 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, and Hamza read: "wa-lā yaḥsabanna" with the ya' as a reference to an absent third person and a fatha on the sin. In this case, either the pronoun in the verb refers to the Prophet ﷺ, or the estimate is: "wa-lā yaḥsabanna aḥadun" (and let no one think), and "alladhina kafaru" is the first object, and "sabaqu" is the second object. Or "alladhina kafaru" are the agents, and the first object is implied, and "sabaqu" is the second object; the estimate of this aspect is: "wa-lā yaḥsabanna alladhina kafaru anfusahum sabaqu" (and let not those who disbelieve think themselves to have escaped). Or "alladhina kafaru" is the agent and "an" is elided, so the estimate is: "wa-lā yaḥsabanna alladhina kafaru an sabaqu," and "an sabaqu" takes the place of the two objects.

Al-Farisi said: this is as Sibawayh interpreted the saying of the Most High: ﴿Say: Do you command me to worship other than Allah?﴾ [al-Zumar: 64], the estimate being: "an a'bud" (that I worship).

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Similar to it is the saying of the poet:

"Ala ayyuhadha al-zajiri an uhdira al-waghā..."

Abu 'Ali said: "an" has been deleted along with its complement in the place of the agent. Ahmad ibn Yahya recited in this regard:

"Nothing startled us except a little (camel) driven with a rope, and my knowledge of him is as a smith who works the bellows."

Ibn 'Amir alone of the seven read: "annahum lā yu'jizūn" with a fatha on the alif of "annahum." Its basis is that it is estimated to mean "li-annahum lā yu'jizūn" (because they do not escape), that is: do not think their escape is a given, because they will not be saved. The majority read: "yu'jizūn" with a sukun on the 'ayn. Some people, as related by Abu Hatim, read: "yu'ajjizūn" with a fatha on the 'ayn and a shaddated jim. Ibn Muhaysin read: "yu'jizūnī" with a kasra on the nun, and its meaning is "yu'jizūnī" with the pronoun attached. Al-Zajjaj said: the preferred reading is a fatha on the nun, and it is permissible to read it with a kasra, on the basis that the meaning is "innahum lā yu'jizūnanī" (indeed they will not make me unable), and the first nun is deleted because of the meeting of two nuns, as the poet said:

(p-225) "You see him like the thaghām plant, perfumed with musk, who harms the (women) who weep when they weep for me."

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The verse belongs to 'Amr ibn Ma'dikarib. Abu al-Hasan al-Akhfash, regarding the saying of Mutammim ibn Nuwayra:

"And I surely know, without doubt, that I... for calamities. So do you see me waver?"

said: this is permissible under necessity. Some people said: the first nun has been deleted, and its deletion is not permitted, because it is the place of the i'rab. Abu al-'Abbas al-Mubarrad said: I see that in cases like this the second is deleted, and so he would say regarding the verse of 'Amr ibn Ma'dikarib.

In the codex of 'Abd Allah it reads: "wa-lā yaḥsabu alladhina kafaru annahum sabaqu innahum lā yu'jizūn." Abu 'Amr al-Dani said: with a ya' from below and without a nun in "yaḥsabu."

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Al-Tabari mentioned it with a nun.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 8, verse 60–61:

The Exalted said:

﴿And prepare against them whatever you are able of power and of steeds of war, by which you may terrify the enemy of Allah and your enemy and others besides them whom you do not know; Allah knows them. And whatever you spend in the cause of Allah will be repaid to you in full, and you will not be wronged.﴾ ﴿And if they incline to peace, then incline to it [also], and rely upon Allah. Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.﴾

The address in this verse is to all the believers. The pronoun in His saying, "for them" (lahum), refers either to those to whom the covenant is returned (alladhina yunbadhu ilayhim al-'ahd), or to those who cannot be overcome (alladhina la yu'jizuna), according to the interpretation of whoever interpreted it so in this world. It is also possible that it refers to all the disbelievers who were commanded to be fought at that time, and then the verse continued to apply to the community in general, since the command to fight all disbelievers has been directed.

'Ikrima, the freed slave of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "Power (quwwa) is male horses, and the steeds of war (ribat) are females." This is a weak opinion. A group said: "Power is archery," and they cited the hadith of 'Uqba ibn 'Amir that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, power is archery. Indeed, power is archery. Indeed, power is archery." As-Suddi said: "Power is weapons." At-Tabari went to the generality of the word, and he mentioned from Mujahid that he was seen preparing for war with a sack (jawaliq) beside him, and he said: "This is of the power."

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is the correct view. Horses, mounts in general, what is carried upon them, weapons of all kinds, fine armour, equipment and expenses are all included in power, and the Muslims were commanded to prepare whatever they were able of that. Since horses were the root of wars and their burdens, and goodness is bound to their forelocks, and they are the strongest of strengths and the fortresses of horsemen, Allah singled them out for mention as an honour, in the manner of His saying: ﴿Whoever is an enemy to Allah and His angels and His messengers and Gabriel and Michael﴾ [al-Baqara: 98], and in the manner of His saying: ﴿Fruit and palm trees and pomegranates﴾ [al-Rahman: 68], and this is common. Similar to it is the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "The earth has been made for me a place of prostration and a means of purification," which is in al-Bukhari and others, while in Sahih Muslim he said: "The earth has been made for me a place of prostration, and its dust a means of purification." He mentioned the dust in the sense of particular emphasis on it, since it is the greatest part of the earth, along with its inclusion in the generality of the other hadith. Since arrows are among the most effective of what is used in war, the most piercing against the enemy and the closest to reaching souls, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) singled them out for mention and drew attention to them. It has been narrated from him (ﷺ) that he said: "Allah, the Exalted, admits three Muslims to Paradise by one arrow: its maker, the one who seeks reward in making it, and the one who shoots it." 'Amr ibn 'Anabasa said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Whoever shoots an arrow in the cause of Allah, whether it hits the enemy or misses, it is like freeing a slave." And the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Shoot and ride, but that you shoot is dearer to me than that you ride."

Ribat al-khayl is the plural of rabt, like kalb and kilab. Its being numerous is not common unless the horses are many. It is permissible that ribat be a verbal noun from rabata, like sahha sihaman and the like, because the verbal nouns of the unaugmented triliteral verb are not regular. If we make it a verbal noun from rabata (the augmented form), then the binding of horses and keeping them is something each person does for the sake of another's action, so the believers bind themselves to one another. When each one of them binds a horse for the sake of his companion, a bond (ribat) has been formed among them, and that is what the verse urges. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever keeps a horse ready in the cause of Allah is like one who extends his hand with charity without withdrawing it." The hadiths on this meaning are numerous.

Al-Hasan, 'Amr ibn Dinar and Abu Hayawa read: "wa min rubut," with a damma on the ra' and the ba', which is the plural of ribat, like kitab and kutub. The commentators thus state it, but regarding its plural while it is a verbal noun, there is room for consideration.

﴿Turhibun﴾ means: you frighten and intimidate. Al-rahba is fear. Tufayl al-Ghanawi said:

"Woe to the mother of a tribe, you struck at their throats, the Banu Kilab, on the morning of terror and dread."

From it comes "rahib" (monk) of the Christians. It is said: "rahiba" meaning he feared, so "turhibun" is transitive by means of the hamza.

Al-Hasan and Ya'qub read: "turahhibun," with a fatha on the ra' and a shadda on the ha', transitive by doubling. It is also narrated from Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala'. Abu Hatim said: 'Amr claimed that al-Hasan read "yurhibun" with a ya' at the beginning and without shadda, and it is thus transitive by doubling. Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ikrima read: "tukhzuna bihi 'aduwwa Allah" (you disgrace by it the enemy of Allah).

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

At-Tabari mentioned this as an explanation, not as a recitation, while Abu 'Amr al-Dani affirmed it as a recitation.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿the enemy of Allah and your enemy﴾ mentions two attributes, although they are close, since their meanings differ, and by mentioning both the censure is strengthened and the aspects of our hostility toward them become clear. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami read: "'aduwwan lillah" with tanwin on "'aduwwin" and a lam in the written text. The intended meaning of these two attributes is those among the disbelievers who are near and close, whose enmity is still active. It is also permissible that they be intended to mean all disbelievers. This is clarified by their differing over His saying: ﴿and others besides them﴾, the verse. Mujahid said: the reference in "and others" is to Qurayza. As-Suddi said: to the people of Persia. Ibn Zayd said: the reference is to the hypocrites. A group said: the reference is to the jinn. A group said: they are every enemy of the Muslims other than the group whom the Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded to scatter, along with those behind them.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This disagreement should properly be based on the meaning that arises from His saying: ﴿whom you do not know﴾. If we take His saying ﴿whom you do not know﴾ in its generality, and we negate the believers' knowledge of this group referred to as a whole, and knowledge in the sense of recognition only takes one object, then among the differing views regarding "and others" none remains except the view of the one who said "the reference is to the hypocrites" and the view of the one who said "the reference is to the jinn." If we take His saying ﴿whom you do not know﴾ as a clear metaphor, or something similar by which the negation of knowledge of them is conveyed, then the views are acceptable, and knowledge is transitive to two objects.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This second view seems to me closer to the truth. At-Tabari preferred that the reference is to the jinn, and he cited what is narrated that the neighing of horses frightens the jinn, and that Satan does not enter a house in which there is a horse for jihad, and similar things. In this, if it is accepted, there is room for consideration. The more important aspect of these verses is that their meaning should appear in everything that strengthens the Muslims against their enemy from among mankind, namely those who wage war and those who defend disbelief. Their dread of the Muslims is what benefits Islam and its people. The fear of the jinn is of no use for the rise of Islam, and it is very far removed from the subject. The better interpretation is that when the Muslims prevail and become strong, those enemies who neighbour them and wage war against them are awed by them; then, when this condition reaches those of the disbelievers who are farther away, awe enters them even if the Muslims do not intend to terrify them. Those are "the others."

It is fitting that His saying ﴿whom you do not know﴾ be understood as meaning: "You do not know them as frightened and awed, nor do you think this of them, while Allah knows them in that state." It is also fitting that the reference be to the hypocrites by way of censure of them and warning about the evil of their condition, so that everyone who knows hypocrisy in himself becomes suspicious of himself when he hears the verse; and their fear and dread have great benefit for the rise of Islam and its exaltation.

His saying ﴿from beside them﴾ (min duniham) is equivalent to your saying: "other than these." "Duna" in the speech of the Arabs, and "min dun," imply the absence of what follows them from the matter in which the speech is. From it is the proverb: "And the sheep's bleat was set in front of 'Ubayda."

Blessed and Exalted is He, by the promise to the believers regarding their spending in the cause of Allah, that the expenditure will certainly be repaid in full, meaning it will be recompensed and rewarded for it. The fulfilment of this is in the Hereafter, though it is possible that Allah may recompense some of the believers in this world with a multiplied recompense in addition to the recompense of the Hereafter.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if they incline to peace, then incline to it﴾, the verse. The pronoun in "they incline" refers to those to whom the covenant is returned on equal terms. "Janaha al-rajul ila al-amr" means a man leaned toward the matter and gave his hand to it. From it comes the word "jawanih" for the ribs, because they lean over the viscera; and "janah" for the tent-cover; and "janahat al-ibil" when the camels bend their necks while walking. Dhu al-Rumma said:

"When he dies upon the saddle, I revive his spirit with your remembrance, and the loosened camels bend their necks."

"Janaha al-layl" when the night approached and lowered its ropes to the earth.

From it is the saying of al-Nabigha:

"Leaning ones, who are certain that their tribe, when the two hosts meet, is the first to prevail."

That is, inclining. Labid said:

"The bending of the one who is perishing upon his hands, prostrate, gazing at the notches of the blades."

The majority of people read: "lil-silm" with a fatha on the sin and a shadda. 'Asim, in the narration of Bakr, read: "lis-silm" with a kasra and a shadda. Both are dialects for making peace. It is also said "salam" with a fatha on the sin and the lam, though I do not know it as a recitation.

The majority of people read: "fajnah" with a fatha on the nun, which is the dialect of Tamim. Al-Ashhab al-'Uqayli read: "fajnuh" with a damma on the nun, which is the dialect of Qays. Abu al-Fath said: this recitation is the analogical one, because fa'ala, when it is intransitive, has its imperfect with a damma on the 'ayn as the more regular form, as qa'ada yaq'udu is more regular than jalasa yajlisu.

The pronoun in "laha" is feminine, since al-silm means peacemaking and truce. It is also said: al-silm is feminine like al-harb, as al-Nahhas mentioned, while Abu Hatim said: al-silm may be masculine.

Qatada, al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan, 'Ikrima and Ibn Zayd said:

This verse is abrogated by the verses of fighting in Bara'a (Surat al-Tawba).

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It may be admitted that its abrogation by them does not follow, by taking this to refer to those with whom reconciliation is permissible, while those in Bara'a refer to the idol-worshippers. This is the view of al-Tabari. The view of the majority is also correct, if the inclination toward peace with the Arabs was established in the early period of Islam, and then the verse of Bara'a abrogated that and their covenants were returned to them. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that it is abrogated by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So do not weaken and call to peace while you are the superior ones﴾ [Muhammad: 35], the verse.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This view is far-fetched as a saying of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, because the two verses are Medinan, and His saying ﴿and rely upon Allah﴾ is a command that implicitly contains a warning.

The fulfilment of this is in the Hereafter, though it is possible that Allah may recompense some of the believers in this world with a multiplied recompense in addition to the recompense of the Hereafter.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if they incline to peace, then incline to it﴾, the verse. The pronoun in "they incline" refers to those to whom the covenant is returned on equal terms. "Janaha al-rajul ila al-amr" means a man leaned toward the matter and gave his hand to it. From it comes the word "jawanih" for the ribs, because they lean over the viscera; and "janah" for the tent-cover; and "janahat al-ibil" when the camels bend their necks while walking. Dhu al-Rumma said:

"When he dies upon the saddle, I revive his spirit with your remembrance, and the loosened camels bend their necks."

"Janaha al-layl" when the night approached and lowered its ropes to the earth.

From it is the saying of al-Nabigha:

"Leaning ones, who are certain that their tribe, when the two hosts meet, is the first to prevail."

That is, inclining. Labid said:

"The bending of the one who is perishing upon his hands, prostrate, gazing at the notches of the blades."

The majority of people read: "lil-silm" with a fatha on the sin and a shadda. 'Asim, in the narration of Bakr, read: "lis-silm" with a kasra and a shadda. Both are dialects for making peace. It is also said "salam" with a fatha on the sin and the lam, though I do not know it as a recitation.

The majority of people read: "fajnah" with a fatha on the nun, which is the dialect of Tamim. Al-Ashhab al-'Uqayli read: "fajnuh" with a damma on the nun, which is the dialect of Qays. Abu al-Fath said: this recitation is the analogical one, because fa'ala, when it is intransitive, has its imperfect with a damma on the 'ayn as the more regular form, as qa'ada yaq'udu is more regular than jalasa yajlisu.

The pronoun in "laha" is feminine, since al-silm means peacemaking and truce. It is also said: al-silm is feminine like al-harb, as al-Nahhas mentioned, while Abu Hatim said: al-silm may be masculine.

Qatada, al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan, 'Ikrima and Ibn Zayd said:

This verse is abrogated by the verses of fighting in Bara'a (Surat al-Tawba).

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It may be admitted that its abrogation by them does not follow, by taking this to refer to those with whom reconciliation is permissible, while those in Bara'a refer to the idol-worshippers. This is the view of al-Tabari. The view of the majority is also correct, if the inclination toward peace with the Arabs was established in the early period of Islam, and then the verse of Bara'a abrogated that and their covenants were returned to them. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that it is abrogated by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So do not weaken and call to peace while you are the superior ones﴾ [Muhammad: 35], the verse.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This view is far-fetched as a saying of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, because the two verses are Medinan, and His saying ﴿and rely upon Allah﴾ is a command that implicitly contains a warning.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 8, verses 62–64:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿And if they intend to deceive you, then sufficient for you is Allah. It is He who supported you with His help and with the believers﴾ ﴿And He brought their hearts together. Had you spent whatever is in the earth entirely, you could not have brought their hearts together, but Allah brought them together. Indeed, He is Exalted in Might, Wise﴾ ﴿O Prophet, sufficient for you is Allah, and for those who follow you among the believers﴾

The pronoun in His saying ﴿And if they intend﴾ refers to the disbelievers about whom it was said: ﴿And if they incline to peace﴾ [al-Anfal: 61]. His saying ﴿And if they intend to deceive you﴾ means: that they show you peace while concealing treachery and betrayal; that is, incline to peace, and do not concern yourself with their corrupt intentions. ﴿Then sufficient for you is Allah﴾ means: He is sufficient for you and grants you victory and manifestation, and this is a pure promise. ﴿Supported you﴾ means: strengthened you. ﴿And with the believers﴾ means: with the Helpers (al-Ansar), by the indication of His saying ﴿And He brought their hearts together﴾ and what follows, and this is a reference to the enmity that existed between the Aws and the Khazraj in the wars of Bu'ath. So Allah the Exalted brought their hearts together upon Islam, and returned them loving one another for the sake of Allah. This blessing was enumerated as a consolation for Muhammad (ﷺ): that is, just as your Lord showed kindness to you at first, so He does likewise in the end.

Ibn Mas'ud said: this verse was revealed concerning those who love one another for the sake of Allah. Mujahid said: when two loving ones meet, and they shake hands and laugh together, their sins fall away. 'Abdah ibn Abi Lubabah said to him: "Indeed this is trivial." He said to him: "Do not say that, for Allah says: ﴿Had you spent whatever is in the earth entirely, you could not have brought their hearts together﴾." 'Abdah said: "So I knew that he was more learned in jurisprudence than I."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

All of this is a fine application (tamaththul) of the verse, not that the verse was revealed concerning that. Rather, the statements of the exegetes concur that it concerns the Aws and the Khazraj, as we have mentioned. Yet if someone went to the generality of the believers among the Muhajirun and the Ansar, and made the bringing together (ta'lif) that which was from all of them into mutual love, so that the harmony of the Aws and the Khazraj would be a part of that, it would be permissible. And every bringing together in Allah follows that bringing together which existed in the early period of Islam. Sahl ibn Sa'd related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The believer is one who bonds with others (ma'lafah), and there is no good in one who does not bond with others nor is bonded with."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Resemblance is the cause of affection: whoever is among the people of goodness loves his like, and they love him.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿O Prophet, sufficient for you is Allah, and for those who follow you among the believers﴾.

Al-Naqqash said: this verse was revealed at al-Bayda', in the expedition of Badr, before the fighting. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that it was revealed concerning the Aws and the Khazraj specifically. He said: it is also said that it was revealed when 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, embraced Islam and the Muslims reached forty; this was stated by Ibn 'Umar and Anas, and so it is, on this account, Meccan.

﴿Hasbuka﴾ in the speech of the Arabs, and "shar'uka" mean: sufficient for you, and "yakfika" (suffices you). And al-muhsib means: the sufficient one. A group said: the meaning of this verse is: Allah suffices you and those among the believers who follow you suffice you, so that "man" in this interpretation is in the nominative, conjoined to the name of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. 'Amir al-Sha'bi and Ibn Zayd said: the meaning of the verse is: Allah is sufficient for you and sufficient for those among the believers who follow you, so that "man" in this interpretation is in the accusative position, conjoined to the position of the kaf (you), because its position is accusative in meaning relative to "yakfika", which took the place of "hasbuka". It is also valid for "man" to be in the genitive position, with an omitted element estimated, as if he said: "and [sufficient is] for whoever...". This is like the saying of the poet:

Do you think every man, or fire blazing at night, is fire?

The estimate is: "and every fire" (wa-kulla nar). This manner of omitting the mudaf (the governed noun) is disliked, and its place is poetic necessity. The line is also narrated as "wa-naran". Like this is the saying of the poet:

When war comes and the staffs split apart, then sufficient for you, and al-Dahhak, is a sharpened sword.

"Al-Dahhak" is narrated in the nominative, "al-Dahhak" in the accusative, and "al-Dahhak" in the genitive. The nominative is conjoined to his saying "sayf" (sword) with an intended postponement, as the poet said: "...upon you, and the peace of Allah" (in another line). In this case "al-Dahhak" is one who suffices the addressee, and the accusative is conjoined to the position of the kaf in his saying "hasbuka"; and "al-Muhannad" in this case is one who suffices the addressee; and "al-Dahhak" in the genitive is by an estimated omission, as if he said: "so sufficient for you and for al-Dahhak."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 8, verse 65–66:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿O Prophet, urge the believers to fight. If there are twenty of you who are steadfast, they will overcome two hundred; and if there are a hundred of you, they will overcome a thousand of those who disbelieve, because they are a people who do not understand.﴾ ﴿Now Allah has lightened your burden, for He knows that there is weakness among you. So if there are a hundred of you who are steadfast, they will overcome two hundred; and if there are a thousand of you, they will overcome two thousand, by the permission of Allah. And Allah is with the steadfast.﴾

(p-235) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Harridh﴾ means: urge them and incite them. Al-Naqqash said: it has also been read as "Harris" with an unpointed sad, and the meaning is close. The word "harid" (the one near to destruction) is a distinct word and has nothing to do with this one.

A group of the exegetes said: the meaning is: urge them to fight until it becomes clear to you which of them has abandoned it, that he was [already] urged.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is a view that does not fit with, nor is it necessarily implied by, the wording, and al-Zajjaj inclined towards it.

Fighting was already obligatory upon the believers by other than this verse, and this verse only contains the command to the Prophet ﷺ to urge them to an act that had already become obligatory upon them from elsewhere.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿In yakun﴾ up to the end of the verse is in the form of a report, which implicitly contains a promise conditional upon a condition, because His saying: ﴿If there are twenty of you who are steadfast﴾ is equivalent to saying: if twenty of you are steadfast, they will overcome; and implicit within it is the command to be steadfast. The ʿayn of "ʿishrūn" was vowelled with kasra because the ratio of twenty to ten is the ratio of two to one; just as the first of "two" (ithnān) came with kasra, the ʿayn of ʿishrūn was given kasra, and then this became regular in the plurals of the units of ten. The one with fatha, like arbaʿa, khamsa and sabʿa, has its first plural letter with fatha, and the one with kasra, like sitta and tisʿa, has its first plural letter with kasra. This is the view of Sibawayh. Others held that "ʿishrūn" is the plural of ʿishr al-ibil (the watering of camels, which is the interval of nine days), for when there were ten and ten, there were ʿishr and ʿishr and two days of the third, and this was collected under ʿishrūn, as Imru' al-Qays said:

﴿...﴾ thirty months in three years [of] states

(p-236) when there was in the thirty a year and a year and part of the third.

Reports from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, and other Companions, are consistent that the obligation for one to stand against ten was a decree from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, upon the believers; then, when that became hard for them, the obligation was lowered to one standing against two.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is abrogation (naskh), for it is the lifting of an established ruling by another legislative ruling, and implicit within it is lightening, since this is the abrogation of the heavier by the lighter. Some people held that the obligation for one to stand against ten was by way of recommendation (nadb) to the believers, and then it was lowered, when it became burdensome, to one against two. This too is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father. Many exegetes said: this is lightening (takhfif), not abrogation, since no legislative ruling for the obligation of ten was ever established. Makki said: it is rather like the lightening of breaking the fast while travelling, for if he fasted he would not sin and it would suffice him.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

There is room for consideration in this, and there is no barrier to calling it abrogation when what was abrogated was permissible; this was taken into account in the case of the charity before private consultation (ṣadaqat al-najwā). In this verse, the lightening is abrogation of the obligation of standing against ten; and whether standing against ten was obligatory or recommended, it is in every case a legislative ruling. The judge Ibn al-Tayyib mentioned that when a ruling is abrogated in part, or in part of its attributes, or its number is changed, it is permissible to call it abrogation, because then it is no longer the first, being other than it; and he mentioned a disagreement on this.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

What appears to me in this is that the term abrogation is applied to the first ruling only when it is qualified, not absolutely; and this was taken into account in the abrogation of prayer toward Bayt al-Maqdis.

(p-237) Hamza, al-Kisa'i and ʿAsim read: ﴿in yakun minkum mi'ah﴾ in both places with the yā' (masculine), in accordance with the masculine marker, and Kharija narrated it from Nafi'.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is according to the meaning, because those who are in that hundred are men; so this is in the sense of the context, like His saying: ﴿Whoever comes with a good deed, for him is ten times its like﴾ [al-An'am: 160], since its likes are good deeds. Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Ibn ʿAmir read: ﴿in takun minkum mi'ah﴾ with the tā' in both places, in accordance with the feminine marker.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is according to the wording and the intent, as if he meant: if there is a group whose number is a hundred. Abu ʿAmr read with yā' at the beginning of the verse and with tā' at its end: in the first he took into account "yaghlibū", and in the second he took into account "ṣābirah". Abu Hatim said: al-Aʿraj read ﴿in takun﴾ with tā' from above, ﴿minkum ʿishrūn ṣābirūn﴾, and made all of them with tā'.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Except His saying: ﴿wa-in yakun minkum alf﴾, for there is no disagreement on the yā' from below. His saying: ﴿lā yafqahūn﴾ means: they do not understand their right course nor the purpose of their fighting; they intend by it only worldly victory, so they fear death if they stand firm; whereas one who fights to win or to be martyred, and so goes to Paradise, is firmer of foot without doubt.

Al-Mufaddal narrated from ʿAsim: ﴿wa-ʿulima﴾ with a ḍammah on the ʿayn and a kasrah on the lām, in the passive form. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu ʿAmr, Ibn ʿAmir, al-Kisa'i, Ibn ʿAmr, al-Hasan, al-Aʿraj, Ibn al-Qaʿqaʿ, Qatada and Ibn Abi Ishaq read: ﴿ḍuʿfan﴾ with a ḍammah on the ḍād and sukūn on the ʿayn. ʿAsim, Hamza, Shayba and Talha read: ﴿ḍaʿfan﴾ with fatha on the ḍād and sukūn on the ʿayn; and their disagreement is the same in Surat al-Rum. ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar read: ﴿ḍuʿufan﴾ with ḍammah on both the ḍād and the ʿayn, and al-Naqqash mentioned it. These are verbal nouns (maṣādir) with one meaning. Abu Hatim said: whoever vowels the ḍād with ḍammah may also vowel the ʿayn with ḍammah; it is a dialect. Sibawayh reported that ḍaʿf and ḍuʿf are two dialects, like faqr and fuqr. al-Zahrawi reported from Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAla' that he said: ḍammah on the ḍād is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz, and fatha on it is the dialect of Tamim, and there is no difference between them in meaning. al-Tha'alibi said in his book "Fiqh al-Lugha": ḍaʿf with fatha on the ḍād refers to the intellect and judgement, and ḍuʿf with ḍammah refers to the body.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is a view that the recitation refutes; and Abu Ghalib ibn al-Tayyani mentioned it without attribution.

Abu Ja'far Ibn al-Qaʿqaʿ also read: ﴿ḍuʿafā'﴾ in the plural, like ẓarīf and ẓuraf'ā', and al-Naqqash related it from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father. His saying: ﴿wa-Allahu maʿa al-ṣābirīn﴾ is a report which implicitly contains a promise and an exhortation to steadfastness, and from it is understood a warning to whoever does not endure that he will be overcome.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 8, verse 65–66:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿O Prophet, urge the believers to fight. If there are twenty of you who are steadfast, they will overcome two hundred; and if there are a hundred of you, they will overcome a thousand of those who disbelieve, because they are a people who do not understand.﴾ ﴿Now Allah has lightened your burden, for He knows that there is weakness among you. So if there are a hundred of you who are steadfast, they will overcome two hundred; and if there are a thousand of you, they will overcome two thousand, by the permission of Allah. And Allah is with the steadfast.﴾

(p-235) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Harridh﴾ means: urge them and incite them. Al-Naqqash said: it has also been read as "Harris" with an unpointed sad, and the meaning is close. The word "harid" (the one near to destruction) is a distinct word and has nothing to do with this one.

A group of the exegetes said: the meaning is: urge them to fight until it becomes clear to you which of them has abandoned it, that he was [already] urged.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is a view that does not fit with, nor is it necessarily implied by, the wording, and al-Zajjaj inclined towards it.

Fighting was already obligatory upon the believers by other than this verse, and this verse only contains the command to the Prophet ﷺ to urge them to an act that had already become obligatory upon them from elsewhere.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿In yakun﴾ up to the end of the verse is in the form of a report, which implicitly contains a promise conditional upon a condition, because His saying: ﴿If there are twenty of you who are steadfast﴾ is equivalent to saying: if twenty of you are steadfast, they will overcome; and implicit within it is the command to be steadfast. The ʿayn of "ʿishrūn" was vowelled with kasra because the ratio of twenty to ten is the ratio of two to one; just as the first of "two" (ithnān) came with kasra, the ʿayn of ʿishrūn was given kasra, and then this became regular in the plurals of the units of ten. The one with fatha, like arbaʿa, khamsa and sabʿa, has its first plural letter with fatha, and the one with kasra, like sitta and tisʿa, has its first plural letter with kasra. This is the view of Sibawayh. Others held that "ʿishrūn" is the plural of ʿishr al-ibil (the watering of camels, which is the interval of nine days), for when there were ten and ten, there were ʿishr and ʿishr and two days of the third, and this was collected under ʿishrūn, as Imru' al-Qays said:

﴿...﴾ thirty months in three years [of] states

(p-236) when there was in the thirty a year and a year and part of the third.

Reports from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, and other Companions, are consistent that the obligation for one to stand against ten was a decree from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, upon the believers; then, when that became hard for them, the obligation was lowered to one standing against two.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is abrogation (naskh), for it is the lifting of an established ruling by another legislative ruling, and implicit within it is lightening, since this is the abrogation of the heavier by the lighter. Some people held that the obligation for one to stand against ten was by way of recommendation (nadb) to the believers, and then it was lowered, when it became burdensome, to one against two. This too is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father. Many exegetes said: this is lightening (takhfif), not abrogation, since no legislative ruling for the obligation of ten was ever established. Makki said: it is rather like the lightening of breaking the fast while travelling, for if he fasted he would not sin and it would suffice him.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

There is room for consideration in this, and there is no barrier to calling it abrogation when what was abrogated was permissible; this was taken into account in the case of the charity before private consultation (ṣadaqat al-najwā). In this verse, the lightening is abrogation of the obligation of standing against ten; and whether standing against ten was obligatory or recommended, it is in every case a legislative ruling. The judge Ibn al-Tayyib mentioned that when a ruling is abrogated in part, or in part of its attributes, or its number is changed, it is permissible to call it abrogation, because then it is no longer the first, being other than it; and he mentioned a disagreement on this.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

What appears to me in this is that the term abrogation is applied to the first ruling only when it is qualified, not absolutely; and this was taken into account in the abrogation of prayer toward Bayt al-Maqdis.

(p-237) Hamza, al-Kisa'i and ʿAsim read: ﴿in yakun minkum mi'ah﴾ in both places with the yā' (masculine), in accordance with the masculine marker, and Kharija narrated it from Nafi'.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is according to the meaning, because those who are in that hundred are men; so this is in the sense of the context, like His saying: ﴿Whoever comes with a good deed, for him is ten times its like﴾ [al-An'am: 160], since its likes are good deeds. Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Ibn ʿAmir read: ﴿in takun minkum mi'ah﴾ with the tā' in both places, in accordance with the feminine marker.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is according to the wording and the intent, as if he meant: if there is a group whose number is a hundred. Abu ʿAmr read with yā' at the beginning of the verse and with tā' at its end: in the first he took into account "yaghlibū", and in the second he took into account "ṣābirah". Abu Hatim said: al-Aʿraj read ﴿in takun﴾ with tā' from above, ﴿minkum ʿishrūn ṣābirūn﴾, and made all of them with tā'.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Except His saying: ﴿wa-in yakun minkum alf﴾, for there is no disagreement on the yā' from below. His saying: ﴿lā yafqahūn﴾ means: they do not understand their right course nor the purpose of their fighting; they intend by it only worldly victory, so they fear death if they stand firm; whereas one who fights to win or to be martyred, and so goes to Paradise, is firmer of foot without doubt.

Al-Mufaddal narrated from ʿAsim: ﴿wa-ʿulima﴾ with a ḍammah on the ʿayn and a kasrah on the lām, in the passive form. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu ʿAmr, Ibn ʿAmir, al-Kisa'i, Ibn ʿAmr, al-Hasan, al-Aʿraj, Ibn al-Qaʿqaʿ, Qatada and Ibn Abi Ishaq read: ﴿ḍuʿfan﴾ with a ḍammah on the ḍād and sukūn on the ʿayn. ʿAsim, Hamza, Shayba and Talha read: ﴿ḍaʿfan﴾ with fatha on the ḍād and sukūn on the ʿayn; and their disagreement is the same in Surat al-Rum. ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar read: ﴿ḍuʿufan﴾ with ḍammah on both the ḍād and the ʿayn, and al-Naqqash mentioned it. These are verbal nouns (maṣādir) with one meaning. Abu Hatim said: whoever vowels the ḍād with ḍammah may also vowel the ʿayn with ḍammah; it is a dialect. Sibawayh reported that ḍaʿf and ḍuʿf are two dialects, like faqr and fuqr. al-Zahrawi reported from Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAla' that he said: ḍammah on the ḍād is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz, and fatha on it is the dialect of Tamim, and there is no difference between them in meaning. al-Tha'alibi said in his book "Fiqh al-Lugha": ḍaʿf with fatha on the ḍād refers to the intellect and judgement, and ḍuʿf with ḍammah refers to the body.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is a view that the recitation refutes; and Abu Ghalib ibn al-Tayyani mentioned it without attribution.

Abu Ja'far Ibn al-Qaʿqaʿ also read: ﴿ḍuʿafā'﴾ in the plural, like ẓarīf and ẓuraf'ā', and al-Naqqash related it from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father. His saying: ﴿wa-Allahu maʿa al-ṣābirīn﴾ is a report which implicitly contains a promise and an exhortation to steadfastness, and from it is understood a warning to whoever does not endure that he will be overcome.

**Ibn 'Atiyya's commentary (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 8, verses 67–69:**

God, Exalted and Majestic, says:

﴿It is not for a Prophet to have captives until he has inflicted a massacre in the land. You desire the goods of this world, but God desires the Hereafter. God is Mighty, Wise.﴾ ﴿Had there not been a prior decree from God, a great punishment would have touched you for what you took.﴾ ﴿So eat of what you have gained, lawful and good, and fear God. Indeed God is Forgiving, Merciful.﴾

In my view, this verse contains a rebuke from God, Exalted and Majestic, directed at the Companions of His Prophet ﷺ. The meaning is: it was not fitting for you to do this deed, which necessitated that the Prophet have captives before he had inflicted a massacre. The address is to them, and for this reason the address continues with ﴿you desire﴾. The Prophet ﷺ did not order the sparing of men during the battle, nor did he ever desire the goods of this world. Rather, the majority of those who engaged in the fighting did it. The mention of the Prophet ﷺ in the verse points to his entering into the blame, in that he did not forbid it when he saw it from the 'arish (the shelter), and Sa'd ibn Mu'adh disapproved of it. However, the Prophet ﷺ was occupied by the suddenness of the matter and the manifestation of victory, so he left off forbidding the sparing of captives. For this reason, the Prophet ﷺ and Abu Bakr wept when this verse was revealed. Many of the commentators (mufassirun) hold that this reproach was caused by the suggestion of those who advised the Prophet ﷺ to take ransom. That is because when the Messenger of God ﷺ gathered the captives of Badr, he consulted his Companions about them. Abu Bakr al-Siddiq said: "O Messenger of God, they are your kinsmen. Perhaps God will guide them to Islam later. So accept ransom from them and spare them, and the Muslims will be strengthened by their wealth." (p-239) 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, said: "No, O Messenger of God! Rather, let us strike their necks, for they are the leaders of disbelief." 'Abdullah ibn Rawahah said: "Rather, let us put them in a valley abundant with firewood and then set it alight upon them." Sa'd ibn Mu'adh had said, while he was with the Messenger of God ﷺ in the 'arish and had seen the taking of captives: "Inflicting slaughter was dearer to me than sparing the men." The Messenger of God ﷺ took the word of Abu Bakr, may God be pleased with him, and inclined to it, and then this verse was revealed, informing that the better and more awe-inspiring course for all the disbelievers was the killing of the captives of Badr. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with both of them, said: "This verse was revealed while the Muslims were few. When they increased and their authority became strong, the ruling on captives was revealed: ﴿then either grace afterward or ransom﴾ [Muhammad: 4]." Al-Tabari and others mentioned that "the Messenger of God ﷺ, when his Companions spoke about the captives in the manner mentioned, entered and did not answer them. Then he came out and said: 'God, Exalted, softens the hearts of some men and hardens the hearts of other men until they are harder than stones. Your example, O Abu Bakr, is the example of Abraham, who said: ﴿Whoever follows me is of me, and whoever disobeys me, indeed You are Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [Ibrahim: 36]. And the example of Jesus, who said: ﴿If You punish them, indeed they are Your servants; and if You forgive them, indeed You are the Mighty, the Wise﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 118]. And your example, O 'Umar, is the example of Noah, who said: ﴿My Lord, leave not upon the earth from among the disbelievers an inhabitant﴾ [Nuh: 26]. And the example of Moses, who said: ﴿Our Lord, obliterate their wealth and harden their hearts so they will not believe until they see the painful punishment﴾ [Yunus: 88].'" Then the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "You are today such that no man of them escapes except by ransom or the striking of the neck." In this hadith, 'Umar, may God be pleased with him, said: "The Messenger of God ﷺ inclined to what Abu Bakr said and did not incline to what I said."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This is evidence for the mention of "inclination" (hawa) in what is correct.

A group read ﴿ma kana li-nabiyyin﴾ with the definite article. The majority of people read ﴿li-nabiyyin﴾. Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' alone read ﴿an takuna﴾ with the feminine marking of the verb, in consideration of the wording of "captives" (asra). The rest of the Seven and the majority of people read ﴿an yakuna﴾ with the masculine marking, in consideration of the meaning of "captives." The majority of people and the Seven read ﴿asra﴾. Some people read ﴿usara﴾, which al-Mufaddal transmitted from 'Asim, and it is the recitation of Abu Ja'far.

The analogical rule (qiyas) and the general pattern is that the plural of asir (captive) is asra. Likewise every fa'il in the sense of maf'ul (passive participle), and what is made analogous to it even when not in the sense of maf'ul, such as marid (sick) and marda (sick, plural), when these are also things into which a person is compelled and which overtake him by force; he is in them in the position of the passive. As for its plural as "usara," it is similar to "kusala" as the plural of "kaslan" (lazy). "Kaslan" is also pluralized as "kasla" by analogy with "asra" as the plural of "asir." This was stated by Sibawayh, and both are anomalous (shadhdhan). Al-Zajjaj said: "Usara" is the plural of "asra," so it is a plural of a plural.

The majority of people read ﴿yuthkhina﴾ with a sukun on the tha'. Abu Ja'far, Yahya ibn Ya'mur, and Yahya ibn Wuthab read ﴿yuthakhkhina﴾ with a fatha on the tha' and a shadda on the kha'. Its meaning in both readings is: he exaggerates in killing. Inflicting a massacre (ithkhan) occurs only in killing and wounding and what is of that kind.

Then He addressed the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ, saying: ﴿You desire the goods of this world﴾, that is, its wealth which presents itself and comes to hand, and what is meant is the wealth taken from the captives. ﴿But God desires the Hereafter﴾, that is, the work of the Hereafter. The genitive (mudaf) is elided, and the genitive-complement (mudaf ilayh) is placed in its position. Ibn Jammaz read ﴿al-akhirati﴾ in the genitive case, on the assumption of an elided mudaf. This may be compared with the words of the poet:

"Do you think every man (is equal to him), and a fire blazing by night is (equal to) fire?"

(p-241) This is according to the assumption: "and every fire."

Al-Tabari and others mentioned that "the Messenger of God ﷺ said to the people: 'If you wish, take ransom for the captives, and seventy of you will be killed in the battle according to their number; and if you wish, they will be killed and you will be safe.' They said: 'We will take the wealth, and seventy of us will be martyred.'" 'Abd ibn Humayd mentioned with his chain of transmission that Gabriel descended upon the Prophet ﷺ with the choice given to the people in this manner.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

According to both reports, the matter of this choice is from God, for it is an announcement of the unseen. When they were given the choice, how then does the reproach occur afterward with His words: ﴿a great punishment would have touched you for what you took﴾? What I say about this is: the rebuke to the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ in His words: ﴿It is not for a Prophet﴾ up to His words: ﴿great﴾ is only concerning the sparing of men at the time of the rout, out of desire to take wealth from them. And the whole rebuke, when considered, is only directed at the people. At that time 'Umar, may God be pleased with him, was killing and urging killing, and did not see sparing as right. Then Sa'd ibn Mu'adh said: "Inflicting a massacre is dearer to me than sparing the men." The Messenger of God ﷺ made these two (men) among those saved from a punishment that would have descended. Among the things that indicate some of them were eager for wealth is the statement of al-Miqdad when the Messenger of God ﷺ ordered the killing of 'Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ayt: "My captive, O Messenger of God!" And the statement of Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr to the one who was capturing his brother: "Tighten your hold on him, for he has a wealthy mother." And other stories of them besides this. When the captives were gathered and driven to Medina, the Messenger of God ﷺ carried out the killing upon al-Nadr and 'Uqbah, and granted grace to Abu 'Izzah and others, and began to deliberate about the rest of them, then the choice came down from God, Exalted. The Messenger of God ﷺ then consulted (his companions). 'Umar, may God be pleased with him, passed over his first opinion about killing. Abu Bakr, may God be pleased with him, saw the benefit in the strength of the Muslims through the ransom money, and the Messenger of God ﷺ inclined to the opinion of Abu Bakr, may God be pleased with him. Both opinions were independent reasoning (ijtihad) after a choice was given, so no rebuke descended upon any of this. The commentators mentioned that the verse was revealed because of this consultation and these opinions. That is contested by what I have mentioned. Likewise they mentioned in these verses the permission of spoils for this community. I do not say that, because God's ruling permitting spoils to this community had already occurred before Badr, namely in the expedition in which 'Amr ibn al-Hadrami was killed. What was innovated at Badr was only the sparing of men for the sake of wealth. And what God graced in it was the attachment of the ransom of the disbeliever to the spoils whose permissibility had already been established.

(p-242) The reasoning of the commentators is that the people were given a choice between two matters, one of which was not good, as a test for them. They chose the lesser, so the rebuke occurred. It was not a choice between two equal levels. This is like what was brought to the Messenger of God ﷺ on the night of the Night Journey, two vessels, and he chose the superior one.

And ﴿Mighty, Wise﴾ are two attributes that come from the context of the verse, because by might and wisdom His will is completed in perfection and fulfilment. Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: "The asra are those who are not bound when they are taken, and the usara are those who are bound by tying."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

Abu Hatim related that he heard this from the Arabs, and Abu al-Hasan al-Akhfash also mentioned it, but said: "The Arabs do not recognize this, and both are the same among them."

As for God's words: ﴿Had there not been a prior decree from God﴾ to the end of the verse, a group said: the prior decree is the Qur'an, and the meaning is: had it not been for the Book that preceded, so that you believed in it and affirmed it, the punishment would have touched you for your taking this ransom. Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, al-Hasan as well, and Ibn Zayd said: the prior decree is God's forgiveness for the people of Badr of what they had previously or subsequently done of their sins. Al-Hasan, Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with both of them, Abu Hurayrah, and others said: the decree is what God had decided from eternity regarding the permissibility of spoils and ransom for Muhammad ﷺ and his community, whereas these had been forbidden for all other nations. A group said: the prior decree is God's pardon for them in this specific sin. A group said: the decree is that God, Exalted and Majestic, decreed not to punish anyone for a sin he committed in ignorance. This is a weak opinion, contradicted by passages of the Shari'ah. Al-Tabari mentioned from Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn Husayn ibn 'Ali ibn Abi Talib that the prior decree is that He does not punish anyone for a sin except after a prohibition of it, and they had not yet been prohibited. A group said: the prior decree is what God decreed of the erasure of minor sins through avoiding major sins.

Al-Tabari held that all these meanings enter under the wording and that it encompasses them, and he avoided restricting it to one meaning over another. (p-243) The lam in ﴿la-massakum﴾ is the response to ﴿law-la﴾ (had it not been). ﴿Kitabun﴾ is nominative as the subject of an inceptive sentence, and the predicate is elided. This is likewise the case of the noun that follows ﴿law-la﴾. Its estimate according to Sibawayh is: "Had there not been a prior decree from God that rescued you." The ﴿ma﴾ in His words ﴿fima﴾ is intended either as the captives or the ransom, and it is a relative pronoun. In ﴿akhadtum﴾ there is a pronoun referring back to it, and it may be verbal-noun (masdariyyah), in which case it needs no returning pronoun. It is related that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Had a punishment descended in this matter, 'Umar ibn al-Khattab would have been saved from it." In another hadith: "and Sa'd ibn Mu'adh." That is because their opinion had been that the captives should be killed.

His words ﴿So eat of what you have gained﴾ up to the end of the verse are a clear text permitting the wealth taken from the captives and attaching it to the spoils whose permissibility had previously been established.

His words ﴿lawful and good﴾ are two circumstantial clauses (hal) referring to ﴿ma﴾ in His words ﴿mimma﴾. It is also valid for them to be from the pronoun in ﴿ghanimtum﴾. It is possible that ﴿halalan﴾ is the direct object (maf'ul bihi) of ﴿fakulu﴾.

﴿And fear God﴾ means: be cautious in acting hastily according to human desire and appetite in another incident. The words ﴿And fear God﴾ come as an eloquent interjection in the midst of the speech, because His words ﴿Indeed God is Forgiving, Merciful﴾ are connected in meaning with His words ﴿So eat of what you have gained, lawful and good﴾.

This is evidence for the mention of "inclination" (hawa) in what is correct.
