Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 8, verse 70–71:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿O Prophet, say to those prisoners who are in your hands: If Allah knows any good in your hearts, He will give you better than what was taken from you, and He will forgive you. Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ ﴿But if they intend to betray you, they have already betrayed Allah before, so He gave you power over them. Allah is All-Knowing and All-Wise.﴾

It is narrated that the prisoners of Badr informed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that they had an inclination toward Islam, that they hoped for it, and that if they were ransomed and returned to their people, they would commit to drawing them to Islam and would strive toward that end and what is similar to this aim. So this verse was revealed concerning that. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: The prisoners in this verse were 'Abbas and his companions. They said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "We have believed in what you have brought, and we testify that you are indeed the Messenger of Allah; we will surely give you sincere counsel regarding our people." So this verse was revealed.

The majority of readers recited: "min al-asra" (مِنَ الأسْرى). Abu 'Amr alone among the Seven recited: "min al-usara" (مِنَ الأُسارى), and this is the reading of Abu Ja'far, Qatada, Nasr ibn 'Asim, Ibn Abi Ishaq, and it is reported differently from al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan and al-Jahdari. Ibn Muhaysin recited: "min lasra" (مِنَ لَسْرى) with idgham (assimilation). The meaning of the speech is: if this is in earnest from you, and Allah knows from your souls good and Islam, He will replace for you something better than the ransom you were given, and He will forgive you all that you have committed. Al-A'mash recited: "yuthibukum khayran" (يُثِيبُكم خَيْرًا). The majority of readers recited: "ukhidha" (أُخِذَ) with a damma on the hamza and a kasra on the kha'; Shayba ibn Nisah and Abu Hayawa recited: "akhadha" (أخَذَ) with a fatha on both. It is reported that the prisoners of Badr ransomed themselves at forty ounces each, except 'Abbas, who was ransomed for one hundred ounces.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The ounce (uqiyya) is forty dirhams. Qatada said: they ransomed them for four thousand each. 'Ubayda al-Salmani said: the ransom of the prisoners of Badr was one hundred ounces, the ounce being forty dirhams, and in dinars six dinars. It is reported that 'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib said: "This verse was revealed concerning me and my companions." And when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave him from the wealth of Bahrain as much as he could carry, he said: "This is better than what was taken from me, and I hope that Allah will forgive me." Al-Tabari also traced to 'Abbas that he said: "It was revealed concerning me when I informed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) of my Islam and asked him to reckon with me for the twenty ounces that were taken from me before the ransom, but he refused and said: 'That is spoils (fay'),' so Allah replaced that for me with twenty slaves, all of whom trade with my wealth." And it is reported from 'Abbas that he said: "I would not wish that this verse had not been revealed even if I had the whole world, for Allah has given me from what was taken from me, and I hope that He will forgive me."

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿But if they intend to betray you, they have already betrayed Allah﴾ — the verse.

It is a statement that he was commanded to say to the prisoners and to set its meaning before them. The meaning: if they are sincere, He will do such-and-such with them; and if they conceal betrayal of what they claimed to be entrusted with of the covenant, then let that not please them nor let them be at ease with it, for Allah is watchful over them (bi'l-mirsad), the One whom they betrayed before by their disbelief and their neglect of reflecting upon His signs, which He had made clear to them in a manner by which they could attain understanding; so it became like an established covenant. Thus their recompense for their betrayal of Him was that He enabled the believers over them and made them prisoners in their hands. His saying, the Exalted: ﴿All-Knowing, All-Wise﴾ are two fitting attributes, meaning: All-Knowing of what they conceal of sincerity or treachery, All-Wise in what He recompenses them with.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

As for interpreting this verse by the story of 'Abdullah ibn Abi Sarh, it requires examination. If the story of 'Abdullah ibn Abi Sarh is cited as an example, just as examples of that may be cited in our own age, then it is good; but if it is cited as the reason for the verse's revelation, then it is an error, because the matter of Ibn Abi Sarh became evident only on the day of the conquest of Makkah, whereas this verse was revealed right after Badr.

Abu 'Amr alone among the Seven recited: "min al-usara" (مِنَ الأُسارى), and this is the reading of Abu Ja'far, Qatada, Nasr ibn 'Asim, Ibn Abi Ishaq, and it is reported differently from al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan and al-Jahdari. Ibn Muhaysin recited: "min lasra" (مِنَ لَسْرى) with idgham (assimilation). The meaning of the speech is: if this is in earnest from you, and Allah knows from your souls good and Islam, He will replace for you something better than the ransom you were given, and He will forgive you all that you have committed. Al-A'mash recited: "yuthibukum khayran" (يُثِيبُكم خَيْرًا). The majority of readers recited: "ukhidha" (أُخِذَ) with a damma on the hamza and a kasra on the kha'; Shayba ibn Nisah and Abu Hayawa recited: "akhadha" (أخَذَ) with a fatha on both. It is reported that the prisoners of Badr ransomed themselves at forty ounces each, except 'Abbas, who was ransomed for one hundred ounces.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The ounce (uqiyya) is forty dirhams. Qatada said: they ransomed them for four thousand each. 'Ubayda al-Salmani said: the ransom of the prisoners of Badr was one hundred ounces, the ounce being forty dirhams, and in dinars six dinars. It is reported that 'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib said: "This verse was revealed concerning me and my companions." And when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave him from the wealth of Bahrain as much as he could carry, he said: "This is better than what was taken from me, and I hope that Allah will forgive me." Al-Tabari also traced to 'Abbas that he said: "It was revealed concerning me when I informed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) of my Islam and asked him to reckon with me for the twenty ounces that were taken from me before the ransom, but he refused and said: 'That is spoils (fay'),' so Allah replaced that for me with twenty slaves, all of whom trade with my wealth." And it is reported from 'Abbas that he said: "I would not wish that this verse had not been revealed even if I had the whole world, for Allah has given me from what was taken from me, and I hope that He will forgive me."

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿But if they intend to betray you, they have already betrayed Allah﴾ — the verse.

It is a statement that he was commanded to say to the prisoners and to set its meaning before them. The meaning: if they are sincere, He will do such-and-such with them; and if they conceal betrayal of what they claimed to be entrusted with of the covenant, then let that not please them nor let them be at ease with it, for Allah is watchful over them (bi'l-mirsad), the One whom they betrayed before by their disbelief and their neglect of reflecting upon His signs, which He had made clear to them in a manner by which they could attain understanding; so it became like an established covenant. Thus their recompense for their betrayal of Him was that He enabled the believers over them and made them prisoners in their hands. His saying, the Exalted: ﴿All-Knowing, All-Wise﴾ are two fitting attributes, meaning: All-Knowing of what they conceal of sincerity or treachery, All-Wise in what He recompenses them with.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

As for interpreting this verse by the story of 'Abdullah ibn Abi Sarh, it requires examination. If the story of 'Abdullah ibn Abi Sarh is cited as an example, just as examples of that may be cited in our own age, then it is good; but if it is cited as the reason for the verse's revelation, then it is an error, because the matter of Ibn Abi Sarh became evident only on the day of the conquest of Makkah, whereas this verse was revealed right after Badr.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 8, verse 72:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Indeed, those who believed and emigrated and strove with their wealth and their lives in the way of Allah, and those who gave shelter and helped — those are allies of one another. And those who believed but did not emigrate, you have no obligation of allegiance to them until they emigrate. And if they seek your help in matters of religion, then it is incumbent upon you to help, except against a people between you and whom there is a covenant. And Allah is Seeing of what you do.﴾

(p-246) The purpose of this verse and what follows is to explain the ranks of the Emigrants (muhajirun), the Helpers (ansar), the believers who did not emigrate, the disbelievers, and the emigrants after Hudaybiyya, and to mention the kinship of some of them with others. He first mentioned the Emigrants, for they are the foundation of Islam. Consider 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, giving them precedence in consultation. Hajara (emigrated) means: he forsook his family and relatives, and they forsook him. And (jahadu) (strove) means: they exerted themselves against those who exerted themselves in fighting them. ﴿Those who gave shelter and helped﴾ are the Helpers. Awa (gave shelter) means: he prepared a dwelling (ma'wa), which is a refuge and a safeguard. So Allah's judgment regarding these two groups is that some of them are allies of others. Many of the exegetes said: this allegiance is support, assistance, and the joining of hands, and on this al-Tabari explained the verse. What they said is a necessary implication of the wording. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, Qatada, Mujahid, and many others said: this allegiance is in inheritance. That is because the Prophet (ﷺ) established brotherhood between the Emigrants and the Helpers, and there was also a brotherhood of kinship among the Helpers, and there was also brotherhood among some of the Emigrants. So when an Emigrant died and had no Emigrant kinsman in Medina, his Helper brother would inherit from him; and if he had a Muslim ally who had not emigrated, that one would not inherit from him, since there was no allegiance between him and his Emigrant relative, so he would not inherit from him. Ibn Zayd said: their affair remained so until the conquest of Mecca, after which they inherited from one another again, since there was no more emigration.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This group held that this is the purpose of the verse. As for whoever held that it concerns mutual support and assistance, he takes Allah's negation of their allegiance toward the Muslims to be a description of the situation, not that Allah decreed categorically that there is no allegiance at all between the Emigrants and them. That is because their situation, when they were far apart in regions, required that if some calamity befell one of them, he would not find the other nor benefit from him; so in this respect the negation of allegiance applies. In both interpretations, the verse urges the Bedouins to emigrate, as said by al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan. As for whoever sees allegiance as inheritance, it is a ruling from Allah that negates allegiance in inheritance. They said: this ruling was abrogated by His saying, blessed and exalted: ﴿And those related by blood are closer to one another﴾ [al-Anfal: 75], and the verse.

Jumhur al-Sab'a and the people read "wa-wilayatihim" with a fatha on the waw, and "al-wilaya" also with a fatha on the waw. (p-247) Al-Kisa'i read "wa-wilayatihim" with a fatha on the waw, and "al-wilaya" with a kasra on the waw. Al-A'mash and Ibn Wathhab read "wilayatihim" and "al-wilaya" with a kasra on the waw, and this is the reading of Hamza. Abu 'Ali said: the fatha is more excellent, because it concerns religion. Abu al-Hasan al-Akhfash said: "the kasra in it is a dialect," but that is not so. Al-Asma'i charged al-A'mash with error (lahhana) and considered him mistaken, because if it is a dialect, then it is not an error.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Especially since one cannot suppose of him anything but that he transmitted it. Abu 'Ubayda said: al-wilaya with a kasra is from "walitu al-amr ilayhi" (I took charge of the matter), so it refers to authority (sultan), while al-wilaya (with fatha) refers to the one who is a mawla; it is said: "mawla bayyin al-wilaya" with a fatha on the waw.

As for His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And if they seek your help﴾: it means: if these believers who did not emigrate ask you to help them against a people of disbelievers, then it is obligatory upon you to help them, except if they ask you for help against a disbelieving people with whom you have made a treaty and a covenant to refrain from war; then do not help them against them, because that would be treachery, a breaking of the covenant, and an abandonment of keeping the pact and fulfilling it. The reading is "fa-'alaykumu al-nasru" with a raf' on the ra', and it is permissible to read "fa-'alaykumu al-nasra" as an incitement (al-igra'). I do not know it to be a recognized reading.

The majority of the people read "wallahu bima ta'malun" in address to the believers. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami and al-A'raj read "bima ya'malun" with the ya', in reference to the third person.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 8, verses 73–75:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿And those who disbelieve, some of them are allies of others. Unless you do this, there will be fitnah (turmoil) on earth and great corruption.﴾ ﴿And those who believed and emigrated and strove in the way of Allah, and those who sheltered and helped – those are the believers in truth. For them is forgiveness and generous provision.﴾ ﴿And those who believed after [that] and emigrated and strove with you – those are of you. And those of [blood] relationship are more entitled to each other in the Book of Allah. Indeed, Allah is Knowing of all things.﴾

(p-248) This is a ruling that the disbelievers' allegiance is one, and that is by combining inheritance, mutual support and assistance. This expression is an encouragement and a rousing of souls, just as you say to someone whom you want to take a stand: "Your enemy is striving," meaning: so strive yourself.

Al-Tabari, in his tafsir of this verse, related from Qatadah that he said: "Allah refused to accept the faith of one who believed and did not emigrate, and that was at the beginning of Islam." This is also mentioned fully in the tafsir of His saying, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Indeed, those whom the angels take in death while wronging themselves – they will say, "In what [condition] were you?" They will say, "We were oppressed in the land." They will say, "Was not the earth of Allah spacious so you could emigrate therein?" For those, their refuge is Hell, and wretched is the destination.﴾ [al-Nisa': 97].

What appears from the Shari'ah is that the ruling for a believer who abandons emigration while knowing its obligation is the ruling of a sinner, not the ruling of a disbeliever. His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Indeed, those whom the angels take in death while wronging themselves﴾ [al-Nisa': 97] refers only to those who were killed among the disbelievers. Concerning them the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I am free of every Muslim who dwells among the polytheists, [such that] their fires do not see each other," the hadith with its varied wordings. Qatadah's statement refers only to one who would stand waiting and say: "Whoever prevails, I will be with him." Likewise it is mentioned in the book of al-Tabari and al-Kushshi.

The pronoun in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Unless you do this﴾ is said to refer to the allegiance (al-muwarathah) and its commitment.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is one from which fitnah occurs only from a distance and through many intermediaries. It has also been said that it refers to support (al-mu'azarah) and assistance (al-mu'awanah) and the joining of hands, and from this fitnah occurs closely, so it is more emphatic than the first. It also appears that it refers to keeping the covenant and the pact which is contained in His saying: ﴿except for a people between you and them is a pact﴾ [al-Anfal: 72]; and if this is not done, then it is itself the fitnah. It may also be that the pronoun refers to the victory of the Muslims who seek help in the religion, and it is permissible that the pronoun refers generally to all that has been mentioned.

Fitnah: the trial of war and what accompanies it of raids, expulsion and captivity.

Great corruption (al-fasad al-kabir): the manifestation of shirk. Most of the readers read "kabir" with a single dot on the ba'. Abu Musa al-Hijazi, from al-Kisa'i, read it with a three-dotted tha'. Abu Hatim al-Madani narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited: "wa fasadun 'arid" (and corruption, vast). A group read: "wa-alladhina kafaru ba'duhum awla bi-ba'din" (and those who disbelieve, some of them are closer to others).

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And those who believed and emigrated﴾ is a verse which contains the specification of the emigrants and the helpers and their honouring with this great description. "Haqqan" (truly) is in the accusative as an absolute object emphasising what precedes it. Describing the provision as "generous" means that it does not become spoiled or tainted; what is meant by it is the food of Paradise, as al-Tabari and others have mentioned; and the necessary implication of the wording is the negation of blemishes from it, and what they mentioned is included within that.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿from after﴾ means: from after al-Hudaybiyyah and the Pledge of al-Ridwan. That is because emigration after that was of a lower rank than emigration before it, and it was called "the second emigration," since war laid down its burdens for about two years, then there was the Conquest of Mecca, and concerning it he (ﷺ) said: "There is no emigration after the Conquest." Al-Tabari said: the meaning is: from after I have made clear to you the ruling on allegiance.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

So the barrier between the two emigrations was the revelation of this verse. Allah, blessed and exalted, informs in this verse that they are among the first in support and the rest of the rulings of Islam.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿and strove with you﴾ is an expression which implies that they are followers, not originators; and His saying: ﴿then those are of you﴾ is likewise; similar to it is his saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "The client of a people is from them," and "the son of a people's sister is from them."

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And those of [blood] relationship﴾ to the end of the surah. Those previously mentioned said: it concerns inheritance, and it abrogates the earlier ruling mentioned that a Muhajir inherits from an Ansari; and by this final verse it became obligatory that a man inherits from his relative even if he did not emigrate with him. A group, among whom is Malik ibn Anas, may Allah have mercy on him, said: the verse is not about inheritance; and this is an escape from giving inheritance to the maternal uncle, the paternal aunt and the like. Another group said: it concerns inheritance, but it was abrogated by the clarifying verse of inheritance.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿in the Book of Allah﴾ means: the Qur'an, i.e., that is established in the Book of Allah. It has been said: the meaning is: in the Book of Allah that preceded, on the Preserved Tablet. And ﴿Knowing﴾ is an attribute suitable to the enforcement of these rulings.

The tafsir of Surah al-Anfal is complete, by the success of Allah, and praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.
